title: 16. Drivers shaping the future of breeding
section: 1 A connected change in the breeding system
text:
1 A connected change in the breeding system
Breeding is likely to be shaped by the interaction of functional genomics, automated phenotyping, machine learning, lower-cost genomic information and changes in farming and breeding organisations. These drivers change more than the size of a prediction problem. They influence which traits are observed, which populations contribute information, who controls access, and how rapidly genetic decisions can be evaluated and revised.
This chapter presents a perspective as of November 2026. Published examples establish what has been demonstrated; the implications and scenarios below are reasoned expectations, not forecasts of adoption rates or guaranteed genetic gain. The current-developments chapter examines specific methods. Here the focus is how developments combine to reshape the breeding system, including its scientific and software requirements.
Climate, disease pressure, welfare, environmental constraints, labour and market demands also determine the direction of change. Better measurement and prediction do not decide which outcomes should be rewarded. A breeding objective must translate these priorities into explicit targets and trade-offs.

title: 16. Drivers shaping the future of breeding
section: 2 Functional genomics: from association to informed models
text:
2 Functional genomics: from association to informed models
Farm Animal Genotype–Tissue Expression (FarmGTEx) is an international programme to map genetic regulation of molecular traits across farm-animal tissues and populations (Fang et al., 2025). It extends the information available beyond marker–performance associations towards tissue, expression and splicing contexts. The cattle regulatory atlas discussed in genomic-feature priors provides an earlier concrete example (Liu et al., 2022). Related work is developing in plants: Lei et al. (2025) analyse a multitissue maize transcriptome resource and its regulatory associations. These are related scientific directions, not identical experimental designs.
The opportunity is to connect a variant to a molecular process and then to a breeding trait. This can inform marker-effect priors, groups of covariance components, candidate mechanisms and experimental priorities. It may be particularly valuable when information has to transfer between populations or when a trait is expensive to measure. Within a well-connected reference population, ordinary markers can already tag much of the relevant variation; additional biological interpretation need not produce a large accuracy gain.
A regulatory association is not proof that expression mediates the production trait. Linkage disequilibrium, shared regulation, tissue sampling and population structure can produce alternative explanations. Colocalisation, fine-mapping, perturbation experiments and validation in relevant tissues and environments provide different forms of evidence. They should not be replaced by a single annotation score described as a causal probability.
For model development, a useful direction is partial pooling of biological information: let annotations influence prior distributions while retaining uncertainty and a background genetic component. Tissue, breed and environment effects need not transfer unchanged. Estimating annotation weights from the evaluation data itself also makes them fitted parameters, which belong inside the validation procedure. These issues connect directly to variance-component inference and genomic-feature priors.

title: 16. Drivers shaping the future of breeding
section: 3 Phenomics: breeding for trajectories and responses
text:
3 Phenomics: breeding for trajectories and responses
Sensors, milking and feeding robots, cameras, spectra and laboratory assays can turn intermittently measured outcomes into repeated descriptions of behaviour, growth, physiological state and exposure. Automated feeding and robotic-milking studies already illustrate the derivation and genetic analysis of new traits (Bérat et al., 2025; Graham et al., 2024). These examples establish feasibility for particular measurements and populations, not universal benefit from every data stream.
An important prospective change is the target itself: from a lifetime total or a single observation towards a trajectory, stability across environments, response to challenge or recovery. Such targets could support breeding for robustness, health and resource efficiency. They require an explicit definition of exposure and opportunity to respond. A low observed disease count can reflect resistance, low exposure or incomplete recording.
Measurement becomes part of the inferential model. Device, farm and software effects may be associated with family, management and selection. More records do not automatically separate these effects, and a million sensor observations do not represent a million independent animals. Joint genetic and environmental factor models, random regression and observation models for events or counts are therefore likely to matter alongside conventional repeatability models. The phenomics chapter develops these choices and their measurement, missingness and validation requirements.
The strategic implication is that well-designed phenotyping may become a more valuable marginal investment than increasing marker density on an already well-genotyped reference. That is a resource-allocation hypothesis to test for each breeding programme, rather than a general ordering of technologies.

title: 16. Drivers shaping the future of breeding
section: 4 ML and AI: several distinct contributions
text:
4 ML and AI: several distinct contributions
Artificial intelligence (AI) has at least four roles that should be evaluated separately:








Role
Potential contribution
Evidence needed




Measurement and feature extraction
Derive traits from images, sound, spectra and time series
Reference-measurement agreement and stability across farms, devices and biological groups


Molecular representation
Predict regulatory consequences or learn sequence features
Species-, tissue- and variant-specific assessment, followed by trait-level validation


Genetic and phenotypic prediction
Learn nonlinear effects, interactions and heterogeneous responses
Comparison with strong statistical baselines under the intended information pattern


Scientific software assistance
Help develop code, interfaces, documentation and analysis workflows
Independent numerical references, reproducible builds, tests and review



Sequence-to-function systems illustrate the second role. AlphaGenome combines long sequence context with multiple molecular prediction tasks (Avsec et al., 2026). Its reported human and mouse work is evidence about regulatory prediction, not evidence that the same model predicts livestock breeding values or crop performance. Adapting such representations to agricultural species requires appropriate training information and validation.
A promising design is a hybrid: learned measurement or biological representations feed a statistical model that explicitly accounts for relationships, repeated records, selection and uncertainty. Other applications may justify end-to-end prediction. Neither architecture is intrinsically best. Compare the quantity that will be used in selection, not only a proxy loss function. Predicting an animal’s phenotype from contemporaneous sensor data is a different task from predicting its transmissible genetic merit before those measurements are available.
For estimation, flexible learned effects can also compete with genetic and environmental covariance components. Model capacity does not resolve identifiability. Uncertainty must account for relevant training and tuning, and validation must protect against repeated animals, relatives, farms, time periods and pretrained-data overlap where these threaten the intended comparison. See model checking and validation.
AI-assisted software development may shorten implementation cycles. It also makes independent qualification more important: plausible code and a successful fit do not establish the equations solved, the statistical target or the validity of a reported uncertainty interval. The qualification framework applies regardless of how the implementation was produced.

title: 16. Drivers shaping the future of breeding
section: 5 Lower-cost genomics: coverage, design and uncertainty
text:
5 Lower-cost genomics: coverage, design and uncertainty
Historical sequencing-cost data document major technological cost reductions, but those data do not constitute current agricultural service prices or the complete cost of collecting and analysing a sample (National Human Genome Research Institute, n.d.). Future budgets must include sampling, extraction, libraries, failed assays, reference panels, computation and storage. Falling cost per base does not guarantee falling cost per useful breeding decision.
Arrays, low-pass sequencing with imputation, and longer-read technologies offer different information. Lamb et al. (2021) provide a proof of concept for cattle genomic prediction using low-coverage portable Nanopore sequencing. Wider adoption must still be justified for the population, variant classes, reference panel and quality requirements involved. Structural variation and more representative genome references are further opportunities, with corresponding demands on variant representation and model comparability.
If genomic information becomes affordable for more commercial animals, the reference can better represent deployment conditions. This could improve evaluation of health and environmental traits outside elite nuclei. It also creates design choices: more individuals, greater sequencing depth, wider environmental coverage, more informative relatives, or better phenotypes. Evaluate these choices jointly. Imputation quality and rare-variant coverage can differ by ancestry, so a larger reference is not automatically an equitable or representative one.
Methods and software will need to preserve dosage and imputation uncertainty where consequential, support evolving variant sets, and distinguish population coverage from marker count. The scientific requirements remain those in genomic models and missing data and selection.

title: 16. Drivers shaping the future of breeding
section: 6 Structural change: who records, learns and benefits?
text:
6 Structural change: who records, learns and benefits?
Farm size, specialisation, automation and contractual relationships affect which animals are recorded and how genetics are deployed. The direction and pace vary between species, regions and production systems. Where farms adopt integrated recording systems, connected data streams can improve evaluation; where recording is concentrated in a narrow subset of farms, the apparent information gain can coincide with a narrower representation of the target population.
Breeding organisations may combine genetic resources, proprietary reference data, phenotyping platforms and analytical services. As one documented company example, Genus describes investment in precision data collection, genomic evaluation and additional trait streams (Genus plc, 2025). This is company-reported strategy, not independent evidence of comparative predictive performance.
Consolidation can finance expensive research and connected reference populations, but it can also change access, bargaining power and incentives to share data. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)’s seed-market analysis documents concentration and policy responses, while finding that its relationship with prices and innovation is not uniform (OECD, 2018). That plant-sector evidence should not be treated as a measured effect for every livestock industry, or as a prediction that consolidation will necessarily improve or damage genetic progress.
Cooperatives, public infrastructure, commercial platforms and shared research consortia offer different ways to organise these resources. The statistical consequences include selective recording, changing connectedness, proprietary calibration procedures and restricted opportunities for external validation. Cross-organisation analysis may require federated or distributed methods, but moving computation instead of records does not automatically solve privacy, harmonisation or population-comparability problems.
Useful agreements specify access to raw and derived records, consent and permitted use, correction of errors, portability, provenance and independent assessment. Open interfaces and auditable exports can preserve scientific comparability even when the underlying data cannot be public.

title: 16. Drivers shaping the future of breeding
section: 7 From improved prediction to sustained genetic progress
text:
7 From improved prediction to sustained genetic progress
For a simplified single-trait selection scheme, expected response per year is often expressed as
\[
\Delta G_{\mathrm{year}}\approx
\frac{i\,r\,\sigma_A}{L},
\]
where \(i\) is selection intensity, \(r\) the accuracy of the selection criterion, \(\sigma_A\) additive genetic standard deviation and \(L\) generation interval. This is a schematic decomposition, not a complete account of overlapping generations, multiple pathways, mating or multitrait constraints; its selection-index foundations are discussed by Hazel (1943). Breeding objectives, selection and mating develops the response algebra, contribution constraints and mating decisions.
The drivers can act on different terms. Earlier genomic information can shorten generation intervals; broader recording can improve accuracy; wider candidate screening can change selection intensity. Gains cannot be added independently: shorter cycles and strong selection can also accelerate relatedness and reduce future variation. Multi-objective selection and mating design therefore need to account for inbreeding, diversity, welfare and robustness alongside current production merit.
Changing farming systems also changes the target environment. A genotype ranked for performance in a high-input nucleus may not have the same ranking under heat, disease or resource limitation. Modelling genotype-by-environment interaction and validating transfer become important when the future production system differs from the reference. See multitrait and longitudinal models.

title: 16. Drivers shaping the future of breeding
text:
8 Implications for methods and software
The resulting research agenda is broader than replacing best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) with a single new algorithm. It includes biologically informed hierarchical models, structured multitrait and longitudinal covariance, uncertainty for learned or imputed inputs, transfer across populations and environments, and breeding-programme design. Prediction and variance-component estimation need separate qualification; estimating more biological components requires information to identify them.
Software should make these developments assessable through stable model and data contracts, explicit prediction targets, modular observation and covariance models, versioned feature pipelines and reproducible execution. Large-scale inference needs matrix-free or sparse representations, controlled approximation, hardware-aware execution and transparent resource accounting. New computing hardware is useful where measured end-to-end workloads benefit, rather than because a method has an AI label. The large-scale computation chapter develops these requirements.
For gsuite, these are directions for continued development and qualification, not a claim that every model described here is already implemented. The useful long-term contract is that a user can identify the fitted model, trace its data, understand its assumptions, assess uncertainty and compare its results with an independent reference.

8.1 A connected methodological response
The statistical response to these drivers is developed in the model chapters, rather than implied by a technology label:



New information or condition
Change in the modelling problem
Where the inference is developed




Functional annotations and molecular atlases
Learned effect distributions, component sharing and molecular versus variant-level information
Functional priors and estimation


Sensor and robot measurements
Joint genetic trajectories, measurement uncertainty and high-dimensional covariance
Phenomics and multitrait models


Learned representations
Uncertainty in features and prediction-time information restrictions
Prediction uncertainty and validation


Broader genomic coverage
Uncertain input genotypes, base conventions and cross-population transfer
Genomic models and genetic bases


Changing farms, environments and breeding populations
Recording, selection and target-population assumptions
Missing data and selection and breeding decisions



These developments can be combined, but each additional layer needs information to identify its parameters. Progress comes from a defensible joint model and evidence for the intended decision, not merely from joining more data streams.

title: 16. Drivers shaping the future of breeding
section: 9 Plausible outcomes and evidence to seek
text:
9 Plausible outcomes and evidence to seek
Several outcomes can coexist: integrated commercial platforms, shared public functional resources, and locally adapted programmes using interoperable tools. Their relative success will depend on reliable phenotypes, population coverage, economics and governance as well as predictive algorithms. No single ownership structure or model family follows inevitably from technological progress.
Evidence of progress should therefore include prospective accuracy and calibration, realised response and correlated responses, diversity, transfer to commercial conditions, and the total cost and distribution of benefits. A programme that improves a retrospective prediction score without improving selection decisions has not yet demonstrated the relevant breeding benefit.






Implementation in gsuite



Existing prediction, estimation and computational methods provide a substantial base for these developments; the implementation overview connects them to the current interfaces. The wider capability directory also links association, mapping, scoring, Bayesian inference and simulation tools. Integration of functional atlases, raw phenomics, learned representations and breeding decisions remains a set of model- and workflow-development tasks, with separate validation for each intended use.

title: Qualification framework: establishing correctness and scientific value
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: Qualification framework: establishing correctness and scientific value
section: 1 Three different claims need three kinds of evidence
text:
1 Three different claims need three kinds of evidence
A method can be algebraically correct, statistically inappropriate for a data collection process, and computationally impractical at the intended scale. Conversely, a fast implementation can agree with another program while both share an error. Qualification must separate these possibilities.
Numerical correctness concerns whether the specified equations and outputs are computed to the declared accuracy. Inferential validity concerns prediction, estimation and uncertainty under stated model and sampling assumptions. Practical value concerns predictive performance, interpretation or resource savings for an intended application.
This framework describes how to assess those claims. It is not a statement that all existing methods have passed every assessment. Completed evidence has its own dated and scoped record, described at the end. The general principles connect numerical analysis with genomic benchmarking (Daetwyler et al., 2013; Higham, 2002).

title: Qualification framework: establishing correctness and scientific value
text:
2 Define the object being qualified
Specify the model family, observation pattern, covariance parameterization, relationship construction, prediction target and inferential operation. Coefficient solving, variance estimation and prediction-error variance (PEV) calculation are different operations; success in one does not establish the others.
Also identify the representation, numerical backend, approximation policy, input contract and reported result. A test of dense complete-data genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP) does not automatically qualify packed single-step estimation with missing traits. An animal-model oracle can support an exact marker-model reduction only when the reduction and reconstructed target are checked.
Freeze the expected invariants and acceptance rules before examining results. Use an existing declared residual or uncertainty gate when evaluating a replacement algorithm; do not relax it retrospectively to obtain a pass.

title: Qualification framework: establishing correctness and scientific value
text:
3 Layer 1: independent algebraic references
On small deterministic problems, construct the model from its scientific definition with explicit matrices. Compare the conditional mixed equations and marginal covariance formulation, not two wrappers around the same solver. Independent derivations expose coding and normalization mistakes that repeated execution of the same implementation cannot reveal.







Quantity
Independent reference or identity




Fixed effects and BLUP
Dense marginal GLS/BLUP versus complete mixed equations


Genomic animal values
Gaussian marker model versus its induced animal covariance


Pedigree marginal precision
Dense submatrix inverse versus a Schur-complement action


REML objective
Marginal determinants/quadratic versus complete-equation identity


Score
Analytic derivative versus finite differences of the same objective


Curvature
Analytic information versus the appropriate reference definition


PEV and contrasts
Complete-system inverse or target solves, including fixed effects


Missing traits
Direct observed covariance versus the selected complete model



These checks should include heterogeneous scales, nontrivial cross-covariances and unobserved prediction targets. An identity covariance with one intercept is insufficient to expose many ordering and incidence errors.
Finite-difference derivative checks need several reasonable step sizes to separate truncation error from roundoff. The objective and derivative must use the same parameter scale, active set and normalization. Average information is not generally the observed Hessian, so testing them for equality would itself be incorrect (Gilmour et al., 1995; Higham, 2002).

title: Qualification framework: establishing correctness and scientific value
section: 4 Layer 2: invariance, reductions and invalid requests
text:
4 Layer 2: invariance, reductions and invalid requests
Equivalent representations should agree after mapping back to the same scientific identities. Useful invariants include permutation of input records, permutation of animal or trait order, consistent allele reversal and a full-rank basis transformation with the covariance transformed appropriately.
Test reductions such as one trait from a multitrait model, zero additional components where the boundary is supported, or genomic and marker formulations at matching scale. A rank-changing boundary needs its own derivation and likelihood treatment; it is not an arbitrary small positive variance.
Invalid input and infeasible requests should produce an explicit outcome: duplicate identities, unmatched alleles, indefinite supplied covariances, non-estimable targets, exhausted iteration limits and unavailable uncertainty operations. An output file alone is not evidence of an accepted result.
Failure controls should show that under-solving and nonfinite operations are rejected. Successful cases establish that a route can pass; failure controls establish that the acceptance mechanism is capable of saying no.

title: Qualification framework: establishing correctness and scientific value
text:
5 Layer 3: repeated simulation for inference
Parameter recovery and uncertainty coverage require repeated datasets. One simulation that estimates a variance near its generating value does not establish unbiasedness, calibration or nominal coverage.
For an estimator \(\hat\theta_b\) over \(B\) replicates, report bias and root mean squared error (RMSE) against a declared target. For interval coverage, if \(\hat c\) is the fraction of intervals containing that target, a binomial Monte Carlo standard error is approximately \(\sqrt{\hat c(1-\hat c)/B}\) for independent replicates. The number of replicates must support the precision of the claimed conclusion.
For prediction, distinguish repeated draws of effects and records at fixed pedigree/genotypes from simulations that regenerate the population. They assess different conditional and population-level questions. Include PEV or interval calibration, prediction error, bias and dispersion, not only correlation with truth. When covariances are estimated, evaluate both plug-in and any broader uncertainty target explicitly (Kackar and Harville, 1984).
Include difficult but relevant settings: weakly identified components, boundary variances, high trait correlations, uneven recording and selection. The generating target must be explicit under selection or time-varying parameters. A founder parameter and a selected-cohort variance are not necessarily the same estimand.

title: Qualification framework: establishing correctness and scientific value
text:
6 Bayesian posterior computation
On a small Gaussian model, check posterior means and covariance against an analytic distribution. For finite mixture examples, enumeration or another independent calculation can test allocation probabilities and normalization. With estimated hyperparameters, compare the intended joint posterior rather than only conditional coefficient solutions (Habier et al., 2011; Sorensen and Gianola, 2002).
For Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), assess multiple independently initialized chains, mixing, effective sample size and Monte Carlo error for the reported scientific quantities. Posterior standard deviation measures uncertainty in the quantity; Monte Carlo standard error measures uncertainty from finite sampling. Successful numerical updates and visually stable traces alone do not prove adequate exploration. Simulation-based recovery and interval calibration address further inferential questions under the specified prior and data-generating design.
For variational methods, optimization convergence does not establish agreement with the exact posterior or calibrated uncertainty. Check relevant means, variances and predictions against tractable references and clearly identify which approximation is being qualified.

title: Qualification framework: establishing correctness and scientific value
text:
7 Layer 4: approximations and stochastic precision
An approximate preconditioner should be assessed with the same original equations and acceptance rule as the reference solve. An approximate target kernel, such as a truncated relationship construction, needs an additional assessment of model sensitivity. Do not combine these into one generic “approximation error” number.
For randomized derivatives or uncertainty, separate Monte Carlo variability from deterministic inner-solve error. Compare with exact references where tractable, use independent random replications to assess reported stochastic precision, and retain solve accounting. A single fixed seed provides a reproducible realization, not evidence about an error distribution (Avron and Toledo, 2011; Hutchinson, 1989).
If tuning adapts the number of probes, target allocation or solve accuracy, assess that complete adaptive procedure. Existing prediction residual and PEV precision gates remain separate; neither substitutes for the other.

title: Qualification framework: establishing correctness and scientific value
text:
8 Layer 5: deployment-aligned prediction validation
Choose the split from the application: future generations, new families, populations or environments. Define which phenotypes, genotypes and covariates are available at the actual decision time. All phenotype-dependent feature discovery, weighting, tuning and covariance fitting belong inside the training procedure for the claimed validation design (Daetwyler et al., 2013; Runcie and Cheng, 2019).
Use appropriate baselines with the same information. For feature priors, compare the unannotated model, informative features and defensible null or misspecified features. A feature chosen after viewing the test results has not been independently validated. Trait availability and residual correlation can particularly distort multitrait validation (Runcie and Cheng, 2019).
In field data, true breeding values are not directly observed. State the assumptions behind phenotype-based accuracy measures and partial/whole-data comparisons such as the linear-regression (LR) method (Legarra and Reverter, 2018). Report calibration and prediction error alongside correlation. Predictive success does not by itself establish a causal biological interpretation of a genomic component.

title: Qualification framework: establishing correctness and scientific value
text:
9 Layer 6: performance and reproducibility
Compare accepted work at matching targets and numerical requirements. Record complete elapsed time and phase breakdowns, physical central processing unit (CPU) allocation, runtime libraries, data placement, memory metric and variability between runs. Setup must be included unless the claim explicitly concerns amortized repeated use.
Count operator applications, factorization work, right-hand sides (RHS) used in solves and refinements, including derivative and uncertainty calculations. An outer iteration count alone cannot explain total work. State which resources are measured versus estimated; sampled process-tree resident set size (RSS), GNU Time RSS and scheduler high-water marks are different quantities.
Preserve small deterministic qualification cases separately from opt-in representative-scale studies. Resource-intensive campaigns need an explicit design and budget; they should not be launched merely because a model can be expressed. A benchmark result applies to its frozen workload and environment, not automatically to the full model family.

title: Qualification framework: establishing correctness and scientific value
section: 10 How an evidence record should be written
text:
10 How an evidence record should be written
A useful record includes the scientific specification, code and runtime identity, data provenance, expected target, reference method, acceptance criteria, observed errors, work counts and result status. Record failures and unavailable outputs as well as positive results. A corrected implementation needs fresh evidence for the affected behavior; a theoretical argument or documentation edit is not that evidence.
Conclusions should name their scope: for example, agreement for a supplied- covariance prediction target under a particular missingness pattern, rather than “the entire model is validated.” A reference comparison should say whether it checks predictions, likelihoods, derivatives, uncertainty or parameter estimates. These results need not all follow from one another.



Resource
Role




Theory chapters
Define models and assumptions, including methods beyond current software


Algorithmic reference
Derive representations, computational steps and acceptance quantities


Existing model evidence index
Locate recorded evidence with its original scope


Existing capability catalog
Interpret model/backend/inference status


Recorded qualification limits
Preserve unresolved and negative results



The last three resources describe software evidence; they are not prerequisites for discussing a model’s theory. They also must not be silently promoted by new theoretical material. This separation allows the notes to cover the field broadly while keeping claims about completed software work precise.

title: The development of genetic evaluation: problems and solutions
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: The development of genetic evaluation: problems and solutions
text:
1 A continuing prediction problem
The development of genetic evaluation is not a sequence in which every new method invalidates its predecessor. Selection indices, best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP), genomic models and biologically informed priors address related prediction problems with different information and assumptions. Their connections help explain when two methods should agree and when differences are scientifically meaningful.
This perspective complements the formal models in Chapters 1–9 and the dated current-developments chapter. It is a selective account of ideas rather than an exhaustive priority history.

title: The development of genetic evaluation: problems and solutions
section: 2 Selection indices: combining information for a breeding objective
text:
2 Selection indices: combining information for a breeding objective
Let the centered breeding objective be \(H=c^\top a\), with economic or scientific weights \(c\), and let \(z\) contain centered information available at selection. Among linear indices \(I=b^\top z\), minimizing mean squared error gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}(z)b=\operatorname{Cov}(z,H).
\]
The index therefore weights information by its covariance with the objective and by redundancy among information sources. Combining traits is not simply averaging their phenotypic ranks. Hazel’s selection-index treatment established a foundational genetic framework for this problem (Hazel, 1943).
The distinction between a breeding objective and the information used to predict it remains important. A cheap early-life measurement can contribute to selection without being an economically weighted trait itself.

title: The development of genetic evaluation: problems and solutions
section: 3 BLUP: incorporating environmental adjustment and relationships
text:
3 BLUP: incorporating environmental adjustment and relationships
Mixed models extend the covariance-based prediction principle while allowing unknown fixed effects, related animals, unequal information and complex record structures. For a random target \(u\), the connection is
\[
\hat u=\operatorname{Cov}(u,y)V^{-1}(y-X\hat\beta).
\]
Environmental adjustment and genetic prediction are solved jointly. Information can pass through relationships, including to animals without records. The meaning of unbiasedness and the role of selection assumptions require care; BLUP is not conditionally unbiased for every realized breeding value (Henderson, 1975; Robinson, 1991).
Pedigree precision provides a computationally important representation of these relationships. Its sparse construction uses parental transmission and innovation variances rather than a dense inverse of a stored relationship matrix (Henderson, 1976). Statistical structure and computational structure become closely connected, but remain distinct concepts.

title: The development of genetic evaluation: problems and solutions
text:
4 Estimation of the covariance structure
Prediction formulas condition on covariance parameters. Estimating those parameters from the same population introduces another inferential layer. Restricted likelihood accounts for the fixed-effect space in covariance estimation (Patterson and Thompson, 1971). Sparse and average-information algorithms make repeated likelihood calculations practical (Gilmour et al., 1995; Johnson and Thompson, 1995).
This does not remove finite-sample uncertainty or boundary difficulties. A plug-in prediction error variance can omit uncertainty from covariance estimation (Kackar and Harville, 1984). Bayesian analysis instead integrates over parameters under explicit priors, with its own computational and inferential requirements (Sorensen and Gianola, 2002). These remain alternative approaches rather than interchangeable names for the same calculation.

title: The development of genetic evaluation: problems and solutions
section: 5 From expected relationships to genomic information
text:
5 From expected relationships to genomic information
Pedigree relationships describe an inheritance expectation. Marker data add information about realized sharing and linkage with causal variation. Dense marker regression allows heterogeneous effect distributions, while Gaussian marker regression connects directly to a genomic relationship covariance (Meuwissen et al., 2001; VanRaden, 2008).
The marker-effect and animal-effect representations can give the same genetic predictions when coding, scale and covariance assumptions agree. Conversely, changing shrinkage, centering, blending or the reference population can change the model. Genomic prediction also combines relationship, linkage disequilibrium (LD) and cosegregation information whose persistence across generations differs (Habier et al., 2013).

title: The development of genetic evaluation: problems and solutions
section: 6 Single-step: combine information rather than discard relatives
text:
6 Single-step: combine information rather than discard relatives
Genotypes are usually available for only part of a pedigree. A joint relationship model retains records and relationships from non-genotyped animals while updating genetic covariance with genomic information (Aguilar et al., 2010; Christensen and Lund, 2010).
This development makes the compatibility of reference populations central: genomic and pedigree relationships cannot be combined meaningfully by name alone. Genomic adjustment, base assumptions and residual genetic components must be specified. Equivalent latent or marker formulations can reduce dense matrix work without changing the intended joint distribution (Legarra et al., 2014).

title: The development of genetic evaluation: problems and solutions
text:
7 Richer phenotypes and biological information
Multitrait and random-regression models express information sharing across outcomes and time. They replace a collection of unrelated analyses with a joint covariance structure, while increasing identification and validation demands (Meyer, 1998; Meyer, 2001). Reaction norms connect genetic predictions to environmental conditions rather than assuming one ranking everywhere (Su et al., 2006).
Feature information extends a different part of the model: the distribution of genomic effects. Grouped covariance components and annotation-dependent mixtures express different hypotheses about how biological information should alter shrinkage. Neither provides a causal interpretation merely by assigning a biological label. See genomic-feature priors.

title: The development of genetic evaluation: problems and solutions
section: 8 What remains invariant, and what remains open?
text:
8 What remains invariant, and what remains open?
Across these developments, the essential discipline is to identify the target, specify the information available, derive its joint distribution and assess the resulting inference. Computational feasibility can motivate a new representation or approximation, but does not by itself justify changing the scientific target.
Open questions include prediction across populations, estimation under changing selection regimes, uncertain annotations and efficient uncertainty calculation at evaluation scale. Large-scale Monte Carlo single-step covariance estimation illustrates continuing algorithmic progress (Bermann et al., 2025). Its existence does not make the identification or selection assumptions unnecessary.
The next methodological step should therefore be judged against an explicit scientific question and an evidence standard, rather than against novelty of terminology. The algorithmic reference connects the equations to computation; the qualification framework states how that computation and its inferential properties can be established.

title: 13. Current developments in animal-breeding prediction and estimation
section: 1 What should count as a methodological advance?
text:
1 What should count as a methodological advance?
The central tasks remain prediction of genetic merit, estimation of genetic and environmental variation, and quantification of uncertainty. Developments change the information available, the assumptions connecting populations and traits, or the computational cost of inference. A more elaborate model is useful when it improves the relevant scientific decision, not simply because it contains more markers or parameters.
This is a selected perspective as of November 2026, rather than an exhaustive ranking of software or methods. It connects research directions to the prediction, estimation and validation foundations already developed.
Distinguish three outcomes. Predictive improvement concerns performance on the intended target population. Improved estimation concerns the parameters and uncertainty describing that population. Biological insight concerns the interpretation of variants, features and mechanisms. These outcomes can diverge: highly correlated markers can predict well without identifying a causal variant, and an informative feature can improve variance partitioning without materially changing within-family prediction.

title: 13. Current developments in animal-breeding prediction and estimation
section: 2 Prediction: retain the joint information while scaling computation
text:
2 Prediction: retain the joint information while scaling computation
The joint pedigree/genomic framework and its computational connections are reviewed by Legarra et al. (2014). An application of the algorithm for proven and young (APY) to a large genotyped population is given by Garcia et al. (2020).
Single-step evaluation places genotyped and non-genotyped animals in a joint relationship model. Modern computational work asks how to retain that target while avoiding dense storage or excessive repeated solves. The alternatives include marker-effect representations, sparse conditional pedigree operations, retained factorizations, matrix-free products and approximate relationship constructions. The relevant distinctions were derived in Chapter 4.
An improved representation can preserve the exact covariance model. An APY approximation to the target relationship need not. A cheaper preconditioner may leave the target unchanged while altering the cost of convergence. These must be assessed separately, using original-system acceptance and the final scientific prediction target.
The practical objective is not minimum time per preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) iteration. A useful evaluation accounts for preparation, factorization, preconditioner setup, operator applications, reconstruction, uncertainty and output. It also checks whether changes in computational policy remain reliable for other pedigree structures, trait counts and blending rules. See Chapter 11.

title: 13. Current developments in animal-breeding prediction and estimation
section: 3 Prediction across generations, breeds and populations
text:
3 Prediction across generations, breeds and populations
The roles of relationship, linkage disequilibrium (LD) and cosegregation information are analyzed by Habier et al. (2013). Cross-breed prediction and heterogeneous marker shrinkage are evaluated by Erbe et al. (2012).
Within a closely related population, markers carry information about both realized relationships and association with causal variants. Transfer to more distant populations changes the usefulness of those signals. A larger reference population can help, but adding samples from another population is not automatically beneficial under a model that assumes identical effects.
One modelling template is
\[
m^{(b)}=m^{(0)}+\delta^{(b)},
\]
where \(m^{(0)}\) is shared and \(\delta^{(b)}\) represents population-specific deviation. This is a hierarchical assumption to estimate and validate, not an automatic correction for population differences. A multivariate model with correlated population-specific effects expresses a related idea.
Transfer can fail through allele alignment, imputation, LD mismatch, frequency differences, environmental change or genuinely different effects. Functional information may make some marker information more portable, but should be tested in forward-generation or across-population validation rather than inferred from a random split of close relatives.

title: 13. Current developments in animal-breeding prediction and estimation
text:
4 Sequence information and biological prioritization
Sequence data increase the opportunity to include causal variation, but also increase the number of correlated, rare and imperfectly imputed predictors. Adding all variants under unchanged shrinkage need not yield the best use of the information. Possible responses include feature-specific kernels, annotation-dependent effect distributions and explicit treatment of known large-effect loci.
In a 2025 simulated livestock study, Yang and colleagues compared genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP), two-component GBLUP, support-vector regression and random forests with varying amounts of known quantitative trait locus (QTL) information. The two-component models performed best in that design; additional QTL information did not make the machine-learning methods universally superior. This is evidence about that controlled setting, not a ranking for all livestock traits (Yang et al., 2025).
The scientific question is therefore how information enters the model: a separate variance component, a changed inclusion probability, a changed slab variance, or an individual-level molecular predictor. These are developed in Chapter 14.

title: 13. Current developments in animal-breeding prediction and estimation
text:
5 Multitrait, longitudinal and environmental information
Random regression and environmental covariance provide established building blocks (Meyer, 1998; Meyer, 2001; Su et al., 2006). The availability of secondary traits at prediction time also changes the appropriate validation design (Runcie and Cheng, 2019).
Repeated measurements and correlated secondary traits can support prediction of difficult or expensive traits. Factor models and random regression reduce the dimension of the covariance representation, while retaining a clear target such as growth trajectory, environmental sensitivity or response at a particular age. Their assumptions and identification requirements remain those in Chapter 6.
High-throughput measurements create additional problems: changing sensor calibration, measurement error, selective recording and availability of the secondary phenotype at deployment. A secondary phenotype recorded only after the selection decision cannot be treated as if it were available beforehand. Prediction of latent biological performance and prediction of a noisy sensor measurement are different tasks.
For robustness, specify whether the target is performance at an environment, a slope, a contrast between environments, or an index combining performance and stability. A reaction-norm slope is model- and scale-dependent; it is not a universal biological definition of resilience. New environments outside the observed range require an explicit extrapolation assessment.

title: 13. Current developments in animal-breeding prediction and estimation
section: 6 Estimation: fitting the covariance model at evaluation scale
text:
6 Estimation: fitting the covariance model at evaluation scale
Chapter 3 compares likelihood, stochastic, moment-based and prediction-based routes, including genomic method R, Monte Carlo single-step estimation and genetic parameters via predictivity (GPP).
Covariance estimation requires more than solving the prediction equations. Restricted maximum likelihood (REML) derivatives contain trace terms and quadratic forms; an optimizer may evaluate these repeatedly at trial covariances. Exact selected-inverse and selected-solve methods, randomized traces, Monte Carlo REML and matrix-free operations address different parts of this cost.
Bermann and colleagues extended Monte Carlo REML to large single-step models in 2025. Their reported studies include comparison with exact traces in a smaller multivariate model and an application with millions of pedigree animals. The important development is the ability to estimate covariances with joint genomic information while reducing inverse-related work, rather than assuming that a prediction solver alone completes REML (Bermann et al., 2025).
The balance between deterministic and stochastic work needs explicit accounting. Probe variability, inaccurate inner solves and optimizer error are separate. A method can preserve the likelihood target while estimating its derivatives approximately. Its finite-run parameter uncertainty should not be confused with an exact optimization result.

title: 13. Current developments in animal-breeding prediction and estimation
section: 7 Estimation under selection and changing genetic parameters
text:
7 Estimation under selection and changing genetic parameters
An estimate of variation in a founder reference population need not equal the variation among selected animals in a recent cohort. Selection changes allele frequencies and can induce LD; drift, trait definition and environmental change also matter. The desired time-specific parameter must be defined before interpreting differences between estimation procedures.
A 2026 study examined genetic-parameter estimation via predictivity (GPP) under simulated genomic selection and changing trait relationships. This illustrates an emerging alternative to full covariance optimization. Its accuracy formulas, validation population and target time slice require scrutiny; it is not simply another optimizer for the same REML objective. The paper also reports direction-dependent correlation estimates in its experiments. (Gowane et al., 2026).
Predictivity-based quantities, realized cohort parameters and historical-base variance components should not be compared as though they necessarily have identical estimands. Likewise, optimizing predictive correlation does not automatically identify a unique covariance decomposition.

title: 13. Current developments in animal-breeding prediction and estimation
text:
8 Nonlinear and machine-learning methods
Kernels, trees, neural networks and hybrid models offer different ways to represent nonlinear relationships. Their usefulness depends on trait architecture, sample size, information available and deployment population. A nonlinear predictor of phenotype is not automatically an additive breeding value or an estimator of transmissible genetic variance.
Three comparisons are needed: against a well-tuned additive baseline, against a biologically informed linear/Bayesian baseline, and against the proposed method under the same information restrictions. Hyperparameter selection, variant selection and any representation learned from phenotypes belong inside training. Report calibration, reproducibility and computation alongside accuracy. The result of the Yang et al. simulation above is a useful reason to avoid assuming that algorithmic complexity guarantees improvement.

title: 13. Current developments in animal-breeding prediction and estimation
section: 9 Integrating feature information with modern evaluation
text:
9 Integrating feature information with modern evaluation
Feature/background covariance components connect directly to the multiple- component framework. Annotation-dependent marker mixtures connect to hierarchical Bayesian regression. Their integration with single-step, multitrait and longitudinal models requires a complete joint specification: the effect distribution, pedigree/genomic connection and prediction target must remain consistent. This is a statistical development question rather than a restriction to one software package.
A useful qualification sequence is to verify the induced covariance on small examples, test prediction and estimation separately, assess misspecified or uninformative features, and then evaluate representative large data. The advancement claim should say whether the gain is prediction, estimation, interpretability or computation. All four are valuable; they need different evidence.

9.1 From new information to a different estimation problem
The progression is now explicit in the substantive chapters. Functional annotations can replace common marker shrinkage by learned variance functions or mixture probabilities; individual molecular measurements instead enter a joint trait or observation model. FarmGTEx is a source of evidence for such hypotheses, not a universal set of trait-specific covariance weights (Fang et al., 2025). Chapter 14 connects these choices to derivative operators, hierarchical estimation and prediction uncertainty.
Phenomics expands the information about trajectories and correlated traits, while adding measurement and recording processes. The genetic latent-factor work in Melsen et al. (2025) is one methodological development, with a specific plant experimental design. Chapter 15 distinguishes that route from joint estimation with related-animal data and derives targets from the resulting genetic trajectories. New representations must be assessed for both inference and prediction, rather than only for compression or runtime.

title: 13. Current developments in animal-breeding prediction and estimation
section: 10 Unresolved questions and the evidence a next method needs
text:
10 Unresolved questions and the evidence a next method needs
A research direction becomes a useful method when its target, assumptions and advancement criterion are explicit. The following questions connect the existing foundations to future work; they are not claims that their solutions are already established.








Question
Statistical development
Evidence needed




How should uncertain annotations influence shrinkage?
A hierarchy separating annotation quality from trait enrichment
Sensitivity to irrelevant/misspecified features and independent prediction


What transfers between populations?
Shared and population-specific effect distributions
Forward-generation and across-population calibration at matched information


How should changing genetic variation be estimated?
A declared cohort/base estimand and a selection-aware model
Recovery of that estimand under controlled selection and recording


How can many traits and environments be modelled?
Structured covariance with identifiable directions
Covariance recovery, target uncertainty and validation in new conditions


How can precision be allocated at scale?
Separate numerical and stochastic error control for scores and PEV
Exact small references, independent precision assessment and solve accounting



The historical perspective explains how earlier methods addressed related information problems. The algorithmic reference and qualification framework provide the next two steps: derive the computation and establish the scope of its evidence.

title: 13. Current developments in animal-breeding prediction and estimation
section: 11 Selected reading and how to use it
text:
11 Selected reading and how to use it

Implementation in gsuite



Several directions discussed here already have implementations: joint pedigree/genomic prediction through the standalone command, packed covariance estimation, structured multitrait models and Bayesian marker/annotation models. The capability overview distinguishes those routes from additional methods in the wider ecosystem. Citing a published method in this chapter does not mean that a matching implementation, or every combination with single-step and longitudinal models, is available.


Next: genomic-feature information and priors.
For applications to automated measurements and high-dimensional traits, see large-scale phenomics.
For the combined implications of technologies, data access and industry structure, see drivers shaping the future of breeding.

title: 11. Large-scale computation and approximation
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: 11. Large-scale computation and approximation
section: 1 The large object need not be stored
text:
1 The large object need not be stored
For sparse direct computation see Chen et al. (2008); for iterative and matrix-free linear algebra see Saad (2003).
The covariance representation \(V=ZKZ^\top+R\) defines a model independently of whether \(V\) is materialized. Dense \(n\times n\) storage grows quadratically; a generic dense factorization grows cubically. Sparse mixed-model equations can be much smaller computationally, but factor fill depends on connectivity and ordering rather than only the input nonzero count.
A matrix-free method computes products with \(C\) or \(V\) through incidence, relationship and residual operators. It saves storage but must repeatedly apply those operators. Packed marker products avoid an explicit dense \(G\) and can reuse a genotype representation across traits or right-hand sides.

title: 11. Large-scale computation and approximation
text:
2 Factorization, repeated solves and PCG
Preconditioning and Krylov iteration are treated systematically by Saad (2003). Their use does not remove the need for a scientifically correct target system.
A retained sparse factor amortizes analysis and numerical factorization over many right-hand sides. Changing covariance parameters may preserve sparsity analysis while requiring a new numerical factor. Selected uncertainty and trace calculations can require many solves beyond the prediction solve.
For a symmetric positive definite (SPD) target system, preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) uses a compatible SPD preconditioner to change convergence, not the target equations. The preconditioner may be approximate; its setup cost, application cost and effect on iteration count all belong in the total budget. Changing preconditioners changes finite stopping behavior, so verify the reconstructed original-system residual rather than assuming that a preconditioned norm proves the required acceptance.
Independent trait/channel right-hand sides can sometimes be batched to reuse memory traffic and factors. Batching does not imply that all traits are independent: the operator must still apply their genetic and residual covariance.

title: 11. Large-scale computation and approximation
text:
3 Distinguish statistical and numerical approximations








Approximation
What can change?
Required assessment




Approximate PCG preconditioner
Convergence path and finite stopping error
Original-system acceptance and total work


Approximate relationship or APY target precision
The fitted covariance model
Prediction/likelihood sensitivity to approximation


Low-rank covariance truncation
Available genetic directions
Rank sensitivity and target-population validation


Randomized trace estimation
Numerical derivative/curvature estimates
Probe uncertainty, solve error and optimizer behavior


Stochastic PEV estimation
Reported uncertainty estimates
Target-specific precision and calibration


Genotype imputation
Predictor information and sometimes covariance
Imputation assumptions, alignment and uncertainty



A stochastic diagonal used only to construct a preconditioner is not a stochastic estimate of the final predictions or their prediction-error variance (PEV). It can preserve the same target equations and acceptance gates. This does not prove that every probe count or model combination is qualified.

title: 11. Large-scale computation and approximation
section: 4 Trace estimation has two sources of error
text:
4 Trace estimation has two sources of error
Stochastic trace estimation was developed by Hutchinson (1989). Avron and Toledo (2011) analyzes sample requirements for implicit symmetric positive semidefinite matrices; those relative-error guarantees should not be transferred automatically to every derivative operator.
For suitable independent zero-mean unit-covariance probes \(z_b\),
\[
\operatorname{tr}(B)=E(z_b^\top Bz_b),\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{tr}(B)}=\frac1m\sum_{b=1}^m z_b^\top Bz_b.
\]
Monte Carlo error decreases with probe count under the corresponding moment conditions, but products involving an inverse may also have iterative solve error. More probes do not automatically remove bias from insufficiently solved systems. Reusing probes across parameter evaluations can stabilize comparisons, but induces dependence that must be respected when assessing precision.
Randomized derivatives and randomized uncertainty have different scientific roles. Their precision controls and solve accounting should be reported separately, not inferred from prediction convergence.

title: 11. Large-scale computation and approximation
text:
5 Hardware and reproducible performance
Sparse triangular solves, marker decoding and dense products have different memory-access patterns. Physical cores, simultaneous multithreading, memory bandwidth, non-uniform memory access (NUMA) placement and Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (BLAS)/OpenMP runtime choices can change timings without changing the model. Thread counts alone do not establish comparable hardware use.
Record the node central processing unit (CPU) model, allowed CPU mask, physical-core allocation, runtime versions and placement settings. Avoid universal affinity or memory-placement prescriptions: a measured interleaving benefit on one system need not transfer to another. Separate setup from repeated operations and include end-to-end time.

5.1 Richer covariance models create different computational workloads
An annotation-weighted covariance can apply \(K_a v=W D(W^\top v)\) without forming a dense animal matrix. Its parameter derivative has the same pattern with derivative weights. Shared marker passes can therefore serve several estimation directions, but increasing annotation count still adds derivative, trace and optimization work. A packed prediction product alone is not a complete covariance-estimation algorithm.
For phenomics, separate genetic dimensions, trait count, basis size and record count. Reduced-rank covariance can save parameters and operations by imposing structure; a structured operator representation can instead preserve a specified model while changing storage. Distinguish these cases when comparing timings. Include measurement extraction and representation learning in end-to-end costs where they are required for deployment. See functional derivatives and phenomics estimation.

title: 11. Large-scale computation and approximation
text:
6 Resource accounting
Sparse animal-model restricted maximum likelihood (REML) illustrates why factorization and repeated right-hand-side (RHS) solves need separate accounting (Johnson and Thompson, 1995). For large single-step covariance estimation with Monte Carlo operations, see Bermann et al. (2025).
Report factor dimensions and fill, resident marker cache, right-hand-side batch width, iteration count, operator applications and backend solve RHS. Refinement counts describe backend correction work and cannot be recovered from PCG iteration counts alone. Distinguish measured counters from inferred averages.
Memory metrics also differ: a sampled sum of process resident set size (RSS) is not the same as GNU Time maximum RSS or a Slurm/cgroup high-water mark. Preserve the metric, sampling interval and possibility of shared-page double counting.
For route-specific controls and limits see the solver guide, packed single-step REML and prediction-error guide.






Implementation in gsuite



Sparse-direct and matrix-free execution, packed marker products, retained factors and specified stochastic estimation are implemented through the solver routes and packed REML. The execution reports record phase timings, memory and placement information. Exact/stochastic uncertainty and approximate preconditioning have separate controls and qualification; backend coverage identifies which combinations are available. Hardware-policy benefits remain dependent on the workload.


Next: checking and validation.
For the derivations behind the operator, elimination, REML and uncertainty calculations, see the algorithmic reference.
For applications to automated measurements and high-dimensional traits, see large-scale phenomics.

title: 9. Genetic bases, groups, metafounders and crossbreeding
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: 9. Genetic bases, groups, metafounders and crossbreeding
section: 1 A breeding value needs a reference population
text:
1 A breeding value needs a reference population
Additive genetic effects, relationship coefficients and genetic variances are defined relative to a reference. Conventional pedigree relationships usually take recorded founders to be unrelated and non-inbred relative to their stated base. That is a modelling convention about unrecorded ancestry, not a claim that the animals have no common ancestors.
Genomic centering also selects a reference: changing allele frequencies changes the coordinate system and potentially the covariance model. A statement such as “heritability is 0.3” or “these animals are unrelated” is incomplete without the trait scale, base and population assumptions. See genomic models for marker coding and normalization.
Distinguish the genetic base from the reporting base. Subtracting a common reference-cohort mean from displayed breeding values can leave all pairwise differences unchanged. Changing founder relationships, population means or genetic variance is a change to the model unless an explicit transformation establishes equivalence.
For a pure coordinate transformation \(a^*=s a+c\mathbf1\), with fixed \(s,c\), the covariance becomes \(s^2\operatorname{Var}(a)\). Prediction errors and their covariances must transform consistently. A group-specific base change is not generally represented by one common display offset.

title: 9. Genetic bases, groups, metafounders and crossbreeding
section: 2 Genetic groups describe base mean differences
text:
2 Genetic groups describe base mean differences
One genetic-group representation is
\[
a=Q_g g+v,\qquad E(v)=0,
\]
where \(g\) contains base-group means and \(Q_g\) contains inherited group contributions. The deviations \(v\) require a declared covariance model. This separates a mean model from the within- and across-group covariance assumptions. Genetic groups in an animal model are developed by Westell et al. (1988).
Unknown parents may be assigned to groups using defensible information such as origin, cohort or selection pathway. Contributions are then propagated through known ancestry. An observed breed label on each animal is not automatically the same design as ancestry contributions from unknown-parent groups.
If group effects are fixed, columns of \(ZQ_g\) can be confounded with the intercept or management effects. Constraints select a parameterization; they cannot create connectedness between otherwise disconnected populations. Compare estimable contrasts or total genetic values under aligned constraints rather than raw group and animal coefficients separately.
Assigning random priors to group means is a different hierarchical model. It imposes shrinkage and a covariance on those means. Merely calling a group “genetic” does not specify that covariance or distinguish mean differences from different genetic variances.

title: 9. Genetic bases, groups, metafounders and crossbreeding
text:
3 Metafounders describe ancestral covariance
Metafounders extend the ancestry model by representing relationships within and between ancestral populations (Legarra et al., 2015). A relationship matrix \(\Gamma\) describes those ancestral relationships. This differs from fitting fixed group means while retaining unrelated-founder covariance assumptions.
A schematic Gaussian decomposition illustrates the distinction:
\[
a=B a_M+\eta,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(a_M)=\sigma_A^2\Gamma,\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(a_M,\eta)=0.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{Var}(a)=
\sigma_A^2B\Gamma B^\top+\operatorname{Var}(\eta).
\]
Here \(B\) propagates ancestral contributions. In an actual metafounder pedigree construction, the innovation variances in \(\eta\) must also follow the compatible inheritance recursion. One cannot generally obtain that model by adding an arbitrary low-rank matrix to an ordinary pedigree relationship while leaving all other quantities unchanged.
\(\Gamma\) needs an admissible covariance structure and an explicit scale. Its elements are not a table of observed breed proportions. Estimation from markers depends on the genomic reference convention; pedigree labels alone do not reveal the magnitude of ancestral genomic relationships. Genetic variance, inbreeding and relationship coefficients must be interpreted on the resulting base. Values from different base conventions should not be compared as though they measured an identical quantity.
Metafounders can address a specified ancestral-population problem. They do not repair incorrect parentage, eliminate selection-history requirements or supply missing cross-population validation.

title: 9. Genetic bases, groups, metafounders and crossbreeding
section: 4 Pedigree and genomic compatibility in single-step
text:
4 Pedigree and genomic compatibility in single-step
In single-step models, \(A_{gg}\) and the replacement genotyped covariance must refer to compatible domains, scales and bases. Aligning average diagonal and off-diagonal moments can be useful, but does not guarantee that every population-specific covariance or allele-frequency difference is reconciled.
Genetic groups affect the mean structure; metafounders affect ancestral covariance. Their contributions must be carried consistently through pedigree elimination, genomic adjustment and the treatment of non-genotyped animals. An implementation that silently retains the old founder precision while changing the genomic base does not establish a coherent joint model.
Qualification should distinguish an equivalent reparameterization from a new base assumption. For the former, predictions and target covariance should agree after transformation. For the latter, differences may be scientifically intended and need population-level validation. The Schur-complement identities in genomic models still apply to a correctly specified joint covariance; they do not determine that covariance on their own.

title: 9. Genetic bases, groups, metafounders and crossbreeding
section: 5 Purebred merit and crossbred performance are different targets
text:
5 Purebred merit and crossbred performance are different targets
An animal selected within a nucleus may be intended to improve performance of crossbred commercial offspring. Genetic merit for the two settings need not be perfectly correlated. Differences in allele frequencies, dominance and genetic background can matter, alongside differences in production environment. Joint genomic evaluation of purebred and crossbred performance is developed for a two-breed system by Christensen et al. (2014).
As a simple model for animals in one parental line, define genetic effects for purebred and crossbred performance jointly:
\[
\operatorname{Var}
\begin{pmatrix}a^{P}\\a^{C}\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\sigma_P^2&r_{PC}\sigma_P\sigma_C\\
r_{PC}\sigma_P\sigma_C&\sigma_C^2
\end{bmatrix}\otimes K.
\]
This is a multitrait representation on a declared parental-animal domain, not a complete terminal-cross model. It makes the target distinction explicit: when \(r_{PC}\) is below one, selection on purebred merit alone is not equivalent to selection on crossbred merit. Estimation requires information connecting the two performance settings. Differences in management and recording should not automatically be attributed to breed-specific genetic effects.
More detailed models can distinguish breed of origin of alleles and the parental populations through which effects are transmitted. These require appropriate ancestry, phasing and relationship information, and uncertainty from inferred origin may be consequential. A pooled genomic kernel with a breed fixed effect is not automatically equivalent to such a model.

title: 9. Genetic bases, groups, metafounders and crossbreeding
section: 6 Breed composition, heterosis and non-additive effects
text:
6 Breed composition, heterosis and non-additive effects
Breed composition can enter the mean model, while heterosis and recombination effects describe other features of a crossbreeding design. They should not be absorbed into an additive genetic effect merely because all are associated with ancestry.
For illustration, if parental breed-origin probabilities are \(q_s\) and \(q_d\) and the transmitted origins are independent, expected between-breed heterozygosity is
\[
h=1-\sum_k q_{s,k}q_{d,k}.
\]
This gives \(h=1\) for a first cross between two distinct pure breeds and \(h=1/2\) for the corresponding backcross under these assumptions. Offspring breed fractions alone are insufficient to distinguish all crossing histories. This quantity concerns breed origin, not observed heterozygosity at every locus.
A regression on such a crossbreeding covariate is a mean model. A dominance relationship kernel instead specifies covariance among individual non-additive effects; it is not a substitute for every systematic crossbreeding effect. For genomic additive/dominance covariance, see Vitezica et al. (2013) and genomic models.

6.1 More molecular information does not remove population differences
An annotation derived in one breed or tissue can be used as a sharing hypothesis, but it does not establish identical effect sizes, enrichment or measurement properties in another population. Model cross-population borrowing through declared covariance or hierarchical assumptions and assess it against the relevant purebred or crossbred target.
Broader sequencing and commercial phenotyping can improve population coverage, while also introducing different imputation quality, devices and management conditions. Keep genetic-base compatibility separate from those observation and transfer assumptions. The genotype-uncertainty example and functional-prior chapter identify distinct parts of this joint problem.

title: 9. Genetic bases, groups, metafounders and crossbreeding
text:
7 Information, validation and reporting
Record founder definitions, group assignments, ancestry fractions, relationship normalization, genetic-variance scale, constraints and the intended offspring population. Retain stable animal identities when adding ancestral entities. Changing those entities must not silently change the interpretation of output rows or uncertainty targets.
Small references should check group-incidence propagation, covariance symmetry and admissibility, inheritance recursions and prediction transformations. Reference calculations for metafounders must implement the same innovation variance convention, not only match ancestral matrix dimensions.
Deployment validation should include relevant breeds, crossbred generations, management systems and cohorts. Random splits dominated by one connected line cannot establish across-line comparability. Assess bias and dispersion as well as correlation, and uncertainty of between-population contrasts where such comparisons are scientifically identifiable. See missing data and selection and model checking and validation.






Implementation in gsuite



Groups, fixed/combined base contributions and supplied metafounder covariance are implemented through the standalone model declarations, with worked YAML examples. Gamma estimation has a specific pseudo-EM contract and is distinct from joint REML; packed REML does not currently admit groups or metafounders. Dominance and hybrid combining ability provide additional implemented constructions. They do not by themselves constitute the general breed-of-origin or purebred/crossbred joint model described in this chapter.


Next: breeding objectives, selection and mating.
