title: 7. Missing data, selection and population structure
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: 7. Missing data, selection and population structure
text:
1 The observed-data model
Let \(S\) select the observed entries from a conceptual complete response vector. Then \(y_o=Sy\), \(X_o=SX\), \(Z_o=SZ\) and \(V_o=SVS^\top\). In a Gaussian likelihood, unobserved responses are integrated out: their absence is not represented by a zero response. A missing trait can coexist with observed traits for the same animal and residual unit.
For a residual covariance block, use the covariance submatrix for the observed traits and then invert or factor that block. Selecting a block of the complete precision is generally different: it represents conditional rather than marginal information. The same distinction appears in pedigree Schur complements.
Irregular longitudinal records preserve their actual times and block identities. Rows should not be inserted with arbitrary zero values to create a balanced grid.

title: 7. Missing data, selection and population structure
section: 2 Which missingness process can be ignored?
text:
2 Which missingness process can be ignored?
Let \(D\) describe response observation indicators, with mean coefficients \(\beta\) and covariance parameters \(\theta\) as in Chapter 1. The observed likelihood is proportional to
\[
\int p(y_o,y_m\mid\beta,\theta)\,
p(D\mid y_o,y_m,\psi)\,dy_m.
\]
Under missing at random, the observation mechanism depends on observed rather than unobserved responses, conditional on the variables included in the analysis. With distinct model and missingness parameters, the likelihood for \(\theta\) can ignore that mechanism in the usual ignorable setting. Bayesian ignorability also needs the appropriate prior factorization. See (RUBIN, 1976).
Missing completely at random is stronger: observation does not depend on response values. Missing not at random permits dependence on unobserved values. The observation pattern alone cannot generally establish which mechanism holds. A numerical method’s ability to accept incomplete records is therefore not proof of valid inference under informative recording or dropout.
Missing covariates and unknown genotypes require their own treatment. Deleting responses and imputing predictors are different operations, with different assumptions and potential uncertainty.

title: 7. Missing data, selection and population structure
text:
3 Selection and selective genotyping
Selection based on recorded information can sometimes be handled by including the relevant information and modelling it correctly. Selection on omitted historical records, latent performance or unmodelled criteria can make the observed sample likelihood inappropriate for the claimed population inference. There is no universal statement that best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) or single-step automatically removes all selection bias.
Selective genotyping changes which animals contribute genomic information. Single-step models connect genotyped and non-genotyped animals through pedigree, but require a defensible pedigree/genomic base and adequate modelling of the information driving selection. Check parentage, cohort representation and whether the recorded pedigree omits important selected ancestors.
The foundational selection argument is developed by Henderson (1975). It relies on assumptions; applying its equations is not a substitute for checking the recording and selection history.

3.1 Recording policies change with the technology
Automated systems can observe more records while still selecting which farms, animals, occasions and biological states are represented. Availability of a camera or robot, treatment-triggered recording and removal from production can all be associated with the response process. Greater data volume does not by itself justify an ignorable-recording assumption (RUBIN, 1976).
The deployment information pattern also changes when candidates have sensor or molecular measurements that earlier generations lacked. State which secondary phenotypes are available at selection, which are used to estimate feature representations, and which remain genuinely held out. These distinctions connect phenomics to multitrait validation (Runcie and Cheng, 2019).

title: 7. Missing data, selection and population structure
section: 4 Animals without phenotypes, genotypes or known parents
text:
4 Animals without phenotypes, genotypes or known parents
An animal without a phenotype may remain a valid prediction target or an informative pedigree link. An animal without genotypes is not equivalent to an animal whose centered dosages are all zero. A genomic prediction for that animal requires a joint model, such as pedigree/genomic single-step, or another explicitly justified imputation and uncertainty model.
Unknown parents define founder assumptions relative to a base population. Genetic groups and metafounders are ways to express particular base differences; they are not generic remedies for arbitrary missing pedigree. Their covariance, constraints and genomic compatibility must be specified and qualified.

title: 7. Missing data, selection and population structure
text:
5 Population structure and transport
Allele frequencies, linkage disequilibrium (LD), management systems and genetic effects can differ between training and target populations. Adjusting \(G\) to pedigree moments aligns selected covariance summaries; it does not establish portability of marker effects or eliminate every population difference.
Specify whether the intended task is prediction within families, across families, across generations, across breeds or in new environments. That task should determine both the reference assumptions and validation split.






Implementation in gsuite



Observed trait subsets are implemented in the multitrait pedigree interface and the standalone long/wide input contract. Packed REML integrates missing traits within its declared residual model. Missing responses remain distinct from zero observations. These implementations do not supply a general informative-dropout or selection-mechanism likelihood; the assumptions above remain part of the analysis design.


Next: non-Gaussian traits.
For applications to automated measurements and high-dimensional traits, see large-scale phenomics.

title: 5. Multiple components, correlated effects and identifiability
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: 5. Multiple components, correlated effects and identifiability
section: 1 From one random term to a covariance decomposition
text:
1 From one random term to a covariance decomposition
For independent components, \(V=\sum_k Z_kK_kZ_k^\top+R\). This representation accommodates additive genetics, common family environment, herd, permanent individual environment and additional genetic kernels. The component label does not determine its covariance or imply that it can be estimated separately from all other terms.
A fixed herd effect removes arbitrary mean differences between the observed herds. A random herd effect instead specifies a covariance and shrinkage rule. These choices can alter both estimable genetic contrasts and the allocation of variation. A large number of levels is not, by itself, a reason to treat an effect as random.

title: 5. Multiple components, correlated effects and identifiability
section: 2 Correlated direct and maternal genetic effects
text:
2 Correlated direct and maternal genetic effects
The quantitative-genetic decomposition of maternal and direct effects is developed in Willham (1972). Sparse restricted maximum likelihood (REML) computation for a direct/maternal animal model is illustrated by Johnson and Thompson (1995).
Let \(d\) be direct effects and \(m\) maternal effects on the same animal domain:
\[
y=X\beta+Z_d d+Z_m m+e,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}\begin{pmatrix}d\\m\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_d^2A&\sigma_{dm}A\\
\sigma_{dm}A&\sigma_m^2A\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The observed covariance includes the cross terms \(\sigma_{dm}(Z_dAZ_m^\top+Z_mAZ_d^\top)\). Omitting them is an independence assumption, not a change of solver. Positive semidefiniteness requires \(\sigma_{dm}^2\leq\sigma_d^2\sigma_m^2\). A genetic correlation is undefined when either marginal variance is zero.
Maternal permanent environment is a separate identity-based dam component; it is not a replacement for correlated maternal genetics. Pedigree connections, which animals have records and which dams have several offspring influence how well these effects can be separated.

title: 5. Multiple components, correlated effects and identifiability
section: 3 Repeated records separate some environmental sources
text:
3 Repeated records separate some environmental sources
In a repeatability model, \(y_{it}=x_{it}^\top\beta+a_i+c_i+e_{it}\). If residuals are independent, two records from the same animal share \(\sigma_a^2A_{ii}+\sigma_c^2\); records from different animals share \(\sigma_a^2A_{ij}\). Repetition and relatedness thus contribute different information about permanent environment and genetics. Serial residual correlation can explain additional within-animal covariance and must be considered when interpreting that separation.
With exactly one visit and identical incidence, an unrestricted individual component and residual component enter through their sum. The four-trait benchmark remains a valid supplied-covariance prediction problem, but does not by itself establish that its environmental split can be estimated.

title: 5. Multiple components, correlated effects and identifiability
text:
4 Diagnosing confounding
The information-based argument concerns local identification under regularity conditions (Rothenberg, 1971); boundary and singular cases require separate care. The component covariance identities below also provide direct algebraic counterexamples to identification.
For linear variance components \(V=\sum_k\theta_k B_k\), consider whether the projected matrices \(PB_kP\) have distinguishable directions. Exact dependence produces non-identification; near dependence can cause large component standard errors and sensitivity to constraints. A pedigree kernel close to identity may be difficult to distinguish from an individual identity component in a limited design.
Distinct parameter estimates are not evidence that the design identified them. Examine information eigenvalues, profiles and sensitivity of total covariance and predictions to alternative decompositions. Predictions of a sum of effects may be stable while its named components are unstable.

title: 5. Multiple components, correlated effects and identifiability
text:
5 Structured alternatives and scientific restrictions
A block Cholesky parameterization ensures positive definiteness in the interior. A factor model, diagonal covariance or fixed variance ratio instead imposes substantive restrictions and reduces parameter count. Constraints should be chosen from the scientific design and validation, not solely to make a failed optimizer report convergence.
At a zero component variance, the effect can be absent from the active model. For correlated components, boundary reduction also changes covariance rank. Boundary inference must account for that rank change and the resulting constraints on covariance parameters.

5.1 Information added by annotations and measurement systems
A new annotation label does not necessarily create a new observed covariance direction. Under a variance-function model, local information concerns the projected derivatives \(P V_l P\) for annotation coefficients, after accounting for competing scale and environmental parameters. Strongly correlated or nearly identical feature kernels can leave enrichment weakly determined while total prediction remains stable (Rothenberg, 1971).
For sensor traits, analogous confounding can occur between genetic loadings, permanent environment and device effects. Additional frames from the same animal improve some measurement precision but do not replace relatives, connected devices or repeated biological occasions. Replicated crop designs and related-animal data can separate covariance through different information. A representation learned under one design needs a new identification argument under another. Functional models and phenomics give the corresponding constructions.

title: 5. Multiple components, correlated effects and identifiability
text:
6 Specification record
For each component state its domain, incidence, covariance or precision, scale, correlation with other components, parameters supplied versus estimated, and prediction target. Identify which features of the design distinguish it from the remaining components. This is especially important for overlapping genomic annotations and genetic/non-genetic family effects.






Implementation in gsuite



Multiple independent pedigree/identity components and correlated channels sharing a relationship are implemented in the development component R interface. The pedigree tutorial includes repeatability and direct/maternal examples; standalone models expose further incidence and covariance constructions. General cross-component covariance is not supported by the component R contract. None of these constructors resolves the identification problems described in this chapter.


Next: multitrait and longitudinal models.

title: 3. Variance-component estimation and inference
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: 3. Variance-component estimation and inference
text:
1 Variance-component estimation and likelihood geometry
Restricted likelihood originates with Patterson and Thompson (1971). The derivative-based computations below connect to average-information estimation (Gilmour et al., 1995; Johnson and Thompson, 1995).
For \(V(\theta)\) positive definite and a fixed full-rank \(X\), the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) objective is, up to a constant independent of \(\theta\),
\[
\ell_R=-\tfrac12\{\log|V|+\log|X^\top V^{-1}X|+y^\top Py\}.
\]
Its score for parameter \(\theta_i\) is
\[
s_i=\tfrac12\{y^\top PV_iPy-\operatorname{tr}(PV_i)\},
\]
and the expected information is
\[
\mathcal I_{ij}=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(PV_iPV_j).
\]
These expressions connect identification to computation: indistinguishable projected derivative directions produce singular information. A converged optimizer at one point on a flat ridge does not identify a unique covariance decomposition.
Positive-definite trait covariances can be parameterized as \(\Sigma=LL^\top\) with positive diagonal elements of \(L\), often represented on a log scale. Scores and information must be transformed to the chosen parameter scale. Boundary estimates, such as a zero component variance, require separate interpretation: ordinary interior normal approximations and simple chi-square likelihood-ratio references need not apply.
Likelihood comparisons also require matching observed responses and normalization. The next section explains the restriction on comparing fixed-effect specifications using REML.

title: 3. Variance-component estimation and inference
section: 2 ML, REML and Bayesian analysis answer related questions
text:
2 ML, REML and Bayesian analysis answer related questions
For a unified quantitative-genetics treatment of these inferential approaches, see Sorensen and Gianola (2002).
Maximum likelihood (ML) maximizes the marginal likelihood with respect to both mean and covariance parameters. REML bases covariance estimation on information remaining after accounting for the fixed-effect space. For the same observed responses, ML can compare nested fixed-effect specifications under suitable regularity conditions. REML objectives from different fixed-effect spaces are not ordinary likelihoods for comparing those spaces.
Neither approach guarantees unbiased component estimates in every finite sample, especially with selection, weak identification or boundary solutions. The appropriate objective depends on the inferential question and sampling assumptions, rather than on which optimizer happens to be available.
Bayesian analysis specifies priors on covariance parameters and combines these with the likelihood. Posterior means, modes and credible intervals generally differ from REML estimates and their standard errors. Priors can regularize weakly identified decompositions, but prior-driven identification must be reported as such.

title: 3. Variance-component estimation and inference
text:
3 Iteration, derivatives and constraints
A covariance-estimation iteration commonly requires evaluating predictions, quadratic forms, log determinants and trace contractions. Computing a best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) once is therefore substantially less work than fitting covariance parameters. Repeated trial steps can reuse some structural information while changing numerical factors or covariance operators.
For covariance models linear in the current parameters, the average-information matrix has the familiar form
\[
\mathcal A_{ij}=\tfrac12y^\top PV_iPV_jPy.
\]
For nonlinear parameterizations the appropriate derivatives and curvature terms must be handled consistently; a formula on the variance scale cannot simply be reused unchanged on a log-Cholesky scale. The original algorithm is described by Gilmour et al. (1995).
Step control must keep the covariance admissible. A factorization failure at an inadmissible trial point is not evidence that the initial scientific model is impossible. Conversely, silently adding a ridge to rescue a trial changes the fitted objective unless that modification is explicitly part of the model.

title: 3. Variance-component estimation and inference
section: 4 What constitutes a credible fitted covariance model?
text:
4 What constitutes a credible fitted covariance model?
Boundary likelihood theory can differ from ordinary interior asymptotics; Self and Liang (1987) gives the general nonstandard framework. Its mixture distributions must not be applied without checking the conditions of the particular model.
Inspect the objective, parameter-scale score, active constraints and sensitivity to defensible starting values. Small changes in the objective with large changes in component allocation suggest weak identification. A small optimizer step alone is not a convergence certificate; a boundary solution may require one-sided optimality conditions, such as the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions, rather than interior zero-score conditions.
For component variances and correlations, report the parameterization, boundary estimates and method used for uncertainty. Wald intervals near zero variances or correlations near their limits can be misleading. Profile likelihood, bootstrap and posterior summaries are alternatives with distinct assumptions; none is automatically supplied by having an accepted coefficient solve.

title: 3. Variance-component estimation and inference
section: 5 Contemporary estimation routes at large scale
text:
5 Contemporary estimation routes at large scale
Modern variance-component estimation includes both established likelihood algorithms implemented at larger scale and alternatives with different estimating criteria. The following is a selected overview of published work relevant to genetic evaluation, checked against the literature in November 2026. Publication year alone does not determine which method is appropriate.








Route
What is estimated or approximated?
Evidence and qualification




Sparse direct average-information REML (AI-REML)
Restricted likelihood using structured factors, selected inverse entries or selected solves
Established foundation for complex animal models; fill and repeated solves can dominate cost (Gilmour et al., 1995; Johnson and Thompson, 1995)


Expectation-maximization REML (EM-REML) and hybrid optimization
The same likelihood through different update rules
Useful for initialization or difficult steps; feasibility and convergence depend on the model and parameterization


Stochastic genomic REML, including BOLT-REML
Likelihood derivatives or related calculations using random probes and iterative solves
An established large-data direction; biobank evidence does not establish performance for every pedigree or multitrait model (Loh et al., 2015)


Stochastic Lanczos REML
Iterative approximation and reuse of spectral information for genomic likelihood calculations
Particularly useful when covariance structure permits shifted-system reuse; not every multicomponent model has that structure (Border and Becker, 2019)


Monte Carlo single-step genomic REML (MC-ss-GREML)
Trace-related quantities from simulated effects and repeated joint pedigree/genomic solves
A 2025 extension tested on complex cattle models and a large pedigree/genomic application (Bermann et al., 2025)


Multi-component randomized Haseman–Elston regression (RHE-mc)
Moment equations for multiple covariance components
A scalable alternative criterion, not an algorithm for maximizing REML (Pazokitoroudi et al., 2020)


Genomic method R and genetic parameters via predictivity (GPP)
Parameters inferred from partial/whole-data prediction relationships or predictivity formulas
Recent genomic applications in 2024 and 2026; sampling, selection history, uncertainty and target time slice require assessment (Gowane et al., 2026b; Hollifield et al., 2024)


Bayesian covariance inference
A posterior distribution under specified priors
Sampling and deterministic posterior approximations require their own convergence and calibration checks (Sorensen and Gianola, 2002)




5.1 Which advances preserve the inferential target?
Replacing an exact trace by an unbiased stochastic estimate can preserve the underlying restricted-likelihood target while introducing finite-run error. Probe count, solve tolerance and optimization accuracy then determine how closely that target is approached. Replacing a genomic relationship by a low-rank or algorithm for proven and young (APY) approximation instead changes the covariance supplied to that likelihood unless equivalence is established. These are different sources of approximation; see large-scale computation.
BOLT-REML and stochastic Lanczos methods illustrate developments from large human-genetic datasets. The 2025 MC-ss-GREML work is directly concerned with joint pedigree and genomic animal models. Its simulation-and-solve construction makes the trace computation feasible without claiming that prediction alone completes covariance estimation (Bermann et al., 2025).
Moment-based methods can be especially attractive when fitting many genomic components, but changing the estimating criterion can change finite-sample behaviour, efficiency and uncertainty calculations. A negative unconstrained moment estimate is not a valid variance to insert silently into a prediction model; constrained fitting or a declared inferential treatment is required. Likewise, genotype-based population partitions do not automatically identify all components in a selected, heterogeneous animal population.
Method R uses prediction relationships between partial and complete data to assess a variance setting; GPP uses predictivity and accuracy relationships. Neither should be described simply as faster optimization of the same REML objective. Distinguish a historical-base variance from a realised parameter in a selected cohort. The 2026 GPP paper has a published correction to two figure axis labels; use the corrected article (Gowane et al., 2026a).


5.2 What evidence is needed for an estimation claim?
Separate uncertainty from finite biological sampling, random numerical probes, inexact inner solves and incomplete outer optimization. A coefficient residual checks a solve at the current covariance parameters; it does not establish that the covariance score is sufficiently small or that a posterior approximation is calibrated. Reusing random probes across trial parameters can stabilize comparisons but does not remove their sampling variability.
Report the fitted criterion, admissibility constraints, optimizer stopping rule, probe and solve accounting, and the uncertainty method. Validate parameter recovery and interval behaviour under relevant selection and missingness patterns, then assess representative large models. Reducing the dataset or removing genomic information can change the statistical problem even when the remaining optimization is exact. The qualification framework sets out the corresponding evidence layers.


5.3 New information changes the parameters to be estimated
Functional annotations can replace one common marker variance by several feature variances or a variance function. Phenomics can replace a small trait covariance by genetic and environmental factor structures or covariance functions over time. The restricted-likelihood score remains applicable to a specified Gaussian model, but its derivative operators and parameter space change. Faster traces alone do not identify additional components.
For \(K_a=W D(\alpha)W^\top\), the annotation derivatives are weighted marker cross-products; Chapter 14 derives them. For latent-factor or trajectory models, scale and rotation constraints and derivatives of loadings or basis-coefficient covariances enter the estimation problem (Meyer, 1998; Thompson et al., 2003). Full Bayesian inference can pool weakly informed parameters and integrate their uncertainty, while a penalized or empirical fit needs its corresponding inferential interpretation.
Distinguish fixed external features from features learned using the same phenotypes, and external covariance information from prior assumptions. A preprocessing step that already shrinks predictions cannot simply be treated as equally precise raw observations in another estimation stage. See phenomics for joint and staged alternatives and the information each requires.

title: 3. Variance-component estimation and inference
section: 6 Heritability depends on the target population and scale
text:
6 Heritability depends on the target population and scale
For a single-trait additive model with unit-diagonal relationship in the reference population and independent residual variance, \(h^2=\sigma_a^2/(\sigma_a^2+\sigma_e^2)\). If other environmental components belong to the phenotype, they also enter the relevant denominator. Inbreeding, heterogeneous residuals and reaction norms can make the appropriate prior or phenotypic variance depend on the individual or environment.
Thus a variance ratio computed from a single coefficient is not a universal heritability. State which variance is averaged, which population is referenced, and whether the reported quantity is on an observed or latent scale.






Implementation in gsuite



Implemented estimation includes sparse-direct REML and specified matrix-free stochastic routes in the model catalog, plus packed single-step EM-REML. The solver guide explains the distinction between solving at supplied covariances and estimating them. Packed REML currently uses whole unstructured blocks and excludes several combinations available for prediction, including factor-analytic covariances, serial residuals and genetic bases. The other published estimation methods reviewed here are not all separate gsuite interfaces.


Next: relationship and genomic models.
For recent large-scale and predictivity-based estimation developments, see Chapter 13.

title: 1. General framework, targets and assumptions
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: 1. General framework, targets and assumptions
text:
1 Scope and inferential targets
The statistical framework follows the mixed-model prediction literature (Henderson, 1975; Robinson, 1991), with likelihood and Bayesian treatments developed in Sorensen and Gianola (2002).
This reference assumes working knowledge of linear models, multivariate normal distributions and matrix algebra. Its purpose is to make the statistical and computational choices in a genetic evaluation explicit. For a gradual introduction, see Mixed-model foundations.
The relationship and marker-model families are developed in Chapter 4.
Three questions must be separated: which joint distribution defines the model, which quantities are estimated or predicted, and which numerical representation is used to compute them. Identical likelihoods need not imply identical named effect decompositions; identical predictions need not imply identical uncertainty calculations.
Let the observed-data model be
\[
y=X\beta+\sum_{j=1}^s Z_j u_j+e,
\qquad u_j\sim N(0,K_j(\theta)),\quad e\sim N(0,R(\theta)),
\]
with mutually independent random components. Collect \(Z=[Z_1,\ldots,Z_s]\) and \(K=\operatorname{blockdiag}(K_1,\ldots,K_s)\). Then
\[
V=ZKZ^\top+R.
\]
The covariance parameters \(\theta\) may be supplied or estimated. Unless stated otherwise, \(R\) and \(K\) are positive definite, \(X\) is full column rank, and the covariances are treated as known. The distinction matters: plug-in prediction after restricted maximum likelihood (REML) is not a linear function of the original data in general, and its usual plug-in uncertainty omits covariance-parameter estimation uncertainty.

title: 1. General framework, targets and assumptions
text:
2 Information, estimability and connectedness
For the relationship between local identification and information at regular points, see Rothenberg (1971). Singular boundary cases require separate analysis.
Full rank of \(X\) is sufficient for the formulas below. If \(X\) is rank deficient, only estimable functions of \(\beta\) have invariant estimates. A generalized inverse or an explicit constraint can select coefficients, but does not create information about an unestimable contrast. Software comparisons must align constraints or compare invariant fitted values and contrasts.
Genetic connectedness is also a property of the design and covariance model. If management groups are poorly linked by relatives or shared information, between-group genetic contrasts can have large prediction error even when the equations have a unique numerical solution. Inspect uncertainty for the scientific contrast, not only marginal animal reliabilities.
For covariance parameters, local identifiability can be examined through \(V_i=\partial V/\partial\theta_i\) after removal of fixed-effect directions. If two parameter changes produce the same observed covariance change, their separate interpretation is not supported by these data. Small information eigenvalues indicate weak identification rather than a linear-solver failure.

title: 1. General framework, targets and assumptions
section: 3 Declaring the target before choosing the model
text:
3 Declaring the target before choosing the model
A breeding value is a transmissible additive component relative to a reference population. A total genotypic value may additionally include dominance and interaction effects. A phenotype includes environmental and residual terms. The same fitted model can supply several targets, but their prediction error variances and practical interpretations differ.
Write a scalar target as \(t=l_\beta^\top\beta+l_u^\top u\). Specifying \(l\) requires the individual, trait, environmental condition and time point, where relevant. Predictions for a new herd or a future time point require a joint covariance model connecting that target to the training observations. A label not seen in training is not automatically the same target as a known level with no response.

title: 1. General framework, targets and assumptions
text:
4 Genetic and non-genetic components
The distinction is substantive rather than algebraic. A pedigree, genomic or identity kernel can be used inside a covariance component, but the scientific meaning comes from the effect definition and design. Herd, litter, maternal environment and permanent individual environment can induce substantial covariance without being additive genetic variation.
Independence between components is a modelling assumption. Direct and maternal genetic effects, for example, can be correlated; their cross-covariance belongs in the joint \(K\). Calling two terms separate effects does not imply zero covariance between them.

title: 1. General framework, targets and assumptions
section: 5 Assumptions that need an explicit statement
text:
5 Assumptions that need an explicit statement
The conditional mean, covariance structure and reference population jointly define the analysis. Record how covariates enter the mean, whether environmental effects are fixed or random, whether residuals are independent, and whether relationships are assumed known. State the observation/selection assumptions needed to use the likelihood in the observed sample. Distributional assumptions beyond means and covariances matter for likelihood inference and posterior probabilities even when a linear prediction formula remains available.
Binary, ordinal, count and survival responses generally require observation models beyond the Gaussian linear mixed model (LMM) developed here. A linear analysis of such a response is a separate approximation, with a response-scale interpretation that must not be confused with a latent-scale genetic model. The observation models and their inferential consequences are developed in non-Gaussian traits.






Implementation in gsuite



The general Gaussian framework is implemented through the standalone model specification and several development R adapters. Start with the standalone guide or the pedigree tutorial. The R coverage inventory identifies which combinations each adapter exposes; an arbitrary joint \(K\) in the theory is not automatically a supported input to every adapter.


Next: prediction and uncertainty.

title: Mixed models for genetic evaluation
text:
These notes are for users who need to specify, fit and assess genetic-evaluation models, rather than only run a particular command. They assume familiarity with linear models, matrix algebra and multivariate normal distributions. The introductory notes provide a slower refresher.
The same framework is used throughout: scientific question → assumptions → equations → identifiable parameters → prediction targets → inference → computation → validation → decisions → limitations. Prediction at supplied covariances is separated from covariance estimation. Relationship information, trait structure and computational representation are separate choices rather than competing names for a single method.
Abbreviations and method names are explained in the shared glossary and expanded in the chapter text.

title: Mixed models for genetic evaluation
text:
Implementation and access in gsuite
Software access: these notes, their references and small examples are public. The standalone gsuite application requires a valid licence. The seven public R packages retain their existing terms; development mixed-model R interfaces are not a public standalone release. See the distribution policy. The implementation map below describes numerical coverage separately from access and release status.
Many of the core models and computational methods developed in these notes are already implemented in gsuite and its component packages. This includes pedigree, genomic and single-step prediction, multiple random components, multitrait and longitudinal models, covariance estimation, structured residuals, and selected prediction uncertainty. The notes also develop research extensions and decision problems beyond those existing interfaces.
There are three access paths: the standalone gsuite command with YAML model files, the development mixed-model R interfaces, and task packages such as gbayes. A native algorithm can be implemented before every R adapter exposes it. Availability of prediction, covariance estimation and uncertainty must be checked separately for the selected model and execution route.



Area in the notes
Existing implementation and where to start




General Gaussian prediction and pedigree models (1–2, 4–5)
Fixed-covariance solving, pedigree models, independent components and correlated channels: standalone models, pedigree tutorial, and R coverage.


Covariance estimation (3)
Sparse-direct REML, matrix-free stochastic estimation and packed single-step EM-REML have distinct controls and limits: solver guide and packed REML.


Genomic and single-step models (4)
Packed ssSNPBLUP, supplied-genomic ssGBLUP and APY routes: YAML model examples and raw-genotype APY. Bayesian marker models use the gbayes workflow.


Multitrait, longitudinal and structured covariance (5–7, 15)
Missing trait patterns, random regression, serial residuals and factor-analytic models are implemented through specified routes: multitrait, longitudinal, and standalone coverage.


Genetic bases and additional genetic effects (9)
Groups, metafounders, dominance and hybrid combining-ability constructions: standalone coverage and non-additive models. These do not constitute every crossbreeding model.


Prediction uncertainty and numerical computation (2, 11–12)
Selected direct and stochastic calculations, sparse factors, packed products and resource diagnostics: prediction error, selected contrasts, and execution reports.


Functional priors and high-dimensional genetic models (14–15)
Supplied-kernel component models and annotation-informed Bayesian regression; development Bayesian covariance-mixture and factor models: component coverage and gbayes methods. The general learned variance-function and joint sensor/molecular models in these notes extend beyond that coverage.


Broader theory and future directions (8, 10, 13, 16)
General non-Gaussian animal models, complete selection/mating optimisation and proposed integrated biological pipelines are not established as general user workflows by this implementation map. Chapter notes identify the existing building blocks and the distinction from research extensions.



Each chapter ends with an implementation note linking its theory to the relevant interfaces. The capability overview, model catalog, standalone specification and gbayes contract own the detailed current limits. This map was checked against the interface source and existing example/test coverage; it is not a new numerical qualification of every combination or a claim that development R interfaces are all released in an installable package.

title: Mixed models for genetic evaluation
text:
Reading routes
For a refresher, start with the introductory foundations. The main reference then follows five connected routes:

Statistical foundations: Chapters 1–3 define the model, prediction targets and covariance estimation.
Model structures: Chapters 4–9 develop relationships, multiple components, longitudinal traits, missingness, non-Gaussian responses and genetic bases.
Breeding decisions: Chapter 10 connects evaluation to objectives, expected response, genetic contributions and mating.
Computation and evidence: Chapters 11–12 connect algorithms to numerical acceptance and statistical validation; the algorithmic and qualification companions provide the detailed reference.
Current and future directions: Chapters 13–16 separate methodological developments, genomic-feature priors, phenomics and changes in breeding systems.

The later chapters build on the earlier framework and can be read by topic. They describe research directions without assuming that every method is already available in gsuite.

title: Mixed models for genetic evaluation
text:
Scope of the methods
The notes describe established methods and current research in animal breeding, independently of their availability in any particular software package. The coverage includes models and inference strategies that extend beyond current gsuite interfaces. Scientific assumptions, approximation error and evidence of predictive or inferential benefit remain central throughout.
Chapters 13–16 provide a dated perspective on current developments and models using biological information, large-scale phenomics and the wider drivers of change in breeding. Established approaches and emerging research are distinguished by their evidence, rather than by implementation status.
These notes contain no executable R examples. Existing numerical examples are retained separately in the repository for future practical material.

Robinson, G. K. (1991). That BLUP is a Good Thing: The Estimation of Random Effects. Statistical Science, 6(1), 15–32. https://doi.org/10.1214/ss/1177011926.

title: APY preparation from PLINK genotypes
text:
The complete runnable YAML example (models/multitrait-ssgblup-apy-plink.yml) connects raw PLINK data to native streamed APY preparation and compiled ssGBLUP PCG. Input covariance matrices remain natural covariances. This is prediction with supplied parameters; PEV precision work remains paused.
inputs:
  genotypes: {type: plink, prefix: data/genotypes, id: IID}
  core:
    type: table
    file: data/apy_core_ids.csv
    columns: {individual: sample_id}
relationships:
  A: {type: pedigree, input: pedigree}
  G:
    type: apy
    genotypes: genotypes
    core: core
    centering: sample_mean
    normalization: sum_2p1mp
    scale: 0.95
    offset: 0.0
    independent_ridge: 0.05
    minimum_conditional_variance: 0.0
    row_tile: 256
    marker_tile: 256
  H: {type: single_step, pedigree: A, genomic: G}
execution:
  formulation: ss_gblup
  solver: pcg
  sparse_backend: pardiso
  preconditioner: block_jacobi
  relationship_metadata: prediction_only
  threads: {factor: 1, relationship: 1, decode: 4, genomic_products: 2}
Add the phenotype/pedigree bindings, trait covariances, model and outputs as shown in the complete example. The core CSV contains a header sample_id and one individual ID per row. Its nonempty, unique IDs determine core order; all other mapped FAM samples become noncore in physical FAM order. PLINK id_map supports explicit FID/IID-to-individual mapping, including repeated IIDs in distinct families. Every mapped individual must be an ordinary pedigree individual. Core selection is explicit; automatic selection and marker selection/weights are outside this spelling.


All physical BIM markers have unit weight. Let c be their observed mean BIM allele-1 dosages across all FAM samples, p=c/2 and Z the centered dosages. Missing calls are replaced by c. The covariance before APY approximation is
G = scale * Z Z' / sum(2*p*(1-p)) + offset * 11' + independent_ridge * I.
Only sample_mean and sum_2p1mp are accepted. Scale defaults to 1 and must be positive; offset defaults to 0 and must be nonnegative. Ridge must be explicit and nonnegative. It is an independent genomic ridge. No pedigree moment matching, A22 blending, automatic ridge or conditional-variance clipping is inferred. All-missing markers and zero total normalization fail; individual monomorphic markers contribute zero after centering. APY conditional variances must strictly exceed minimum_conditional_variance, which defaults to zero.
APY keeps the core covariance and core/noncore covariance, replacing noncore conditional off-diagonals with zero. Thus it changes the genomic covariance model; PCG convergence does not eliminate that approximation. Selecting all genotyped individuals as core gives exact G with quadratic core storage.



Python’s centering pass reads one marker at a time. Native preparation uses bounded row/marker tiles, threads.decode for decoding and threads.genomic_products for dense products/core solves. The latter also controls streamed cross products during prediction. Both default to one; multithreaded dense products require native MKL support. The centering pass is serial. threads.relationship controls the sparse pedigree factor; threads.factor retains its compiled direct-factor meaning.
Row and marker tiles default to 256. They control work granularity; there is no hardcoded application RAM ceiling or timeout. Numeric genomic preparation RAM is O(core^2) plus bounded tiles and linear metadata. The core Cholesky factor is reused; no full G, genomic inverse, decoded panel, resident cross block or projection is constructed. Cross storage is O(noncorecore) on disk. Core factorization costs O(core^3), and conditional solves cost O(noncorecore^2). Compiled ssGBLUP prediction defaults to execution.relationship_metadata: prediction_only. It retains the exact H precision diagonal, determinant, pedigree factor and preconditioner, while omitting H covariance diagonals that supplied-parameter prediction never uses. This removes repeated per-non-genotyped-individual covariance actions. An omitted diagonal is absent, not approximated. relationship_metadata: complete restores exact covariance metadata for diagnostics and matched setup comparisons. Automatic covariance starts/reliability calculations that require that metadata must use a complete native relationship; this prediction-only YAML route does not request them. Native constructors keep complete metadata by default. Prepared compiled files use format 6 and must be regenerated from YAML with the refreshed driver.
Genomic preparation and prediction still have independent scaling limits, including core size, cross-file traffic, precision-diagonal preparation and PCG convergence; no industrial APY timing claim follows from this optimization.
Results include native/apy_N_cross.bin and native/apy_N_metadata.csv for each raw genomic preparation. Keep the cross files with the results. The CSV contains numeric pedigree IDs, covariance/precision diagonals and noncore conditional variances; model.json maps these back to source IDs and records core/noncore order. run.json contains phase timing, peak native RSS, thread requests, metadata policy and omitted-column count, core size, cross-file size, normalization and minimum conditional variance. Sources and prepared centers are fingerprinted. Failed preparation can leave partial files in a fresh rejected output directory.
Fixed-covariance compiled prediction also omits unused global REML first/second covariance-derivative matrices and RHS arrays. It retains the same numerical MME, residual precision caches and preconditioner; full estimation keeps its existing derivative assembly. This removes quadratic-in-parameter-count storage from prediction without imposing a memory ceiling. The refreshed native capability is prediction_value_only_assembly.
