  export KMP_AFFINITY=granularity=core,scatter
  "$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/time" -v -o time.txt \
    /path/to/lmt -f para.xml > console.log 2>&1
)
Keep each LMT run directory fresh to avoid priming from results.bin or reusing adjustg2a.bin. GNU time is the existing Conda time package. Data conversion is outside both fit timings. gsuite’s end-to-end timing is in execution.json; LMT’s end-to-end timing is in time.txt. Inspect both native logs for successful convergence. LMT’s explicit cr=-25 setting is the small test’s setting; it is not asserted equivalent to gsuite’s relative 1e-11 and absolute 1e-13 stopping controls. Report the criteria alongside timings, and compare final predictions before drawing performance conclusions.
convert-data reads and validates the YAML inputs, then writes a fresh output directory containing:

Numeric data.csv with four responses, an intercept and effect group columns.
Complete numeric pedigree.csv, individual-major genotypes.txt, its pedigree-ID cross.csv, and frequencies.blkcsv containing mean dosages.
Reversible id-map.csv, record-map.csv and marker-map.csv mappings, a diagnostic missing.csv, and manifest.json with source/output hashes.

Source files remain unchanged. Partial response missingness uses an explicit LMT missing-value threshold; observed zero remains observed. Records with all responses missing follow gsuite’s omission policy. Missing genotypes and fixed markers are rejected rather than imputed or removed. Genotypes retain source sample and marker order and count the first BIM allele.
BED decoding uses bounded sample batches (--sample-batch, default 128). The 150,000 by 40,000 panel produces approximately 6 GB of genotype text, in addition to observations, pedigree and mappings. Conversion is a separate cost from fitting and can be reused when only covariance or solver settings change. An interrupted or failed conversion retains an unaccepted manifest and partial files. Neither command overwrites an existing destination.

title: Separate LMT directives and data
text:
translate reads the YAML and optionally the small conversion manifest. It does not read or rewrite phenotype, pedigree or genotype data, and can run before those data exist. Without a manifest, references default to lmt-data/ beside the XML file. With a manifest, it checks the input/binding contract and records its hash; it does not rehash the large converted files or check whether source contents have changed since conversion. The manifest identifies the converted snapshot, not a live data view.
The initial profile requires four traits, an intercept, one single-step genetic effect, ordinary identity random effects, and full positive-definite covariance matrices in declared trait order. It excludes weighted/structured residuals, random regressions, genetic groups, metafounders and genotype ID maps. gsuite thread/backend settings and requested output tables are not translated into an LMT execution policy. The receipt records source execution settings and the explicit LMT convergence setting. LMT runtime settings must be controlled separately for a benchmark.
The format references are the official LMT guide’s parameter elements, input files, examples and algorithms.

title: Separate LMT directives and data
text:
The reverse adapter admits the explicit four-trait snpblup1 profile generated by this frontend: four intercept equations, genetic, site, family and individual environment effects, supplied positive definite covariance matrices, positive pedigree blending and optional adjustg2a. Unsupported equations, switches and data options are rejected. This is not a general LMT parameter-file importer.
gsuite convert-data para.xml --from lmt --to gsuite --output imported-data \
  --source-data-manifest lmt-data/manifest.json
gsuite translate para.xml --from lmt --to gsuite \
  --data-manifest imported-data/manifest.json --output imported.yml
gsuite validate imported.yml
For files not produced by gsuite, provide --marker-map marker-map.csv instead of --source-data-manifest. The map must contain lmt_column, source_marker, chromosome, position, dosage_allele and other_allele, in marker order. Text dosages cannot identify marker names or alleles by themselves. Conversion reconstructs SNP-major BED, BIM and FAM, checks supplied frequencies against sample mean dosages, and rejects missing/non-012 genotypes and fixed markers. Custom centering frequencies are outside this profile.
The imported model retains LMT numeric animal IDs and trait labels y1 through y4; it does not infer original source names. Directive translation reads control files and manifest metadata, without rewriting or scanning data. Without a manifest it emits a draft with data_ready: false. Source convergence controls are recorded, but their stopping criterion is not declared equivalent to gsuite’s.
Small deterministic reverse-conversion tests compare all animal genetic values with independent marginal BLUP equations at two pedigree blend weights, with partially missing responses. Genotype round trips and unsupported-input rejection are tested separately. These tests do not invoke LMT or certify arbitrary LMT models. Full cross-software prediction and residual qualification remains a separate, executable-specific step.

title: Convert between DMU and YAML
text:
The development standalone frontend provides gsuite import-dmu. It translates a supported DMU 5.x linear-model specification into the existing YAML interface. The DMU driver file can reference other files, so keep its data, pedigree and parameter files available during conversion. A DMU executable is not required. Existing HPC installations do not gain the command until their frontend is updated; check gsuite --help for import-dmu.
The same frontend provides gsuite export-dmu for the reverse conversion. Both commands prepare files; neither invokes DMU.

title: Convert between DMU and YAML
text:
Separate directives and data
The staged commands reuse the same DMU parser and data writer as the combined commands. Convert data once, then translate directives against its manifest:
gsuite convert-data model.yml --to dmu --output dmu-data
gsuite translate model.yml --to dmu --data-manifest dmu-data/manifest.json \
  --output dmu-directives

gsuite convert-data dmu-directives/model.DIR --from dmu --to gsuite \
  --output imported-data
gsuite translate dmu-directives/model.DIR --from dmu --to gsuite \
  --data-manifest imported-data/manifest.json --output imported.yml
DMU directive export writes model.DIR, parameters.txt and a translation receipt in a fresh directory. Data conversion writes tables, coding metadata and manifest.json, without directives. Directive translation reads control files and manifest metadata; it does not rescan the converted tables. Preserve those tables unchanged and validate the resulting model before running it.
The manifest binds input paths, trait/design/relationship definitions and the analysis task. Compatible covariance-value, solver and output edits can reuse the data. Changes to those bindings require another data conversion. Import uses the existing REAL4-compatible float32 interpretation by default; --real-precision float64 is explicit and must match between import stages.
DMU-to-YAML translation without a manifest produces a draft with placeholder data paths and data_ready: false. YAML-to-DMU translation requires the data manifest because factor coding and the missing threshold depend on the data. The existing import-dmu and export-dmu combined commands remain available.
Small deterministic tests compare staged round-trip predictions with independent mixed-model equations, including the original residual. This qualifies the supported conversion path against that reference, not a live DMU executable.

title: Convert between DMU and YAML
text:
Convert and run
gsuite import-dmu /project/dmu/model.DIR --output /project/converted
gsuite run /project/converted/model.yml
The output directory must be fresh and its parent must exist. Conversion writes:

model.yml: the model, natural covariance matrices, execution and outputs.
observations.csv and any pedigree_N.csv files: converted input tables.
conversion.json: source/output hashes, variable mappings, missing-data counts, original execution controls and translation limits.

Edit execution settings in the YAML as usual. The default is one thread with PARDISO; --threads 8 --sparse-backend pardiso sets the generated requests. The normal gsuite validate, describe and run commands apply afterwards. Conversion checks the generated YAML and inputs; numerical convergence is established only by the subsequent fit. A successful import is not a DMU cross-software qualification.
DMU resolves relative filenames from its working directory. The importer uses the DIR file’s parent by default. If those locations differ, supply:
gsuite import-dmu /project/config/model.DIR \
  --base-directory /project/dmu-run --output /project/converted

title: Convert between DMU and YAML
text:
Supported initial subset







DMU specification
Translation




$ANALYSE task 1
REML with supplied starting covariances, or identity starts when omitted


Tasks 11 / 12
Supplied-covariance solve, using compiled sparse direct / PCG


$DATA ASCII (integers,reals,miss)
One combined or two corresponding integer/real files


$VARIABLE
Named columns, or generated I1/R1-style names when absent


$MODEL
Single/multiple traits, trait-specific fixed classes, overall fixed regressions, independent or correlated random effects across traits


Repeated individual ID in distinct random factors
Separate genetic and permanent-environment effects with the same incidence


Zero ABSORB lines
Accepted with or without the historical zero lines


$VAR_STR N PED 1 ASCII ...
Inbreeding-aware sire/dam pedigree relationship


Default random relationship
Independent levels, with trait covariance supplied by $PRIOR


Inline or external $MODEL and $PRIOR
Parsed and included in source provenance



Each random factor may occur at most once per trait. The same factor can occur across traits, including with different incidence columns. Covariance entries use factor-local, lower-triangular coordinates in trait order among the traits containing that factor. The residual block follows the last random factor. The importer transfers natural covariances directly. Supplied-covariance solves require every variance diagonal; omitted off-diagonal entries are zero.
DMU integer codes are normalized as integers. Zero classification codes mask the affected trait’s response. Real responses strictly below miss become missing; equality is retained. A missing required fixed covariate on an otherwise observed row is an import error requiring explicit data editing. Original numeric columns and separate masked response columns are retained in the converted CSV.
Data reals default to the documented DMU REAL*4 precision: values are rounded to float32 before writing decimal CSV. For a known double-input setup, --real-precision float64 retains double precision within the documented input range. Covariance parameters are read at double precision. The chosen setting is recorded, and data files are streamed rather than retained as Python tables.
DMU fixed classes use full indicator spaces. The generated YAML represents those spaces through an intercept and treatment contrasts; fixed coefficient references can differ. Compare fitted values and random effects for equivalence. Additional rank deficiencies remain errors in the existing YAML validator; factor merging or model-specific constraints need explicit preparation.

title: Convert between DMU and YAML
text:
Features requiring further translation
The initial importer rejects nonzero NOCOV, observation weights, nested or random regressions, merged random factors within a trait, binary input, noninbred or phantom-parent pedigree methods, supplied inverse/genomic structures, heterogeneous residual structures, variance restrictions and nonlinear/MCMC directives. In particular, PED 2 is not changed into inbreeding-aware PED 1. An unsupported statistical directive prevents publication of a converted model.
DMU-specific solvers, scaling, preconditioners, stopping and printing controls are recorded separately. They do not select equivalent gsuite algorithms or convergence tolerances. The YAML requests fixed/random estimates, diagnostics and pedigree-based genetic predictions. DMU residual/solution file formats and uncertainty requests are not reproduced by this importer.
The focused tests cover conversion, source preservation, missingness, direct and PCG predictions against independent dense equations, and balanced one-way REML against analytic mean-square estimates. They do not establish agreement with every DMU release or an operational NAV model.
Syntax and input conventions follow the official DMU 5.6 guide. DMU 6 has revised driver keywords and requires a separate import profile.

title: Convert between DMU and YAML
section: Export a YAML model to DMU
text:
Export a YAML model to DMU
gsuite export-dmu /project/model.yml --output /project/dmu-run
The output parent must exist and the destination must be fresh. Run DMU from the resulting directory so its relative filenames resolve correctly. Export creates:

model.DIR, data.txt and parameters.txt: complete ASCII model, data and natural covariance parameters (or REML starting values).
pedigree_NAME.txt: ordinary inbreeding-aware sire/dam pedigrees when used.
levels.csv and records.csv: deterministic integer-to-original-ID mappings and data-line-to-record mappings. Original string IDs can contain spaces.
conversion.json: source/output hashes, trait and channel ordering, random-factor mappings, input precision and translation qualifications.

The export supports the same statistical intersection as the importer: single/multiple traits, categorical fixed main effects, overall fixed numeric regressions, independent-level and ordinary pedigree random effects, including repeatability and correlated factors with separate incidence columns across traits. Channels are reordered into DMU trait order together with their covariance rows and columns. Pedigree sort ranks put parents before offspring.
Solve models select DMU task 11/method 9; REML models select task 1/method 1. REML requires every covariance block to be estimated without constraints. Partial estimation, covariance tying, FA/serial structures, weights, interactions, random regressions, genetic groups, metafounders, uncertainty requests and genomic/single-step models require further translation and are rejected. The original YAML model and inputs are unchanged.
DMU data are exported at documented REAL4 precision; covariance parameters retain double precision. The report gives the maximum rounding change. The exporter chooses two finite negative REAL4 values below all observed responses and required covariates for the missing threshold and missing sentinel. Input values outside that representable range are rejected. Missing responses stay trait-specific. YAML solver/thread/optimizer controls and post-fit truth evaluation are not translated into equivalent DMU controls. DMU solution and residual files are requested, independently of YAML output-table selection.

title: Convert between DMU and YAML
text:
Numerical qualification
Focused export tests compare predictions and fitted values with independently assembled small mixed-model equations and compare variance estimates with an analytic balanced one-way REML reference. They also check ID recoding, covariance permutations, source preservation and export/import equivalence.
This first version follows the DMU 5.6 guide and existing benchmark conventions. The new converter has not yet been validated by running the exported files in DMU. Existing historical DMU benchmarks do not qualify this exporter. A live comparison must check DMU convergence, map SOL using levels.csv, compare fitted values on corresponding records, and compare PAROUT with fitted natural covariances. Fixed coefficients can differ under alternative contrasts. REML likelihood constants and optimizer stopping rules also require separate treatment.

title: Standalone models and YAML examples
text:
Quick start · Installation · Results and diagnostics
The standalone application requires a licence. The model syntax, examples and capability descriptions on this page are public.
One YAML file specifies input files, column bindings, the statistical model, natural covariance matrices, fitting controls, threads and requested outputs. The interface uses schema: gsuite.model/v1-draft. Unknown keys and unsupported combinations are rejected. The YAML specification gives the full syntax and supported combinations.

title: Standalone models and YAML examples
text:
Input and model sections







Section
Meaning




traits
Ordered response/channel names, also used for environments


inputs
All CSV/TSV, PLINK, covariance, assignment and prediction-grid files


relationships
Named pedigree, single-step, APY, dominance, cross-product or supplied relationship models


bases
Optional power, Legendre or Chebyshev regression bases


covariances
Natural variances/covariances or FA loadings and specific variances


model
Observation input, fixed formula, named random effects and residual structure


analysis
task: solve for supplied covariances, or task: reml for estimation


execution
Formulation, solver, factorization, threads and linear-solve tolerances


output
Destination, selected coefficient tables, predictions and optional uncertainty


evaluation
Optional comparison with supplied true genetic values after fitting



Matrices are covariances, never inverses. Inline matrices use one YAML list item per row, for example - [1.0, 0.2]. Their order follows the generated channels; labelled inline or external matrices must match that order exactly. Random/residual matrices must be finite, symmetric and positive definite. Known measurement-error covariance may be positive semidefinite and remains fixed. Under REML, selected matrices are starting values; omitted blocks remain fixed. Otherwise these are fixed supplied values.
Column bindings use neutral logical names such as individual, parent1, parent2, mother, time or environment. IDs remain strings, including leading zeros. Wide phenotypes map trait names to response columns. Long phenotypes use layout: long and responses: {trait: trait_column, value: value_column}. One record ID is one residual occasion: ID/trait pairs must be unique and mapped covariates must agree within an ID. Distinct visits need distinct record IDs. Absent trait rows are missing responses, without imputation. Independent prediction grids remain wide.
For a herd-year fixed effect, bind a prepared herd-year column and use factor(herd_year) in the existing fixed formula. Preparation indexes active factor levels and streams wide designs to a native sparse rank check; it does not construct a dense square matrix of all fixed coefficients. Reference levels and coefficient ordering are unchanged. Memory still depends on design sparsity and factor fill; this does not qualify a complete NAV evaluation pipeline. The packed solver also replaces large dense coarse corrections with a sparse fixed-effect correction and small global aggregates. Fixed effects remain jointly estimated through iteration on data; no phenotype pre-correction is introduced. See the fixed-design limits.

title: Standalone models and YAML examples
text:
Complete ssSNPBLUP example
Save this as model.yml beside the supplied example’s phenotypes.csv, pedigree.csv and genotypes.bed/.bim/.fam. The physical columns in this synthetic example use animal, sire and dam; the logical bindings remain individual, parent1 and parent2 for plant, human and animal datasets. Edit the physical bindings for another dataset. The matrices below are covariances on their natural scale, in the declared [milk, fat] trait order. The example requests eight threads for marker work and one for other phases; request at least eight Slurm CPUs, or edit the YAML to match your allocation.
The included example contains:
example/
  model.yml
  pedigree.csv
  phenotypes.csv
  genotypes.bed
  genotypes.bim
  genotypes.fam
  true_breeding_values.csv
phenotypes.csv has columns record_id,animal,milk,fat,herd,age; pedigree.csv has animal,sire,dam, with 0 for unknown parents. PLINK FAM IIDs match the pedigree individual IDs; BED is SNP-major and BIM lists markers. Repeated observations use distinct record_id values. The example uses NA for one missing response. The truth CSV is optional reference material and is deliberately absent from the model’s inputs.
Save the following complete specification as model.yml beside those inputs. All covariance matrices are supplied values; analysis.task: solve holds them fixed rather than estimating them.
# Tiny synthetic example: covariance matrices follow [milk, fat].
schema: gsuite.model/v1-draft
name: single_step_example
traits: [milk, fat]
inputs:
  observations:
    type: table
    file: phenotypes.csv
    id: record_id
    columns: {individual: animal, site: herd, age: age}
    responses: {milk: milk, fat: fat}
  pedigree:
    type: pedigree
    file: pedigree.csv
    columns: {individual: animal, parent1: sire, parent2: dam}
  genotypes: {type: plink, prefix: genotypes, id: IID}
relationships:
  A: {type: pedigree, input: pedigree}
  H:
    type: single_step
    pedigree: A
    genotypes: genotypes
    genomic: {adjustment: none, polygenic_weight: 0.0, independent_ridge: 0.05}
covariances:
  genetic:
    - [1.0, 0.1]
    - [0.1, 0.04]
  individual_environment:
    - [0.4, 0.02]
    - [0.02, 0.02]
  residual:
    - [2.0, 0.08]
    - [0.08, 0.05]
model:
  data: observations
  fixed: "factor(site) + age"
  random:
    genetic: {group: individual, relationship: H, covariance: genetic}
    individual_environment: {group: individual, covariance: individual_environment}
  residual: residual
analysis: {task: solve}
execution:
  formulation: ss_snp
  solver: pcg
  sparse_backend: pardiso
  preconditioner: qnn_reuse
  pedigree_factorization: ancestral_sweeps
  convergence: {relative_tolerance: 1.0e-10, maximum_iterations: 4000}
  threads: {default: 1, marker_products: 8, marker_setup: 8}
output:
  directory: ../results/example
  tables: [fixed_effects, random_effects, diagnostics]
  predictions:
    genetic_values: {effects: [genetic], levels: all}
From that directory, validate, inspect and fit:
gsuite validate model.yml
gsuite describe model.yml
gsuite run model.yml
The selected outputs are genetic_values.csv, fixed_effects.csv, random_effects.csv and diagnostics.json under ../results/example/. run.json records numerical acceptance, residual checks and native timings; execution.json records whole-workflow timings, result collection and sampled process-tree memory. Check their acceptance fields before using predictions. Repeating the fit requires a fresh output directory, for example gsuite run model.yml --output ../results/example-repeat.
This supplied-covariance model selects packed PCG, exact ancestral pedigree sweeps and Qnn reuse. Change model/task declarations in YAML rather than choosing a different executable. The model specification gives the full syntax for other effects and covariance families.

title: Standalone models and YAML examples
text:
Solver and threads
For fast packed ssSNPBLUP:
execution:
  formulation: ss_snp
  solver: pcg
  sparse_backend: pardiso
  pedigree_factorization: ancestral_sweeps
  preconditioner: qnn_reuse
  threads: 16
A scalar sets every applicable thread request. Override particular operations with threads: {default: 16, decode: 4}. Packed controls are marker_products, marker_setup, decode, pedigree, preconditioner and vectors. Compiled models use factor and relationship; raw-genotype APY also uses decode and genomic_products. A mapping without default uses one for unspecified operations. Request matching Slurm CPUs. Thread settings are phase-specific requests: Python preparation and dependency-ordered pedigree work can be serial.
ancestral_sweeps preserves the full statistical model with a smaller retained pedigree factor and exact peripheral sweeps, including supplied metafounders. full_qnn is available for comparison and is the default. qnn_reuse avoids a second global pedigree factor; shifted_pedigree is the alternative packed preconditioner. Linear PCG tolerances belong in execution.convergence. Ordinary compiled models support direct or PCG solving. Exact/APY ssGBLUP uses compiled PCG and formulation: ss_gblup.

title: Standalone models and YAML examples
text:
Covariance estimation
analysis.estimate selects free covariance blocks; omitted blocks stay fixed. Sparse-direct compiled REML supports unstructured and FA covariance and scalar or separable multivariate serial parameters. Natural starts are transformed internally. analysis.constraints can fix named optimizer coordinates; describe lists them. A fixed Cholesky coordinate is not a fixed covariance entry. Direct optimizer controls include maximum_step and maximum_line_search_reductions.
Packed EM-REML estimates whole unstructured genetic, additional identity-effect and independent residual covariance blocks for ordinary pedigrees. Genetic regression channel width can differ from residual trait width. Its update control is optimizer.step_fraction in (0, 1]. Score traces have their own explicit solve and precision budgets under analysis.traces. Exact traces are small references; stochastic traces require explicit probes, seed, total solve cap and maximum score MCSE. Stochastic convergence also requires an independent final score check. See packed REML controls and limits.
Omit analysis.likelihood to skip global determinant work in packed REML. Optional method: exact requires maximum_dimension; method: slq requires maximum_operator_products, with optional probe/depth/precision controls. It reports the likelihood change from the start to the final covariance state, with separate sampling MCSE and Lanczos-depth sensitivity. It does not control EM updates or certify a global optimum. Unqualified optional likelihood does not reject an otherwise qualified point fit. Compiled direct REML retains its absolute likelihood and line-search acceptance.

title: Standalone models and YAML examples
text:
Model capabilities and limits
The weighted, spatial and non-additive model guide covers observation precision/known error, spatial trials, selected prediction contrasts, additional-effect REML, dominance and hybrid GCA/SCA. It identifies native/YAML coverage and dense-kernel limitations.
The complete examples cover pedigree, packed ssSNPBLUP, exact/APY ssGBLUP, direct/maternal and weighted incidence, regression, external relationships, groups/metafounders, FA, serial residuals and estimation. The specification gives exact syntax and route-specific supported combinations.
Supplied FA uses natural loadings and specific variances with an identified triangular leading loading block; it reduces covariance parameters, not genetic coefficient count. Serial models support scalar or separable trait-by-time AR1 and exponential covariance with actual gaps and missing traits. Compiled models also accept general finite trait-by-visit covariance blocks.
Fixed/random groups, explicit phantom group-parent absorption, combined bases and supplied/estimated Gamma are distinct statistical declarations. Packed ordinary random groups use implicit sweeps; packed fixed/combined groups prepare ordinary inheritance columns once, requiring O(individuals × groups) storage. Metafounders retain every correlated latent base. Gamma pseudo-EM requires an explicit absolute marker base and is separate from joint REML.
Sparse external natural covariance uses a retained sparse inverse-action factor; fill and exact precision-diagonal setup can be costly. Raw PLINK APY uses an explicit ordered core and bounded tiles/file-backed cross products. Industrial APY preparation remains unqualified. Packed REML currently excludes FA, serial/grouped residuals, groups/metafounders and joint PEV requests.
Existing selected exact/stochastic PEV options remain conditional on supplied covariances, with explicit work budgets and separate qualification. Their precision is not improved by this interface cleanup. The model-only validator skips uncertainty cases.

title: Standalone models and YAML examples
text:
Compare predictions with supplied truth
An optional top-level evaluation block makes gsuite run model.yml fit and score in one invocation with evaluation settings in the same YAML. Truth is used only after an accepted fit.
For the 20K gsim dataset, add this alongside model, execution and output:
evaluation:
  predictions: genetic_values
  truth:
    file: true_breeding_values.csv
    columns:
      individual: animal
      trait: trait
      value: true_breeding_value
  subset: heldout
  individual: individual
  genotypes: genotypes

output:
  directory: results/prediction20k-evaluated
  predictions:
    genetic_values: {effects: [genetic], levels: all}
Replace the existing output block rather than declaring it twice. The predictions key references a named output.predictions request with individual levels. truth.columns maps the long truth CSV’s individual, trait and numeric value columns. Its file resolves beside the YAML. individual references a mapped observation column, not the source CSV header. Optional genotypes references a PLINK input; its existing FID/IID-to-individual mapping is reused. No second genotype path or training table is needed.
Run in a compute-node allocation with the model’s requested CPUs:
gsuite run /path/to/dataset/model.yml
Fitting and evaluation use managed $TMPDIR scratch and are collected together at output.directory. Use a fresh result directory. No shell scoring or copy step is needed. execution.threads: 8 still controls the native fit.
subset is heldout, phenotyped or all. An individual is phenotyped if it has any observed response in model.data; repeated rows, long-format rows and fully missing records use that same definition. Held-out individuals have no observed training response in any trait. This option does not mask training phenotypes: the input must already encode the intended training/held-out split. Partially observed traits do not make an individual held out. Truth targets must match the requested prediction levels and traits. Duplicate/nonfinite truth, empty subsets and missing predictions fail explicitly.
evaluation/summary.csv reports Pearson accuracy, Spearman rank correlation, RMSE, mean absolute error, mean prediction-minus-truth bias, and the intercept and slope of truth regressed on prediction. Ideal mean bias/intercept are zero and slope is one. When genotypes is supplied, results are grouped by all, genotyped and non-genotyped targets. evaluation/matched.csv retains every scored pair; evaluation/assessment.json records definitions, hashes and cohort settings. evaluation-inputs/ preserves the frozen evaluation-only targets. No truth centering, rescaling or model tuning is performed.
execution.json includes separate preparation, fitting and evaluation times and workflow memory. Overall acceptance requires a successful requested evaluation as well as fitting. A scoring failure preserves the accepted native fit and its diagnostics; native numerical acceptance and evaluation acceptance remain separate. Acceptance checks a complete labelled comparison, not an accuracy threshold. One simulated dataset does not establish population-level bias or sampling uncertainty.

title: Standalone mixed models with YAML
text:
The standalone gsuite application is offered only to licensed users. This guide, the model specification and small examples remain public. Software access is described in the distribution policy; standalone bundles are supplied separately from public R package downloads.
Use one YAML file for input data, the model, covariance matrices, threads and outputs. The same command runs supplied-covariance solving and REML estimation.

title: Standalone mixed models with YAML
text:
Run a model
On GenomeDK, start inside a Slurm compute allocation with enough CPUs for the threads requested in your YAML. Use your project’s shared installation:
export PATH="/path/to/shared/installation/bin:$PATH"
gsuite run model.yml
No compilation or access to the maintainer’s Conda environment is needed. Input and output paths resolve beside the YAML. Choose a fresh output directory; scratch processing and copying results back are automatic.
To check or inspect a model before fitting:
gsuite validate model.yml
gsuite describe model.yml
See the complete ssSNPBLUP example for input files, covariance matrices, thread settings and outputs.

title: Standalone mixed models with YAML
text:
Find the results
Results are saved to output.directory in the YAML:

Prediction CSVs and requested effect tables contain the estimates.
run.json records numerical acceptance and diagnostics; execution.json reports workflow timings and memory.
Optional truth comparison writes accuracy, bias and calibration to evaluation/summary.csv.

Check acceptance before using estimates. See results and diagnostics for file definitions, failure handling and resource reporting.

title: Standalone mixed models with YAML
text:
Build, validate and distribute
These steps apply to an authorised supplied bundle. Development or validation builds do not automatically become production licensed releases.
Maintainers: inside an extracted source bundle on a compute node, with the build environment activated, run each task separately after the previous one succeeds:
bash build.sh
Builds and installs, reusing compatible native cache entries.
bash hpc_tasks/validate.sh
Runs exact references, truth-evaluation checks and all bundled fixture models.
bash hpc_tasks/build_binary_distribution.sh
Produces a binary archive and validates a fresh installation. Logs and results are collected automatically. See installation and maintenance for prerequisites, acceptance checks and binary installation instructions.

title: Standalone mixed models with YAML
text:
Reference

Model guide: complete YAML example, threads, REML and truth evaluation.
Convert between DMU and YAML: supported ASCII pedigree models, inputs and ID mappings.
YAML specification: all supported declarations and combinations.
GenomeDK validation record: tested installations and qualification limits.

title: gmap software validation
text:
These recorded simulation results assess selected behavior on ten fixed datasets from the shared design. They do not revalidate the statistical method or cover every setting. The use snippets show the current package interfaces. This report step summarizes retained artifacts and does not rerun analyses. The gmap guide describes current inputs and options.


mapping_stat <- gmap::gmap_stat(stat, Glist,
                          phenotype_variance = phenotype_variance)

            regions = regions, method = "multi_effect",

title: Earlier connected genomic evidence and Bayesian parameter learning
text:
This records the earlier connected genomic simulation and separate Bayesian parameter-learning qualifications. The shared genomic simulation has a newer fixed set of ten draws and separate pages for each library. Results from these runs are not pooled with the newer set. Development history, failed runs and exploratory diagnostics are deliberately excluded.


The workflow connects glma, gcorr, gbayes, gscore, gmap and gsea through the gsuite R interfaces. One detailed dataset provides figures and worked results. Ten independently simulated datasets repeat the same fixed design for a small descriptive qualification.
The qualification asks whether the modules can share prepared genomic data, summary statistics and LD resources; whether requested analyses complete; and whether their outputs behave sensibly relative to known simulation truth. A separate five-repetition design qualifies the supported BayesC and BayesR reference-LD recipe. The results are descriptive checks rather than a ranking of competing methods.




10,000 unrelated simulated individuals and 50,000 biallelic markers.
500 independent 100-marker regions with within-region correlation ranging from 0.2 to 0.8.
Three continuous traits with target heritabilities 0.30, 0.40 and 0.35.
Effects enriched in the first 80 regions.
Region 1 contains a shared causal variant for two traits; region 2 contains distinct causal variants.
Three disjoint GWAS samples of 3,000 individuals and 1,000 held-out individuals for prediction.
A pooled LD reference constructed from the 9,000 GWAS individuals. It retains every pair within each simulated region with \(r^2=0\) and no cross-region LD.

Population truth is calculated from the simulated effects and the known population LD, rather than from the observed reference matrix.











Component
Exercised capability
Outcome

All marker fits completed; 150 selected marker/trait comparisons across the ten repetitions agreed with R OLS within \(10^{-9}\)


gcorr

Point estimates completed; truth comparisons, unavailable uncertainty and out-of-range correlations remain visible


gbayes
BayesC and BayesR using sparse reference LD
The supported parameter-learning recipe passed all heritability, effect-recovery, prediction and chain-diagnostic criteria across five simulations


gscore
Ridge, BayesC and BayesR scoring
Held-out scoring completed; truth-effect scoring agreed with simulated genetic values within numerical tolerance


gmap
Regional multi-effect mapping and ABF colocalisation
The deliberately simple shared and distinct causal signals were recovered in all repetitions


gstat and gsea
Gene statistics, ORA, preranked GSEA, competitive regression, bounded MAGMA and Bayesian pathway analysis
All requested gene and pathway statistics completed through the documented saddlepoint gene-tail route



All ten planned repetitions completed. Seeds were fixed in advance and no failed simulation was replaced. Native operation-local thread counts were one.





Use the scalar BayesC and BayesR reference-LD workflow as follows:

Standardize the continuous phenotype and dosage scale, align summary statistics to the LD reference, and retain the allele labels.
Use a matched reference population. The qualification uses 3,000 GWAS individuals and an independent reference of 9,000 individuals.
Construct sparse LD with a 1,000-marker window and \(r^2=0.001\).
Use residual_policy = "reference_ld" and residual_adjustment = 0.9.
Set priors to the intended architecture. Here the expected nonzero proportion is 0.02. BayesR uses variance multipliers \((0,0.01,0.1,1)\) and active-component proportions \((0.012,0.006,0.002)\). Mixture weights use an explicit Dirichlet strength of 5,000.
Run four chains. Use 500 burn-in sweeps, followed by 700 retained sweeps for BayesC or 5,000 for BayesR. Require maximum R-hat at most 1.05 and minimum bulk ESS at least 100 for the reported scalar parameters.

The sampler learns residual variance, marker-effect variance and mixture probabilities. It returns posterior marker effects, PIPs, parameter traces and joint-draw reference heritability. Posterior-mean effects can be passed to gscore() without changing marker order or allele orientation.



Five fixed simulations use 3,000 study individuals, 2,000 markers, 40 causal markers and target heritability 0.30. BayesC is evaluated under a homogeneous normal-effect architecture. BayesR is evaluated under its matching three-component variance mixture. Each simulation receives a separately generated reference panel from the same genotype population. No failed draw was replaced.

Small fixed-seed native checks also show that the BayesC and BayesR transitions agree with the corresponding installed sblr calculations to numerical precision. With complete same-sample LD, posterior mean effects correlate 0.9975 for BayesC and 0.9994 for BayesR with individual-level sblr effects. These checks connect the supported R workflow to its native implementation.



A second fixed five-repetition qualification covers four advanced transitions under their intended data contracts. Block residual learning uses two disjoint summary-likelihood blocks with separate response normalizations. BayesS uses 600 markers, 300 nonzero effects and a known MAF exponent. The multivariate design uses three continuous traits measured on the same 1,800 individuals, complete shared LD, and the observed response cross-product required to learn sampling covariance. Across the ten repetitions:

Mean trait heritabilities were 0.300, 0.398 and 0.349.
Annotation-aware LDSC means were 0.310, 0.439 and 0.394. Baseline LDSC, GNOVA and SumHer generally underestimated heritability in this deliberately nonuniform architecture.
All 40 component credible sets contained the simulated causal marker in the two simple mapping regions.
HESS supplied standard errors for 189 of 600 regional covariance estimates; SUPERGNOVA supplied 600 of 600; the exercised LAVA route supplies none.
Six annotation-category genetic correlations were undefined because an estimated component heritability was nonpositive.
The documented saddlepoint gene-tail route returned all 30,000 requested p-values; 11 calculations used the recorded moment-matching fallback.

Unavailable values and out-of-range genetic correlations are retained in the public tables. They are not clipped, silently replaced or removed.



This evidence covers one continuous-trait simulation design with a predefined LD structure, architecture and sample split. Ten repetitions provide a useful descriptive check, but not precise power, false-positive, coverage or method ranking statements.
The connected qualification does not cover binary traits, population structure, multi-ancestry analysis, realistic LD-reference mismatch, alternative LD windows or \(r^2\) thresholds, MR/SEM/GGM, Bayesian annotation learning beyond the BayesS specialization, arbitrary sampling overlap, LOCO association, every interface option, or complete package/platform qualification. Literature attribution and pedigree/greml/gsolve qualification are maintained separately.



The public workflow presents the retained figures and principal results without executing analyses during website rendering. The published compact tables preserve the aggregate truth comparisons, availability summaries, BayesC/BayesR reference-LD results and extension checks. Current supported calls are documented by the package guides and their focused deterministic tests.
The complete package check was not part of this workflow qualification.

title: Polygenic scoring with gscore
text: gscore applies allele-labelled marker weights to selected people in a gbase Glist. It can produce total scores, scores for named marker sets and several weight columns in one pass. It also constructs clumping-and-thresholding (C+T) weights from aligned GWAS statistics and stored sparse LD. The shared simulation holds out 2,000 individuals for this example. Run the overview loading block first for prefix, Y, bayes_fit, gene_sets, statistics and reference_Glist.

title: Polygenic scoring with gscore
text:
Apply BayesC weights
This page uses the frozen dispatcher bayes_fit$weights artifact from the shared study. Its scoring calls, tables and figures are retained unchanged. The current gbayes fitters return bayesfit objects with coef() and extract() accessors; this tutorial does not establish a direct gscore(bayesfit, ...) conversion or transfer its saved numerical results to a newly fitted model. Preserve the declared allele and effect-coding contract when preparing weights for another analysis.
The gbayes fit provides standardized, portable weights for trait A. The target Glist selects only the held-out people from the same PLINK files. sets contain marker names; the Glist resolves their BED locations and the scorer accumulates their contributions while reading the target panel.
library(gbase)
library(gscore)

holdout_ids <- sprintf("id%05d", 18001:20000)
test_Glist <- gprep(bedfiles = paste0(prefix, ".bed"),
  ids = holdout_ids, nthreads = 4)

prediction <- gscore(bayes_fit$weights, test_Glist,
  sets = gene_sets[1:20], include_total = TRUE,
  coding = "standardized", scale_scores = FALSE,
  control = list(threads = 4))

dim(prediction$scores)
colnames(prediction$scores)[1:6]
The score matrix has 2,000 rows in selected individual order. Its A column is the total BayesC score; the remaining columns are the requested gene contributions. Since scale_scores = FALSE, scores are not standardized again across the target cohort.

title: Polygenic scoring with gscore
text:
Evaluate the held-out score
Join scores to outcomes by individual ID, rather than relying on row position. Here the same trait A score is correlated with all three simulated outcomes; the B and C rows are cross-trait associations, not separately fitted B or C prediction models.
observed <- Y[rownames(prediction$scores), , drop = FALSE]
trait_A_score <- prediction$scores[, "A"]
vapply(colnames(observed), function(trait)
  cor(trait_A_score, observed[, trait]), numeric(1))

title: Polygenic scoring with gscore
section: Construct another score from GWAS evidence
text:
Construct another score from GWAS evidence
clump_threshold() chooses markers by GWAS p-value, LD and distance. It needs an LD resource retaining every pair its requested window could inspect. The main tutorial reference has a 100-variant construction limit, so it cannot be used for a 250 kb C+T window even on this artificial panel. Construct a separate clumping reference with no variant-count limit and a base-pair window at least as wide as the clumping rule:
dir.create("analysis", showWarnings = FALSE)
ct_reference <- gprep(bedfiles = paste0(prefix, ".bed"),
  ids = sprintf("id%05d", 1:18000), nthreads = 4)
ct_reference <- gprep(Glist = ct_reference, task = "sparseld",
  out_prefix = "analysis/clumping-LD",
  max_distance_bp = 250000, max_distance_variants = 0,
  r2 = 0.1, block_size = 128, nthreads = 4)

ct_weights <- clump_threshold(statistics$A, ct_reference,
  p_threshold = 5e-8, r2_threshold = 0.1,
  window_bp = 250000)

ct_prediction <- gscore(ct_weights, test_Glist,
  coding = "standardized", scale_scores = FALSE,
  control = list(threads = 4))
This C+T call is a supported alternative; the displayed scatter and correlations use BayesC weights only. C+T needs the aligned b, seb, p and n fields. Save ct_reference with its LD files for reuse; the clumping resource does not need to be recomputed for each trait.

title: Heritability and genetic correlation with gcorr
text: gcorr works with aligned summary statistics. The convenient ldsc() route uses LD scores and reference metadata already held by a gbase Glist. Other public functions provide GNOVA, SumHer, regional covariance methods, covariance models and Mendelian randomisation when their additional inputs are available. This page uses the three disjoint GWAS cohorts from the shared simulation. Run the overview’s loading block first for statistics, reference_Glist and regions.

ordinary <- ldsc(statistics, reference_Glist,
  what = "rg", block_count = 200L,
  overlap_intercept = 0,
  marginal_intercept = "fixed_one")

title: Heritability and genetic correlation with gcorr
section: Attribute heritability to a marker group
text:
Attribute heritability to a marker group
The first 80 artificial regions form an enriched annotation. Standard stratified LDSC computes an annotation LD-score column; at any marker it includes LD to annotated markers, including LD that crosses the annotation boundary. The residual column covers the remaining marker membership.
enriched_markers <- unlist(regions[1:80], use.names = FALSE)

partitioned <- ldsc(statistics, reference_Glist,
  sets = list(enriched = enriched_markers),
  residual = TRUE, set_model = "stratified",
  what = "rg", block_count = 200L,
  overlap_intercept = 0,
  marginal_intercept = "fixed_one")

subset(partitioned$estimates,
  trait1 == "A" & is.na(trait2) &
    quantity %in% c("h2", "enrichment"))
The trait A rows from this fit show a total h2 of about 0.36, with about 0.267 attributed to the enriched category. enrichment compares a category’s heritability share with its marker share. It is a model-based estimate, not a count of causal variants.

section: Work at regional or covariance level
text:
Work at regional or covariance level
One prepared regional LD object can be reused across methods and trait pairs. The preparation loads the requested regions and verifies their complete eigensystems once in the current R session:
prepared_regions <- gcorr_prepare_regions(reference_Glist,
  regions = regions[1:20])

regional_h2 <- gcorr_hess(statistics$A, prepared_regions,
  maximum_components = 0, minimum_eigenvalue = 0)
regional_h2$estimates
This call illustrates HESS; regional results were not part of the displayed LDSC table. Regional methods require method-specific sample overlap, eigenvalue and inference choices.

title: Association analysis with glma
text: glma scans individual-level genotypes in a Glist. It supports quantitative linear scans, conditional scans, binary logistic scans and two leave-one- chromosome-out (LOCO) background models. Its vegas() function then combines aligned marker evidence within named marker sets using reference LD. This page follows the shared simulation, where each of three traits has a separate 6,000-person GWAS cohort. First run the loading block in that overview to define prefix, Y, simulation, reference_Glist and gene_sets; the snippets below can then be run in order.

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Scan the quantitative traits
The phenotype is named by individual ID, so glma() can match its rows to the selected Glist sample order. A named matrix can scan several traits in the same cohort; this simulation instead uses disjoint cohorts and fits one trait at a time.
library(gbase)
library(glma)

gwas_ids <- list(
  A = sprintf("id%05d", 1:6000),
  B = sprintf("id%05d", 6001:12000),
  C = sprintf("id%05d", 12001:18000)
)

fits <- setNames(vector("list", 3), names(gwas_ids))
for (trait in names(gwas_ids)) {
  study <- gprep(bedfiles = paste0(prefix, ".bed"),
    ids = gwas_ids[[trait]], nthreads = 4)
  phenotype <- setNames(Y[, trait], rownames(Y))
  fits[[trait]] <- glma(phenotype, study,
    method = "linear", threads = 4, block_size = 128)
}

head(fits$A$associations[c("marker", "a1", "a2", "beta", "se",
  "statistic", "p", "status")])
beta is the effect per allele-1 dosage; se and p describe its single-marker test. status distinguishes tested markers from unavailable fits. In this simulated run, large signals were planted at markers including m00050, m00125 and m00175; nearby LD can produce secondary peaks.

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Prepare the shared summary tables
Use gbase::checkStat() to orient the scan results to the LD reference. The driver also supplies chr, pos and allele labels from the same reference metadata before alignment:
metadata <- reference_Glist$sparseLD$marker_metadata
statistics <- lapply(names(fits), function(trait) {
  a <- fits[[trait]]$associations
  raw <- data.frame(
    rsids = a$marker, chr = metadata$chromosome,
    pos = metadata$base_pair_position,
    ea = metadata$allele1, nea = metadata$allele2,
    b = a$beta, seb = a$se, p = a$p,
    n = length(gwas_ids[[trait]])
  )
  checkStat(reference_Glist, raw,
    excludeMAF = NULL, excludeMAFDIFF = NULL, excludeINFO = NULL,
    excludeCGAT = FALSE, excludeINDEL = FALSE, excludeDUPS = TRUE,
    excludeMHC = FALSE, excludeMISS = NULL, excludeHWE = NULL)
})
names(statistics) <- names(fits)
The resulting named list is the common input for gcorr, gbayes, gmap and gene aggregation below.

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Test genes with VEGAS
Each gene is a vector of marker names. vegas() finds them in the Glist and processes all traits while each gene’s LD is available. The saved run used 1,000 artificial genes and a saddlepoint tail calculation.
gene_metadata <- setNames(lapply(names(statistics), function(trait) {
  data.frame(
    set = names(gene_sets),
    sample_size = length(gwas_ids[[trait]]),
    mean_minor_allele_count = vapply(gene_sets, function(markers) {
      p <- simulation$frequencies[match(markers, marker_ids)]
      mean(2 * length(gwas_ids[[trait]]) * pmin(p, 1 - p))
    }, numeric(1))
  )
}), names(statistics))

gene_results <- vegas(statistics, reference_Glist,
  sets = gene_sets, metadata = gene_metadata,
  control = list(tail_method = "saddlepoint"), threads = 4)

head(gene_results$stat$A[c("set", "marker_count", "score",
  "p_value", "p_available")])

title: Association analysis with glma
text:
Other association routes








Question
Public call
Important input or output distinction




Does a marker add signal after a known marker?
glma(..., method = "linear", condition_on = index)
index is a 1-based position in selected Glist marker order.


Is a binary outcome associated?
glma(binary, study, method = "logistic")
Outcome is coded 0/1; beta is a log-odds effect and failures have status.


Is there signal after a polygenic background?
glma(..., method = "infinitesimal_loco")
Produces calibrated score tests with explicit background diagnostics.


Does a selected prior improve the LOCO background?
glma(..., method = "prior_selected_loco")
Records prior selection, refits and effect estimates.



For example, a conditional scan in the same cohort is:
study_A <- gprep(bedfiles = paste0(prefix, ".bed"),
  ids = gwas_ids$A, nthreads = 4)
phenotype_A <- setNames(Y[, "A"], rownames(Y))
lead_index <- match("m00050", unlist(study_A$rsids, use.names = FALSE))
conditional <- glma(phenotype_A, study_A, method = "linear",
  condition_on = lead_index, threads = 4)
head(conditional$associations)
The simulation assigns a separate artificial chromosome label to each 100-marker region. Those labels do not represent real chromosome-scale backgrounds, so this dataset is not a meaningful LOCO example. The full glma guide works through binary, conditional and LOCO examples with a suitable small panel.
Download the top marker associations · download the leading VEGAS genes

title: One genomic dataset, seven R packages
text:
These tutorials follow one connected analysis. gbase prepares a PLINK BED/BIM/FAM panel and a reusable LD reference. The other packages perform association testing, Bayesian regression, genetic correlation, fine-mapping, scoring and gene-level analysis. The pages show actual tables and figures from one seeded simulation, along with the R calls that produced them.
The saved Bayesian stage uses the earlier gbayes() dispatcher and its estimates/weights result contract. It is frozen evidence, not a result from the current six-interface API. The gbayes tutorial introduces the current fitters separately. The original driver, seeds, tables, figures and downstream use of the saved weights remain unchanged.

title: One genomic dataset, seven R packages
text:
The simulated study







Component
Design




Genotypes
20,000 individuals and 50,000 biallelic markers across 500 artificial chromosome labels, one per 100-marker region


Traits
Three quantitative traits, A, B and C


GWAS
Three disjoint groups of 6,000 individuals, one group per trait


LD reference
The first 18,000 individuals; 500 independent 100-marker regions


Prediction
The remaining 2,000 individuals, excluded from GWAS and LD preparation


Gene sets
1,000 artificial genes, two nonoverlapping marker sets per region


Pathways
Three gene collections labelled enriched, background and mixed



The simulation uses deliberately strong signals and simple independent LD regions to make the outputs readable. Effect sizes, p-values and run times are properties of this one simulated dataset. They do not establish calibration or performance on real cohorts.

title: One genomic dataset, seven R packages
text:
Reproduce the complete run
Install the seven source packages and gsim. Download the complete R driver, place it in a new working directory and run:
Rscript run.R --threads=4
The driver creates the PLINK files and phenotypes, computes LD once, and runs all seven package workflows. It saves stage objects under build/benchmarks/genomic-20k-50k-4cores/ and small result tables under benchmarks/genomic_20k_50k/results/. This is a substantial simulation; allow disk space for the packed genotypes and LD files. The tutorial plots and tables were generated from its saved four-thread stage objects. Package installation and compilation are outside the driver.
To inspect a saved stage without repeating the analysis:
cache <- file.path("build", "benchmarks", "genomic-20k-50k-4cores")
stage <- function(name) {
  readRDS(file.path(cache, paste0(name, ".rds")))$value
}

reference_Glist <- stage("sparse_ld_and_scores")
statistics <- stage("gwas_and_checkstat")$statistics
bayes_fit <- stage("bayesian_regression")

base_cache <- file.path("build", "benchmarks", "genomic-20k-50k")
simulation_cache <- if (file.exists(file.path(cache, "data_simulation.rds")))
  cache else base_cache
simulation <- readRDS(file.path(simulation_cache,
  "data_simulation.rds"))$value
prefix <- simulation$prefix
Y <- simulation$simulation$Y
rownames(Y) <- sprintf("id%05d", seq_len(nrow(Y)))

marker_ids <- sprintf("m%05d", 1:50000)
regions <- split(marker_ids,
  rep(sprintf("region%03d", 1:500), each = 100))
gene_sets <- list()
for (r in seq_along(regions)) {
  cut <- 20L + r %% 60L
  gene_sets[[sprintf("gene%04d", 2L * r - 1L)]] <- regions[[r]][1:cut]
  gene_sets[[sprintf("gene%04d", 2L * r)]] <- regions[[r]][(cut + 1L):100L]
}
regions and gene_sets are named marker vectors; pathway_sets in the gsea tutorial contains gene names. These are different units: a gene set identifies markers in the Glist, while a pathway identifies genes already summarized by VEGAS. In an ordinary study, replace prefix, Y, the sample IDs and set definitions with your own data.

title: One simulated dataset across six genomic modules
text:
Completed example and supported recipes



All six modules ran on the same simulated dataset. Pathway analyses use the documented saddlepoint route, which returned all requested gene statistics. The connected 50K-marker BayesC and BayesR fits use declared fixed parameter values. Parameter learning is checked in a separate matched-reference study; see the qualification record for its settings and numerical scope.

title: One simulated dataset across six genomic modules
text:
What this example demonstrates
Start with a simulated population, run GWAS, then reuse its summary statistics and LD for Bayesian regression, genetic correlation, fine-mapping, scoring and pathway analysis. Genetic correlation uses the gcorr R package; the other calls use their current task-package or umbrella interfaces.
This connected example covers glma, gbayes, gcorr, gmap, gscore and gsea. It checks selected calculations and demonstrates representative methods at this scale. It does not establish calibration of every supported method or option. The library-specific qualification pages report a separate fixed set of ten simulations using the same design.

title: One simulated dataset across six genomic modules
text:
One population, explicit sample groups







Setting
Value




Individuals / markers
10,000 / 50,000


Traits
Three continuous traits: A, B and C


Target heritabilities
0.30, 0.40 and 0.35


Genomic layout
500 independent artificial regions of 100 markers


GWAS samples
Three disjoint groups of 3,000; one per trait


Scoring test sample
1,000 individuals excluded from GWAS and LD preparation


LD reference
The pooled 9,000 GWAS individuals


Annotation
1,000 artificial genes; enriched, background and mixed pathway sets


Replicates
One detailed example and an earlier set of ten fixed simulations



The genotype generator has known within-region population LD. It writes one marker at a time to a packed BED file. gsim then generates phenotypes from explicit effects, using bounded reads from the prepared Glist. Neither a full genotype matrix nor a 50,000-by-50,000 LD matrix is created.
The LD reference retains all within-region correlations and treats regions as independent. It shares individuals with the GWAS samples; it is not an independent external panel. Summary-based fits therefore use a pooled-LD approximation to each study’s cross-products. The artificial chromosomes, genes and pathways have no biological interpretation.

title: One simulated dataset across six genomic modules
text:
The connected workflow
These excerpts show the current supported model calls. The retained results use the sample selection, truth construction and effect units defined in the shared design.
# Association: one selected GWAS group and its phenotype.
association <- glma::glma(y, Glist, method = "linear", threads = 1)

# Prepare aligned summaries separately from fitting.
prepared <- gbase::checkStat(stat, Glist)

# Genome-wide genetic correlation from prepared public inputs.
correlation <- gcorr::gcorr(statistics, ld_scores = ld_scores,
                            blocks = blocks, method = "ldsc",
                            overlap_intercept = 0)

# Bayesian regression: fixed declared parameters, four posterior chains.
bayesian <- gbayes::gbayes(statistics$A, Glist, method = "bayesc",
                  prior = prior, control = control)

# Regional mapping after explicit OLS sufficient-statistic preparation.
mapping_stat <- gmap::gmap_stat(statistics, LD_Glist,
                               phenotype_variance = phenotype_variance)
mapping <- gmap::gmap(mapping_stat, LD_Glist, regions = regions,
                method = "multi_effect", prior = prior, control = control)

# Apply allele-labelled weights with explicit coding to held-out individuals.
prediction <- gscore::gscore(weights, test_Glist)

# Aggregate marker evidence, then analyse pathways of genes.
evidence <- glma::vegas(statistics, LD_Glist, sets = genes,
                 metadata = metadata,
                 control = list(tail_method = "saddlepoint"))
gene_stat <- lapply(evidence$stat, function(x) transform(x, gene = set))
pathways <- gsea(gene_stat, pathway_sets, method = "preranked")
The prior and control placeholders differ between Bayesian regression and regional mapping. They are explicit in the script. No universal prior scale is assumed across methods.

title: One simulated dataset across six genomic modules
text:
Results

GWAS: which signals were detected?



Manhattan plots for three linear GWAS scans. Orange triangles mark variants with a nonzero simulated effect for the plotted trait; grey points have zero direct effect. The first 80 enriched artificial regions have a pale blue background.


Each panel shows all 50,000 markers from glma, with a dashed reference line at \(p=0.05/50{,}000=10^{-6}\) for that trait. Positions follow the 500 artificial regions, not human chromosomes. A causal variant need not reach this threshold: most effects are small and each GWAS uses 3,000 individuals. Conversely, a grey marker can be associated through LD with a causal variant; grey significant points are not automatically false-positive associations.
The association summary reports the numbers of causal markers and threshold crossings separately. Each trait has 984 causal markers; 985 distinct markers affect at least one trait. There are three threshold crossings for A, three for B and two for C; all are directly causal in this draw. The 15 direct comparisons with R ordinary least squares remain the independent numerical check of these scans.



Estimated versus true marginal GWAS effects for the three traits, on the raw-dosage scale.


The target here is the marginal effect, \(R_{\mathrm{pop}}B\), which includes LD with other causal variants. The diagonal represents equality. Direct causal effects \(B\) are a different target and are used for the Bayesian comparison below.


Heritability and genetic correlation



Heritability estimates with jackknife uncertainty and true versus estimated genetic correlations. Dashed lines show population truth; LDSC+ann includes the enriched annotation.





Analysis

h2 C




Realized population truth

0.347


Baseline LDSC

The baseline fits underestimate heritability in this draw. Effects are concentrated in the first 80 regions, which also occupy the lower-LD end of the generator. The annotation-aware model represents this heterogeneity and gives estimates closer to truth here. This contrast is about model assumptions; it does not rank software implementations or establish bias across repetitions. SumHer uses ordinary LD scores as tagging weights and one baseline architecture component, explaining its near-identical results to baseline LDSC in this setup.
The uncertainty bars show estimate plus/minus 1.96 jackknife standard errors, using the 500 regions as blocks. They are illustrative normal approximations, not an interval-coverage evaluation. Correlations are imprecise with 3,000 individuals per trait: baseline LDSC gives B/C rg = 1.095 (SE 0.331), and annotation-aware LDSC gives 1.052 (SE 0.228), versus truth 0.726. These out-of-range estimates remain visible; they are not clipped to one.
HESS, SUPERGNOVA and LAVA also returned the requested covariances in 20 predetermined regions. HESS standard errors were unavailable for 40 of the 60 trait-pair/region results because its plug-in genetic/residual matrices did not meet the positive-semidefinite requirement. SUPERGNOVA returned all 60 standard errors. The exercised LAVA covariance route does not return standard errors. Finite point estimates do not remove those uncertainty limitations.



Regional genetic covariance estimates against population truth, and LDSC annotation heritabilities.


Each regional panel contains 20 predetermined regions and three trait pairs. Covariances use phenotype-standardized units. The annotation panel compares the enriched and background contributions to total heritability; the categories are disjoint and exhaustive. Points for regions and traits from the same dataset are dependent. Download the labelled truth comparisons.


Bayesian regression: a supported reference-LD recipe
The scalar BayesC and BayesR workflow was qualified separately across five simulations. Each fit used standardized summary statistics from 3,000 individuals and sparse LD from an independent, matched reference of 9,000 individuals. LD retained a 1,000-marker window with \(r^2=0.001\).
The fit learns residual variance, marker-effect variance and mixture probabilities. The reference-LD residual update is
\[
V_e^{\mathrm{work}}=V_e+0.9V_g,
\qquad
V_g=b^{\mathsf T}R_{\mathrm{ref}}b.
\]
Priors specify an expected nonzero proportion of 0.02. BayesR uses variance multipliers \((0,0.01,0.1,1)\) and active-component proportions \((0.012,0.006,0.002)\). Mixture probabilities use an explicit Dirichlet strength of 5,000. Four chains use 500 burn-in sweeps and retain 700 BayesC or 5,000 BayesR sweeps.
fit <- gbayes::gbayes(statistics, Glist, method = "bayesc", trait = "trait",
  prior = prior,
  control = list(
    residual_policy = "reference_ld",
    residual_adjustment = 0.9,
    estimate_effect_variance = TRUE,
    estimate_weights = TRUE,
    burnin = 500,
    sampling_sweeps = 700,
    seeds = c(101, 102, 103, 104),
    threads = 4
  ),
  posterior = list(reference = LD_Glist,
                   phenotype_variance = c(trait = 1)))

BayesC and BayesR reference-heritability recovery, marker-effect recovery and genetic-score recovery across five simulations.


The exact settings, acceptance criteria and downloadable results are in the qualification record.


Regional mapping and colocalisation
The two regions were selected before fitting. Region 1 contains a shared causal variant; region 2 contains distinct causal variants for A and B. The fitted multi-effect model uses one component, matching this deliberately simple regional truth. ABF colocalisation uses the same complete regional summaries from disjoint samples and its at-most-one-causal-variant-per-trait assumption.
All four regional fits converged. ABF H4 is effectively one for the shared signal, and H3 is effectively one for the distinct signals in this draw. The credible-set summary records set size, completeness, LD checks and whether the known causal marker is included for each region and trait. All four sets contain one marker, the true causal variant, and pass the recorded LD checks.



Regional inclusion probabilities and shared versus distinct causal signals. H3 denotes distinct causal variants and H4 a shared variant.




Pathways
glma::vegas() aggregates marker evidence into 1,000 artificial genes, processing each gene region once for all three traits. The supported workflow uses the saddlepoint tail calculation for all 3,000 gene-by-trait statistics. Every statistic was returned in the detailed example, with no moment-matching fallback.
The retained analysis artifacts also compare ORA, preranked GSEA, competitive regression, the bounded MAGMA route and a scalar Bayesian pathway model. The current direct VEGAS handoff covers ORA and preranked analysis; the covariance- based methods require a separately prepared gene covariance. The enriched pathway covers the simulated enriched regions; the mixed pathway samples genes across the genome, and the background pathway covers regions with lower causal-marker probability. Background does not mean zero genetic effects.



Pathway evidence from the bounded MAGMA route for three traits, and Bayesian pathway inclusion probabilities for trait A. Gene p-values use the saddlepoint approximation.


The enriched pathway has nominal bounded-MAGMA p-values of 0.0086, 0.00077 and 0.0018 for A, B and C. Its Bayesian PIP for trait A is 0.9995, compared with 0.0705 for background and 0.0315 for mixed. ORA, preranked GSEA and competitive regression also show the strongest evidence for the enriched set in this draw. Pathway p-values here are unadjusted; the different methods use different null hypotheses, so their magnitudes do not rank method quality.
P-values and posterior inclusion probabilities answer different questions and are shown on separate scales. One simulated dataset cannot establish pathway false-discovery control, credible-set coverage or comparative power.



Four frequentist pathway summaries for trait A alongside the separate Bayesian PIP scale.

title: One simulated dataset across six genomic modules
text:
Earlier connected results across simulations
Ten datasets repeat the same 10,000-individual, 50,000-marker design. Genotypes, marker effects and phenotypes are regenerated each time. The regions, annotations, sample split, priors, chain lengths and working-noise scale are fixed before these runs. The detailed example above is excluded from the aggregate. No seeds are selected or replaced based on their results.
All ten runs completed. Mean population heritability for trait A was 0.300. These repetitions provide the connected checks for correlation, regional mapping and pathway analysis. The separate five-repetition Bayesian qualification above is the maintained evidence for the supported parameter-learning recipe.
Baseline LDSC, GNOVA and SumHer underestimate heritability on average in this nonuniform architecture. Annotation-aware LDSC changes the mean estimates to 0.310, 0.439 and 0.394 for A, B and C, against mean truths of 0.300, 0.398 and 0.349. Accounting for enrichment reduces systematic underestimation here but can overshoot; it does not improve every trait’s RMSE.



Heritability estimation errors by trait and method, and mean genetic-correlation error across three trait pairs for each simulation.


Each point represents one simulation; short black lines show means. Zero is the estimation-error target. Genetic-correlation errors are first averaged over the three pairs within a simulation, so the pairs are not presented as independent repetitions. Download accuracy summaries.
All 40 component credible sets contain their simulated causal variant; each set contains one marker. Colocalisation assigns probability effectively one to the appropriate shared- or distinct-causal hypothesis in these easy regions. The mean Bayesian pathway PIP is 0.894 for the enriched set, compared with 0.054 for background and 0.038 for mixed. The downloadable tables retain variation across datasets and the other pathway methods.
Across the ten runs, HESS supplies standard errors for 189 of 600 regional covariances, SUPERGNOVA for 600 of 600, and the exercised LAVA route for none. Six annotation-category correlations are undefined because an estimated component heritability is nonpositive. The supported saddlepoint gene-tail route returns all 30,000 gene/trait p-values; 11 use its recorded moment-matching fallback. These availability and fallback flags remain in the downloadable tables.
With only ten simulations, one outcome changes a proportion by ten percentage points. These results are descriptive checks under one non-null design, not precise calibration, a null false-positive assessment or general method rankings. The run status lists every planned seed and its outcome. The linked aggregate tables retain the labelled truth comparisons and numerical availability used above.
