Compute h2 = Vg/(Vg+Ve) at each posterior draw when reporting model-scale heritability. The variance of posterior mean predictions differs from mean posterior Vg.
Each fit$chains[[k]]$individual_bed contains vb_trace, ve_trace, vg_trace, vle_trace, vld_trace, weight_trace, and log-CPO. BED traces include burn-in and every sweep; variance means average all post-burnin sweeps independently of effect thinning. Top-level traces average chains at corresponding sweeps; use per-chain traces for posterior uncertainty and diagnostics. Top-level final_* values average endpoints, not posterior draws. Per-chain scheduling counters are scheduled_marker_updates and scheduled_full_sweeps. Log-CPO uses retained training draws and is distinct from held-out prediction accuracy.
The gact individual-level example shows sparse-trait BayesC/BayesR with training-only preparation and held-out scoring. Its advanced study preserves the original short-run sparse/polygenic comparison and records quantity-specific prediction, variance and mixture diagnostics.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Annotation-informed block-eigen regression
Use sbayes(method = "bayesRC", algorithm = "mcmc", representation = "block_eigen") for a single checked summary trait. Prepare sparse LD and verify the block partition first. This example takes a prepared Glist, its aligned stat table, and a block_table with the first and last marker of each block.
Glist <- gbase::define_ld_blocks(
  Glist,
  data.frame(
    block_id = block_table$block_id,
    first_marker = block_table$first_marker,
    last_marker = block_table$last_marker
  )
)

fitted_markers <- Glist$sparseLD$marker_metadata$marker_id
intercept_design <- matrix(numeric(), nrow = length(fitted_markers), ncol = 0,
                           dimnames = list(fitted_markers, NULL))

rc <- gbayes::sbayes(
  stat, Glist = Glist, method = "bayesRC", algorithm = "mcmc",
  representation = "block_eigen", nit = 1000, nburn = 500, seed = 1,
  annotation = list(component = list(design = intercept_design))
)
coef(rc)
For an annotated fit, use a numeric design with marker IDs as row names and annotation names as column names. Pass it in exact fitted-marker order. The following call shows the legacy gbayes() spelling and controls.
component_design <- as.matrix(annotation_table[fitted_markers, , drop = FALSE])

fit <- gbayes::gbayes(
  stat,
  Glist,
  method = "sbayesrc",
  annotation = list(component = list(design = component_design)),
  control = list(
    eigen_control = list(retained_positive_mass = 0.995),
    block_eigen_residual = list(mode = "all_mix")
  )
)
The block residual update is defined on retained response coordinates: each block uses the squared retained response norm and retained rank. This is an explicit reduced-space likelihood and is not an assertion of identical normalization to GCTB or another SBayesRC implementation. Set retained_positive_mass = 1 to retain every positive eigenvalue. On a full-rank block-diagonal reference with fixed block residuals, this route reduces to the ordinary bayesr sufficient-statistic fit.
fit$diagnostics$block_eigen records block loads, eigensystem decompositions, retained ranks, discarded positive mass and peak dense-block memory. The factors remain native working state; the returned fit is serializable and continuation restores sampler state without serializing dense eigenvectors.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Additional summary engines
The same dispatcher provides focused single-trait summary methods:
point_normal <- gbayes::gbayes(stat, Glist, method = "point_normal")
shrinkage <- gbayes::gbayes(stat, Glist, method = "continuous_shrinkage")
variational <- gbayes::gbayes(stat, Glist, method = "variational")
mixture <- gbayes::gbayes(stat, Glist, method = "mixture_variational")
These retain method-specific controls and outputs. They do not silently inherit all BayesC/BayesR sampling, learning or annotation features.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Multivariate and study-specific fits
Named phenotype columns fit a joint individual-level model:
joint <- gbayes::gbayes(
  data = phenotypes,
  Glist = Glist,
  trait = c("height", "weight"),
  method = "bayesr",
  prior = list(
    effect_covariance = effect_covariance,
    residual_covariance = residual_covariance
  )
)
For summaries, stat may be a named trait list with one shared Glist sparse-LD reference, or a named study list paired with a named list of study-specific Glist references. Study identity remains distinct from trait identity. Local LD operators are preserved; no synthetic union LD matrix is created. Independent and shared-LD sampling assumptions are declared through sampling.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Annotations and continuation
BayesC supports inclusion and variance annotations. BayesR supports component and variance annotations. BayesS scaling uses the same checked variance-model boundary. Multivariate fits additionally support pattern annotations.
Pass a previous fit, or its $continuation member, back through continuation. The model-defining inputs, marker order, prior, annotations and transition controls must remain identical. Continuation restores native chain states and performs zero additional burn-in.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Posterior genetic quantities
An explicitly aligned sparse-LD Glist can define the reference population for posterior genetic covariance and correlation. Heritability additionally requires an explicit phenotype variance; no denominator is inferred.
groups <- setNames(marker_groups, fitted_marker_ids)

fit <- gbayes::gbayes(
  stat,
  Glist,
  method = "bayesr",
  posterior = list(
    reference = Glist,
    partition = groups,
    phenotype_variance = c(height = 1)
  )
)
fit$quantities separates genetic covariance/correlation, heritability, reporting partitions, predictions and per-chain quantities. Partition groups are reporting objects and are independent of covariance-group priors.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Predict selected individuals with uncertainty
Posterior score uncertainty uses an existing target Glist. Its active markers may be a strict subset of fitted markers and may span any number of BED components. Components and markers retain Glist order; requested individuals retain the supplied ID order.
target <- gbase::gprep(
  bedfiles = c("target-chr1.bed", "target-chr2.bed"),
  ids = selected_ids,
  rsids = selected_markers
)

fit <- gbayes::gbayes(
  stat,
  Glist,
  method = "bayesr",
  posterior = list(
    prediction = list(
      Glist = target,
      ids = selected_ids,
      target_set = "validation",
      retain_draws = FALSE
    )
  )
)
The package validates exact fitted-marker availability, coordinates and counted alleles. Component projections use the public gscore::summary interface and are summed into one score. Coverage records fitted, used and omitted markers and the number of active BED components. Reported score covariance is posterior effect uncertainty, not phenotype predictive variance.
Scalar individual-level BED fits also include genetic_variance (VG), vle, vld and h2 directly in fit$posterior. These rows use the original per-chain draws from every post-burn-in sweep, independently of effect thinning. They report posterior mean, SD, credible intervals, R-hat, ESS and Monte Carlo error using the native summary routines. h2 is summarized from each draw’s VG / (VG + VE). Existing effect_variance (VB) and residual_variance (VE) rows retain their effect-thinned parameter draws. Continuation summaries cover the new batch.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Apply portable posterior weights
When genotype coding is identified, fit$weights is directly consumable by gscore(). This includes block-eigen SBayesRC fits; scoring uses the portable posterior mean weights and does not need the fitted eigensystems:
prediction <- gscore::gscore(fit$weights, target)
For pathway or other marker-set scores, pass a uniquely named list of marker IDs. The target Glist resolves their BED locations and the native scorer handles overlapping or cross-file sets in one pass:
prediction <- gscore::gscore(
  fit$weights, target,
  sets = marker_sets,
  include_total = TRUE
)
Weight learning remains with gbayes; score application remains with gscore. Raw association effects are not automatically Bayesian weights, and conventional clumping and thresholding remains gscore::clump_threshold().

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Regional interpretation
gmap::gmap_bed() can consume a saved individual-BED gbayes_fit together with sparse LD prepared from the same Glist samples and physical marker selection:
mapped <- gmap::gmap_bed(fit, Glist, regions)
This interprets global marginal PIPs by region without refitting. Marginal-PIP groups are not component credible sets.
gmap_bed() is specific to individual-BED fits because it verifies the fitted sample selection, BED files and in-sample LD identity. A summary SBayesRC fit remains a whole-reference gbayes_fit; regional BayesC/BayesR or multi-effect models are fitted through gmap() with their own explicit regional likelihood.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Qualification status
The package passed its complete source check with no errors or warnings, focused deterministic tests, an exact Windows DLL-closure and SHA-256 audit, and clean binary loading. The two source-check NOTEs concern installed DLL size and the conservative compiled-code scan of the bundled native DLL closure.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Simple individual-level defaults
Scalar individual BED fits can omit prior: gbayes initializes half the observed phenotype variance as residual variance and half as nominal genetic variance. BayesC starts with inclusion probability .001; BayesR starts with weights (.95,.02,.02,.01) and multipliers (0,.01,.1,1). The marker-scale variance is VG/(m times mixture variance mass), using standardized genotype coding. This is a starting heuristic, not an empirical estimate of heritability or causal count. Variance learning uses df=4 and scale=initial variance/2; mixture learning uses unit Beta/Dirichlet concentrations. These learning priors are separate from initial mixture probabilities. Automatic runs use 1000 burn-in and 2000 sampling sweeps, thinning 5, seeds 1 and 2, one thread, retained diagnostics and full sweeps. Control overrides remain available. Explicit nonempty priors retain the existing opt-in learning controls and require proper learning priors when enabled. Scalar BED responses are centred internally without rescaling; the default likelihood dimension is n-1. The phenotype mean is recorded in provenance. An omitted prior during continuation reuses the saved prior and transition controls. Inspect $prior, $control and $posterior; default sweep counts and the R-hat/ESS screening message do not guarantee convergence.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Exact cross-product BayesC and BayesR
Development only — gbayes 0.1.6. This entry point is not included in the public gbayes 0.1.1 download; it requires a compatible development installation.
For general feature regression, use the existing native sampler without a Glist:
X <- scale(cbind(feature1 = sin(1:30), feature2 = cos(1:30)))
y <- as.vector(scale(sin((1:30)/3)))
fit <- gbayes::blr(crossprod(X), drop(crossprod(X, y)),
                  yy = sum(y^2), n = length(y),
                  method = "bayesR", nit = 5000, nburn = 1000, seed = 10)
coef(fit)

# Multiple responses, with labelled residual and latent marker covariances:
joint <- gbayes::mblr(XX, Xy_matrix, yy=YY, n=n,
                      vb=Vb, ve=Ve, pi=pattern_weights)
gbayes::extract(joint, "effects", chain=1)
The caller prepares consistently centered and scaled XX, Xy and yy, as in the example above; blr() does not transform supplied statistics. The caller supplies matching unique feature labels for XX and Xy; joint Xy also has ordered trait labels, and yy is labelled in that trait order. Scaled eigensystem and Schur-complement checks validate the full PSD/rank contract, including singular XX and consistent Xy. Coefficients and variances retain supplied feature units.
The direct controls and defaults match the other new fitters: nit=1000, nburn=500, nthin=1, nchains=2, ncores=1, seed=1. Retain completed post-burn multiples of nthin and finish all transitions. Scalar pi is the BayesC active probability or complete BayesR mixture vector. With d the declared likelihood dimension, defaults use vb=h2yy/(trace(XX)mixture mass) and ve=(1-h2)*yy/d. This respects arbitrary feature scaling. Joint vb/ve and activity-pattern pi are explicit, with learning off by default. Proper priors enable optional covariance/weight learning; exact same-scale yy is required for residual learning. There is no reference-LD adjustment. C/R reference-LD input uses sbayes/msbayes.
The default declares already centered inputs with likelihood dimension n-1. Other projections require control$likelihoodDimension and coding=list(preprocessing=“residualized”). Coding can additionally store feature-named centers/scales and trait-named intercepts used to prepare the statistics. Dense feature prediction reuses those transformations; phenotype prediction requires intercepts and centered preprocessing. Without saved coding, prediction is unavailable. Neither training means nor nuisance coefficients are inferred from cross-products. Common fits retain labelled axes, per-chain access and actual checkpoint diagnostics. Full coefficient draws and annotation are unavailable here. This replaces the previous scalar blr signature without compatibility aliases.
Exact C/R cross-product fits support native checkpoint continuation:
saveRDS(fit, "cross-product-fit.rds")
more <- gbayes::blr(crossprod(X), drop(crossprod(X, y)), n=length(y),
                     nit=500, continuation=readRDS("cross-product-fit.rds"))
# Use mblr for a saved joint checkpoint. Omitted yy/coding reuse saved values.
gbayes::diagnostics(more)$execution$continuation
Supply XX, Xy and n again; ordered labels, values, scatter, supplied units, coding and likelihood dimension must remain identical. Omitted method, priors, learning flags, thinning, chains and seeds inherit the original model. Omitted yy/coding inherit the checked saved values; explicit NULL is a new value and must match. Final learned parameters remain private checkpoint state.
Nit adds transitions without repeated burn-in. Global thinning survives remainder and repeated splits, including a short segment containing the next retained draw. At most one discarded advance precedes the retained native call. Resumed fits summarize only newly retained draws and remain resumable. Worker count, diagnostic capture, probability and memory budgets may change; model and chain identities stay fixed. Native states/RNG and parameter traces replay uninterrupted runs.
Checked statistics/coding and the bundled gbayes/gbase runtime are fingerprinted before/after fitting; the declared gbase dependency is initialized even for pure cross-products. SaveRDS/readRDS needs no live handles. Current qualification is bundled Windows builds; other layouts report restartState unavailable. Existing feature prediction still requires saved transforms, and phenotype prediction requires centered preprocessing/intercepts. Full effect draws and CM continuation remain unavailable. See the cross-product continuation contract.
Cross-product C/R can also capture posterior quantities:
captured <- gbayes::blr(XX, Xy, yy=yy, n=n, method="bayesR",
  posterior=list(reference="training", partition=feature_groups,
    phenotypeVariance=c(response=outcome_variance)))
gbayes::extract(captured, "geneticCovariance")
gbayes::extract(captured, "partitionCovariance", state="retained")
summary(captured, quantity="quantities")
Use mblr with trait-named denominators for joint models. Reference=“training” selects XX/d with the declared likelihood dimension d; the reported draw-wise component covariance is B’ XX B / d. Centered inputs default to d=n-1. Residualized inputs give a projection-normalized model quantity, not raw population covariance. Feature units remain supplied units; no LD conversion, alleles, new centering or intercept terms are inferred. The fitting operator is shared, with a reporting identity tied to its ordered features, values and divisor.
The common genetic quantity names denote this linear-predictor component. Generic features alone do not justify genetic interpretation. The common heritability output is an explicit-denominator variance ratio, requiring compatible phenotypeVariance; yy is not used to infer that denominator. Genetic interpretation requires an appropriate genetic feature model and units.
Partition labels are disjoint and named in fitted feature order. Partition-only requests report activity; with reference=“training”, full group/trait covariance retains cross-group terms and is not an additive heritability allocation. Correlation moments retain positive-variance conditioning counts. Per-chain moments and pooled native quantity intervals/diagnostics remain separate from parameter summaries. Traces follow retainDiagnostics; moments remain when traces are disabled. Capture is per call, including continuation, and covers only newly retained draws. States/RNG and parameter traces are unchanged. Managed capture budgets and identity checks apply. Full effect draws, per-chain quantity intervals and posterior score capture remain unavailable. Ordinary predict() retains its saved-coding contract. See the cross-product capture contract.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Joint summary IBSS
Development gbayes 0.1.9 exposes native mvSuSiE and MultiSuSiE through msbayes() with algorithm="ibss". These engines do not need the gmap R package. Select one bounded region in Glist or control$markers; full LD is reused or prepared through gbase. A call fits one supplied marker domain; genome-wide region orchestration and set interpretation remain separate.
mv <- gbayes::msbayes(stat, Glist, method="mvsusie", algorithm="ibss",
  sampling=list(dependence="shared_ld"),
  prior=list(covariance=templates), pi=template_weights,
  vb=.2, ve=sampling_covariance, control=list(effects=10))

mp <- gbayes::msbayes(stat, refs, method="multisusie", algorithm="ibss",
  sampling=list(dependence="independent",
    reference=c(EUR="european", AFR="african"),
    phenotype_variance=c(EUR=1, AFR=1)),
  vb=effect_covariance, ve=c(EUR=1, AFR=1), control=list(effects=10))

gbayes::fit_contract(mv)
gbayes::extract(mv,"pips")
gbayes::extract(mp,"anyPip")
gbayes::extract(mp,"componentAssignments")
gbayes::diagnostics(mp)$ibss
mvSuSiE uses one shared Glist, complete common markers and N, and one study per trait. The optional study-named trait mapping is one-to-one. ve is fixed SPD sampling covariance; vb is a nonnegative component scale. The labelled PSD dictionary in prior$covariance may contain singular/private/shared templates. pi supplies template weights. updateB and updatePi default TRUE. Effects use the standardized b/sqrt(n*seb2+b2) convention. Trait PIPs, any-trait assignments and same-marker pair activity retain distinct meanings.
MultiSuSiE treats every study as its own effect axis and requires independent samples, including when studies reuse an LD reference. Named reference catalogs can be reordered; sampling$reference maps study names to them. Observed marker subsets, ordering and N may differ. Effect covariance vb is PSD and its correlation shapes remain fixed. Effect and residual learning default off.
Its checked OLS inputs retain supplied score/information or reconstruct information=(n-1)vy/((n-2)seb2+b2), score=b*information. Reconstruction assumes intercept-only OLS/conventional SE for continuous outcomes. Supply outcome variance via sampling$phenotype_variance or prepared metadata; inferred beta/SE/N initialization is recorded separately and is not sufficient for residual learning. Set sampling$in_sample_ld=TRUE and provide genuine variance for that option. prior$markerWeights is fixed for both engines.
Use nit as the maximum sweeps (when omitted: 500 for mvSuSiE, 200 for MultiSuSiE). Explicit MCMC controls, continuation and posterior capture are rejected. IBSS results retain no sampled chains. MultiSuSiE exposes union anyPip and leaves trait pips unavailable. Objective decreases and iteration exhaustion remain visible; returned residual proposals may differ from the scale actually used for posterior moments. Neither a converged coordinate fit nor a union PIP establishes sharing calibration. See help("summaryIBSS", package="gbayes") for all controls and limits.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Fixed BayesC active-slab means
Keep method="bayesC" and supply marker-named prior$slabMean. The spike is zero; only the active normal slab moves. Supply explicit scalar pi, vb and ve, all fixed. Individual means use original phenotype per saved HWE dosage scale; summary means use standardized phenotype/genotype and must already match the reference counted allele.


Code
m <- setNames(prior_means, fitted_markers)
fit <- bayes(training, Glist, trait="trait", method="bayesC", algorithm="mcmc",
  pi=.1, vb=.02, ve=1, prior=list(slabMean=m),
  nit=1000, nburn=500, nchains=2, seed=42)
summary_fit <- sbayes(stat, LD, method="bayesC", algorithm="vbayes",
  pi=.1, vb=.02, ve=1, prior=list(slabMean=summary_scale_means),
  nit=1000, control=list(tolerance=1e-8))


VB uses a whole-panel product approximation with no MCMC controls. Its fixed point does not establish calibration under LD. Neither route enables joint fitting, marker-prior learning, capture, continuation or gmap conversion. Development gbayes 0.1.16 supports optional exact MCMC residual learning below. Ordinary BayesC MCMC without slabMean or marker probability/variance fields retains its defaults. See the full contract and tools/examples/gbayes/informed-bayesc.R for a runnable saved-input example.

Marker-specific BayesC probabilities and slab variances
Use named prior$markerInclusionProbability instead of scalar pi and/or named prior$markerSlabVariance instead of scalar vb. Each vector covers every fitted marker exactly once. Slab variances are positive absolute variances on the fitted effect scale; probabilities are active probabilities strictly inside (0,1). Scalar and marker forms of the same parameter are mutually exclusive. Keep ve explicit and fixed; optional slabMean defaults to zero.


Code
fit <- sbayes(stat, LD, method="bayesC", algorithm="vbayes", ve=1,
  prior=list(markerInclusionProbability=marker_pi,
             markerSlabVariance=marker_variance,
             slabMean=summary_scale_means))
# The same prior fields work in individual bayes and with algorithm="mcmc".


The existing units, whole-panel VB approximation, fixed-prior restrictions and save/reload/scoring handoff apply. Fixed marker priors remain in input$prior; no artificial global mixture-weight or variance-scale estimate is reported.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Scalar BayesC and BayesR annotations
Use gbayes 0.1.16 for these calls. Designs and supplied frequencies use exact fitted-marker order.


Code
fit_c <- bayes(training, Glist, trait="y", method="bayesC", algorithm="mcmc",
  pi=.1, vb=.02, ve=1, updateB=FALSE, updateE=FALSE, updatePi=FALSE,
  annotation=list(inclusion=list(design=A, learn=TRUE),
                  bayess=list(allele_frequency=af, initial_s=-.5)))
fit_r <- sbayes(stat, LD, method="bayesR", algorithm="mcmc",
  pi=c(.7,.2,.1), gamma=c(0,.1,1), vb=.02, ve=1,
  updateB=FALSE, updateE=FALSE, updatePi=TRUE,
  annotation=list(component=list(design=A), variance=list(design=B)))
extract(fit_c, "annotationCoefficients")
extract(fit_c, "annotationCoefficients", state="retained", chain="chain1")
extract(fit_c, "varianceAnnotation")


Baseline pi learning and BayesC inclusion-slope learning are distinct. BayesR component learning replaces its global weight update. The MAF coefficient is an exponent on fitted-scale variance; no raw-dosage BayesS conversion is inferred. Marker prior probabilities and posterior PIPs remain separate quantities. Capture, continuation, joint C/R annotations and saved mapping remain gated. See the source contract.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Exact residual learning
Set updateE = TRUE in informed scalar BayesC MCMC or independent-provider joint BayesC/BayesR MCMC to learn exact residual variances.
For informed bayes, centered outcomes supply y’y and dimension n-1. For informed sbayes, declare control=list(normalization=list(response_ss=yy, likelihood_dimension=d,in_sample_ld=TRUE)). Keep marker means, probabilities and slab variances fixed. ve is the initial residual variance. VB remains fixed.
For msbayes C/R, declare sampling=list(dependence=“independent”, residual_variance=initial, response_sum_squares=yy, likelihood_dimension=d, in_sample_ld=TRUE), with all three vectors named in provider order. Use existing vb and pattern pi, updateE=TRUE, optional nue and prior$veScale. nue defaults to 4; veScale is a scaled-inverse-chi-square scale, defaulting to a prior mean at the initial variance. Provider residual means are in extract(fit,“parameters”) under provider_residual_variance; retained parameters and terminal scales retain separate provider labels even when several studies map to one trait.
Exact summary learning requires compatible in-sample y’y, scores, full LD and common N within each provider, equal to its LD sample count. External/reference LD, overlap, variable marker N and truncated LD are not admitted. Data provenance and independence remain caller assertions. These extensions do not expose capture, annotations, continuation or saved gmap conversion. See the design contract, installed ?exact_residual_learning, and tools/examples/gbayes/exact-residual.R.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Population shrinkage
Use msbayes with continuous_shrinkage and mcmc for PRS-CSx, JointPRS reference and Panther reference fits. Keep population names in stat and use one common phenotype label in trait:


Code
fit <- msbayes(list(EUR=eur, EAS=eas), list(EUR=ld_eur, EAS=ld_eas),
  trait="height", sampling=list(dependence="independent"),
  method="continuous_shrinkage", algorithm="mcmc",
  prior=list(hierarchy="prs_csx",globalScale=.01),
  nit=1000,nburn=500,nthin=5,nchains=2,seed=42)


All references must already contain the same ordered marker intersection and verified LD blocks. Independent discovery samples, population-specific common N and explicit catalog mappings are required. For JointPRS use hierarchy= “jointprs_reference” and named correlationCaps. For Panther use hierarchy= “panther_reference” plus labelled sharingGroups, pantherRoute and outputPopulation. The supplied categories are not learned sharing probabilities; target mode ignores them. All native estimated population effects are retained.
updateB learns the global scale only; local and normalized residual scales always update. These reference residual transitions are separate from exact in-sample residual learning. Extract effects/empirical effectVariance, parameters, localScales, JointPRS populationCorrelation or Panther groupScales. No spike PIPs are available. Serial chains retain selected diagnostics and final effects, without continuation or gmap interpretation. JointPRS remains experimental; selected mean agreement does not establish mixing. See the full contract, ?population_shrinkage and the saved-input example in tools/examples/gbayes/population-shrinkage.R.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Scalar summary IBSS
Use sbayes with multi_effect and ibss for one bounded region. Prepare OLS summaries with the public gmap helper, retaining original phenotype/design effect units:


Code
prepared <- gmap::gmap_stat(stat, LD, phenotype_variance=vy)
fit <- sbayes(prepared, LD, trait="height", method="multi_effect", algorithm="ibss",
  vb=.02,ve=1,updateB=TRUE,nit=500,control=list(effects=5))
# Alternatively pass ordinary stat plus control$phenotypeVariance=vy.


The full regional marker/allele/coordinate order must match complete LD; the initial route requires positive full-rank LD and caps the domain at 2048 markers by default. It does not perform automatic filtering, score projection or LD repair. Component-variance learning is on by default; residual learning is off. Exact residual learning requires explicit in-sample response scatter/dimension, matching sample count and normalization. It is variational EB, not MCMC.
Extract effects, effectVariance, pips, componentAssignments and componentScales; inspect diagnostics(fit)$ibss for objective/residual traces and inactive/inner convergence flags. Inactive components are not signals, and conditional components do not establish independent causal markers. There are no chains or full effect draws. Save/reload works through RDS; prediction, capture, continuation and saved scalar gmap conversion are not exposed. Direct gmap is the reference workflow. See the contract, ?scalar_summary_ibss and tools/examples/gbayes/scalar-summary-ibss.R.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Weighted elastic net
All four genomic fitters accept named marker penalty multipliers with method = "elastic_net" and algorithm = "coordinate_descent".


Code
fit <- bayes(training,Glist,trait="height",method="elastic_net",
  algorithm="coordinate_descent",nit=10000,
  control=list(lambda=.1,alpha=.6,l1Weights=marker_l1,l2Weights=marker_l2))
joint <- mbayes(training,Glist,trait=c("height","weight"),method="elastic_net",
  algorithm="coordinate_descent",nit=10000,
  control=list(lambda=.1,alpha=.6,covariance=K,
    l1Weights=marker_l1,l2Weights=marker_l2))
# K is a fixed SPD penalty covariance labelled c("height","weight").


Each supplied vector must be finite, nonnegative and named for the entire fitted marker panel. Omitted weights default to ones and are never normalized. Weights apply to saved training empirical-SD coefficients; scalar covariance scales the L1/L2 terms as before. Zero removes a penalty, not a marker. Alpha=0 remains gated; alpha=1 ignores L2 weights. Use diagnostics(fit)$numerical for native and normalized KKT, objective and qualified lambdaMax. An L1-unpenalized marker with nonzero score prevents a finite all-zero threshold. Prediction reuses training coding; weights and exact normalized coefficients survive RDS save/reload. Joint weights are marker vectors shared across traits. L1 uses marginal SDs of K; each L2 weight multiplies the full marker precision block, so zero removes that marker’s cross-trait penalty. K does not weight residuals. Automatic selection/weight estimation remains separate. The new joint native symbol requires rebuilding native gbayes before the R package at the batch checkpoint. See the contract, ?weighted_elastic_net and tools/examples/gbayes/weighted-elastic-net.R.
The scalar summary route uses standardized marginal effects and reference LD:


Code
summary_fit <- sbayes(stat,LD,trait="height",method="elastic_net",
  algorithm="coordinate_descent",nit=10000,
  control=list(lambda=.1,alpha=.6,l1Weights=marker_l1,l2Weights=marker_l2))


Supply the usual b/SE/n table covering every prepared sparse-LD marker and one common GWAS N. This fits a normalized reference-LD quadratic with standardized summary effects, not empirical-SD individual effects. The supplied LD must be PSD for convexity; no PSD certification, repair or projection is performed. Inspect the saved LD/convexity limitations and normalized summary KKT/objective. No training coding/intercept or direct prediction is inferred. Bayesian scale, learning, MCMC, capture and continuation arguments are rejected. The runnable example accepts interface=“sbayes” with stat instead of data in inputs.rds.
Joint summary fitting adds a distinct sampling declaration to the penalty K:


Code
joint_summary <- msbayes(list(height=stat_height,weight=stat_weight),LD,
  method="elastic_net",algorithm="coordinate_descent",nit=10000,
  sampling=list(dependence="shared_ld",covariance=Omega),
  control=list(lambda=.1,alpha=.6,covariance=K,
    l1Weights=marker_l1,l2Weights=marker_l2))


K is the fixed penalty covariance; Omega is the justified sampling-error covariance. Both are SPD and labelled in trait order. For independent providers, declare dependence=“independent” and residual_variance named in provider order. Study-named Glists also use the normal named trait map. This source route admits one full ordered panel per trait (2–32 traits), with common N within each provider; independent providers can have different LD/N. Losses are normalized per provider before adding the same shared-marker penalty. PSD LD is assumed, not certified/repaired. Inspect maximumKktSummary and the normalized objective; there is no further N division, training coding or posterior uncertainty. The example accepts interface=“msbayes” with stat, sampling and penalty K.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
section: Runnable Gaussian and weighted elastic-net examples
text:
Runnable Gaussian and weighted elastic-net examples
Run both fits with a small centered feature matrix. The row names match the phenotype IDs. The named L1 multipliers apply a larger penalty to v.


Code
ids <- paste0("i", 1:4)
X <- cbind(u = c(-1, -1, 1, 1), v = c(-1, 1, -1, 1))
rownames(X) <- ids
training <- data.frame(id = ids, height = c(-1, 1, -2, 2))

fit <- gbayes::bayes(
  training, X = X, trait = "height",
  method = "marker_gaussian", algorithm = "pcg", ve = 1,
  prior = list(markerVariance = c(u = 0.2, v = 0.2))
)
weighted <- gbayes::bayes(
  training, X = X, trait = "height",
  method = "elastic_net", algorithm = "coordinate_descent",
  control = list(lambda = 0.1, alpha = 0.6, l1Weights = c(u = 1, v = 2))
)

coef(fit)       # u = 0, v = 0.666667
coef(weighted)  # u = 0, v = 1.326923
predict(fit, X)


X is a bounded finite matrix with sample row IDs and feature column IDs, already centered in the desired fitting units. The response is centered without rescaling. Keep the training feature-preparation recipe and apply it to target features before predict; no feature standardization or raw-feature transform is inferred. The exact-statistics companion is blr(XX,Xy,yy,n,method=…), using the same two methods and native fitters. Its existing coding can enable generic prediction. Set prior$markerMean to supply Gaussian prior means or elastic-net penalty centers. Elastic-net weights default to one when omitted. For genomic inputs, see the four weighted elastic-net fitters. The prepared-design examples passed on the frozen 0.1.16 build. See the contract, ?prepared_design and tools/examples/gbayes/prepared-design.R.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Streamed and batched scalar mixtures


Code
source <- list(ids=sample_ids,features=feature_ids,sourceId="training-v1",
  readColumns=function(first,last) read_prepared_columns(first,last))
fit <- bayes(training,X=source,trait="height",method="normal_mixture",
  algorithm="vbayes",vb=c(0,.01,.1),pi=c(.8,.15,.05),ve=1,
  control=list(chunkSize=64,fixed=covariates))
batch <- bayes(training,X=source,trait="height",method="laplace_gaussian",
  vb=.1,ve=1,prior=list(laplaceProbability=.5,normalVarianceFraction=.3),
  control=list(models=list(first=list(),second=list(vb=.2))))
coef(batch$fits$first)


A labelled finite matrix can replace the reader descriptor. Each reader result must retain declared sample order and requested feature order, with both axes labelled. Keep the source immutable. The adapter adds an intercept and native QR fits the supplied fixed covariates; target phenotype prediction needs matching covariates. Features retain their supplied units. Priors remain fixed and each candidate is a separate scalar bayesfit; candidates are not traits or selections.
Inspect each fit’s negative-ELBO history and convergence status. Maximum sweeps remains provisional; variational variances are approximate, and no PIPs are exposed. Shared batch work diagnostics must not be summed across their copies. The saved fit omits its reader. Prediction uses new feature matrices. See the contract, ?streamed_prediction and tools/examples/gbayes/streamed-prediction.R.

title: Bayesian genomic regression
text:
Scalar Gaussian co-data
This runnable example learns a diagonal Gaussian prior from two overlapping groups in one co-data set. It uses the supplied feature coding and a fixed residual variance and group penalty.


Code
X <- diag(3)
dimnames(X) <- list(c("a", "b", "c"), c("u", "v", "w"))
data <- data.frame(id=c("c", "a", "b"), height=c(1.4, 3, .2))
fit <- gbayes::bayes(data, X=X, trait="height",
  method="marker_gaussian", algorithm="gaussian", ve=.7,
  prior=list(coData=list(id="annotation",
    groups=list(left=c("u", "v"), right=c("v", "w")),
    globalVariance=1.3, hyperLambda=2)),
  control=list(coding=list(centers=c(u=.1, v=-.2, w=.3),
                          scales=c(u=2, v=.5, w=1))))
coef(fit)
gbayes::diagnostics(fit)$coData
predict(fit, X)


X can also be a labelled dgCMatrix; sparse input is not converted to a dense feature matrix. Coding defaults to zero centers and unit scales. Supply the intended transforms explicitly: this route fits no intercept, leaves outcomes unchanged and does not infer preprocessing. Effects use transformed feature units. Overlapping groups are averaged per feature. globalMode="known_noise_ml" and explicit varianceBounds optionally learn the initial global variance; ve and hyperLambda stay fixed. Both moment RHS and hyper-ridge profiles are explicit options. Use only training outcomes and training-derived coding.
The reportable means are Gaussian conditional means at a learned plug-in prior. Sampling variance in diagnostics is not posterior effect uncertainty; PIPs and posterior variances are unavailable. Prediction uses all fitted features in fitted order, with saved coding and no refitting. No implicit phenotype offset is added. This bounded scalar route has no joint/summary adapter. Automatic tuning and multiple annotation sets are supported below. General selection stays in gscore. See the design contract, ?gbayes::co_data_gaussian and the runnable source example tools/examples/gbayes/co-data-gaussian.R.

Combining multiple co-data sets
Use named sets instead of groups/id. Every set covers all fitted features; groups can overlap within a set. For the same three-feature example:


Code
fit <- gbayes::bayes(data, X=X, trait="height",
  method="marker_gaussian", algorithm="gaussian", ve=1,
  prior=list(coData=list(sets=list(
    A=list(left=c("u", "v"), right=c("v", "w")),
    B=list(odd=c("u", "w"), even="v")),
    globalVariance=1, hyperLambda=c(A=2, B=3),
    normalize=TRUE, normalizeSets=TRUE, weightRule="ecpc_2_switch")))
gbayes::diagnostics(fit)$coData$setWeights
predict(fit, X)


An unnamed scalar hyperLambda shares one fixed penalty; a named vector aligns penalties to sets. The native engine learns group profiles and weights across sets, then fits their combined diagonal Gaussian prior. Normalizing groups and normalizing set weights are independent choices; both enabled give mean prior variance equal to the global variance. Set normalization is post-fit scaling. The same frozen coding and optional shared known-noise ML apply. A one-group set uses a fixed unit profile. Sets are annotations on one outcome, not new traits or model-averaged candidate fits.
Set weights are not posterior activity or sharing probabilities. Inspect the actual route/rank/KKT diagnostics: similar profiles may not identify individual weights. The undefined zero-source profile and solver failures are explicit errors, with no accepted partial fit. Posterior effect variances and PIPs remain unavailable. See ?gbayes::co_data_gaussian, the design and runnable source example tools/examples/gbayes/co-data-gaussian-multi.R.


Tuning from saved feature-group splits
Use hyperLambda=0 with saved partitions of each group’s feature IDs:


Code
groups <- list(left=c("u", "v"), right=c("v", "w"))
pair <- list(inside=list(left="u", right="v"),
             outside=list(left="v", right="w"))
splits <- list(first=pair, reverse=list(inside=pair$outside, outside=pair$inside))
fit <- gbayes::bayes(data, X=X, trait="height", method="marker_gaussian",
  algorithm="gaussian", ve=1,
  prior=list(coData=list(groups=groups, hyperLambda=0, splits=splits)))
gbayes::diagnostics(fit)$coData$tuning


For multiple sets, use hyperLambda=c(A=0, B=3) and splits=list(A=splits) with the earlier named sets. A tunes; B stays fixed. Each split half names every group, with disjoint members covering the full group; character(0) is allowed for an empty half. One-group sets retain their native unit profile and skip tuning. No random splits are inferred. control$tuning adjusts native path and hyper-search controls; maxSplits bounds the total saved pairs.
Zero requests native path-bound construction and raw-gamma held-out equation tuning, followed by the declared full-group fit. It is not a zero-penalty solve. Inspect saved paths, split equations, objective, evaluations and boundary status. Prediction and save/reload do not repeat selection. Search exhaustion and undefined numerical equations return no accepted partial fit.
These partition feature-group equations, not patients: they do not create a validation cohort. Use training outcomes/coding only. Patient CV/refit remains separate in gscore; fixed noise and absent posterior variances/PIPs are unchanged. See the contract, package help and tools/examples/gbayes/co-data-tuning.R.


Learning residual variance
The same scalar co-data family can learn the initial residual and global effect variances jointly, then hold them fixed during annotation fitting:


Code
X <- rbind(c(1,0), c(0,1), c(0,0), c(0,0))
dimnames(X) <- list(letters[1:4], c("u", "v"))
data <- data.frame(id=letters[1:4], height=c(sqrt(7), 1, 1, 1))
fit <- gbayes::bayes(data, X=X, trait="height", method="marker_gaussian",
  algorithm="gaussian",
  prior=list(coData=list(groups=list(u="u", v="v"), hyperLambda=2,
    globalMode="joint_noise_ml", varianceRatioBounds=c(.01,100))))
gbayes::diagnostics(fit)$coData[c("residualVariance", "globalVariance", "globalSearch")]
gbayes::fit_contract(fit)$sampling$varianceLearning


Omit ve, globalVariance and varianceBounds. The bounds constrain the residual/ global ratio, using supplied feature coding. For multiple sets, replace groups with the existing named sets contract; every set receives the same learned pair. Positive penalties and saved-split automatic penalties both compose with this mode. Native fitting learns noise once before groups; it does not re-estimate noise after group tuning or set weighting. No intercept or centering is inferred.
Inspect objective, boundary and identification limits. Proportional-to-identity design Gram matrices and zero outcomes are rejected, and near-flat profiles are not identification certificates. Prediction/save/reload do not retune. No PIPs or posterior parameter/effect uncertainty is added. See the contract, help and tools/examples/gbayes/co-data-noise.R.


Supplied-fold initialization selected in gscore
Use gscore for the workflow and gbayes for numerical fitting:


Code
X <- cbind(u=c(-1,.5,2,-.2,.8,1.4,-.6,.3),
           v=c(.2,1,-.5,.7,1.2,-.8,.4,.9),
           w=c(.6,-.3,.5,1.1,-.7,.2,1.3,-.4))
rownames(X) <- paste0("s",1:8)
data <- data.frame(id=rownames(X), height=c(2,-1,.3,.8,1.5,-.6,2.1,.2))
folds <- setNames(c(1,1,2,2,2,3,3,3), rownames(X))
result <- gscore::co_data_cv(data, X, folds,
  penalties=c(low=.1,medium=1,high=10), ve=1,
  prior=list(coData=list(groups=list(left=c("u","v"),right=c("v","w")),
                         hyperLambda=2)),
  cvControl=list(preprocessing="externally_frozen", retainPredictions=TRUE))
result$selection
predict(result$fit, X)


Multiple sets use the same coData$sets contract; saved feature-group split tuning can also be supplied separately. For noise profiling conditional on the selected ratio, set estimateNoise=TRUE and omit ve. Do not supply coData initializer modes/variances/bounds; gscore selects that pair. Final fitControl reuses CV coding.
This workflow tunes the ordinary ridge initializer. Full-model co-data CV remains planned. gscore independently selects minimum row-weighted MSE with a largest-penalty exact-tie rule and verifies the native provisional profile before refitting. Freeze preprocessing externally and keep patient clusters within folds. No outer test outcomes, learned fold coding or automatic folds enter. CV and refit work/ownership remain saved, including in fit provenance. The final fit is conditional on the selected pair and keeps normal prediction/uncertainty contracts. See the design, package help and tools/examples/gscore/co-data-cv.R.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
There are two routes. A saved individual-level BED gbayes::gbayes() fit can be interpreted by region using LD from the same people and markers. This reuses the global posterior and does not refit it. Alternatively, start with aligned GWAS results and a prepared Glist. Regional LD can be computed on demand; prepared sparse LD is optional. Prepare the statistics, fit each region and trait, inspect marker support, then compare fitted multi-effect components with gmap_coloc_components().
This example requires development installations of gbase, gbayes, gmap and gsim. The website displays saved results and does not run models. The current calls are shown below; a refreshed end-to-end script remains separate work.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
There are two routes. A saved individual-level BED gbayes::gbayes() fit can be interpreted by region using LD from the same people and markers. This reuses the global posterior and does not refit it. Alternatively, start with aligned GWAS results and a prepared Glist. Regional LD can be computed on demand; prepared sparse LD is optional. Prepare the statistics, fit each region and trait, inspect marker support, then compare fitted multi-effect components with gmap_coloc_components().
This example requires development installations of gbase, gbayes, gmap and gsim. The website displays saved results and does not run models. The current calls are shown below; a refreshed end-to-end script remains separate work.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Prepared summary-statistic input
Prepare raw_stat from gact::getGWAS(..., rm.na = FALSE) or supply the same layout yourself, then use stat <- gbase::checkStat(Glist, raw_stat, ...). gmap() consumes stat and that Glist without repeating QC or allele alignment. It accepts a single-study data frame or the gact list of marker-by-study b, seb, n, and z matrices with identical dimnames. Shared marker metadata need not be expanded into a separate genome-wide data frame per study.
fit <- gmap::gmap(stat, Glist, sets = regions, method = "multi_effect")
For beta/SE input, vy is the sample phenotype variance (denominator n - 1), inferred when omitted. Supply a scalar or vector named in study order to override. Conversion assumes intercept-only OLS with one common integer sample size per study within each region. Existing score/information input needs no vy. Requested markers must have usable sufficient statistics in every study; Z-only or imputed-only entries need explicit score/information. gmap constructs native input tables one region at a time and currently fits studies separately. Full LD remains the multi-effect default; existing model-specific QC screens remain opt-in. Without prepared sparse LD, gmap reuses gbase::getLD() to decode and form LD once per region, sharing it across studies and fitting attempts. A genome assembly label is optional and is recorded as unspecified when absent.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Grouped controls
Scientific parameters retain qgg names: h2, mc, pi, gamma, vy, vg, ve, vb, nub, nug, nue. Missing vy is inferred from selected beta/SE/n summaries or prepared metadata; vg=vyh2, Bayesian ve=vy, and Bayesian mixture vb=vg/(mcsum(pi*gamma)). Multi-effect restores working-scale ve=1, initial vb=.02, effect-variance learning, 500 sweeps and objective tolerance 1e-10. Supply suitable ve/vb for different outcome/effect units. Explicit values and control overrides are respected.
fit <- gmap::gmap(stat, G, sets = loci, method = "bayesC",
  learn = list(updateB = TRUE, updatePi = TRUE),
  ld = list(threshold = 1),
  cs = list(threshold = .95, r2 = .5),
  control = list(mcmc = list(nit = 1000L, nburn = 100L, nrun = 4L,
    swap = TRUE, swapprob = .05, swapr2 = .8)), seed = 10)
fit$initialization
fit$diagnostic_summary
fit$ld_swap
Effect-variance learning defaults on for all methods; BayesC/BayesR also weakly learn pi, with residual variance fixed. Full LD is the default; auto uses eigen inference for multi-effect/truncation and dense MCMC for full-LD Bayesian mixtures. Both can compute regional LD on demand. Swaps default to probability .05 and LD r-squared .8. Four chains provide between-chain diagnostics, without guaranteeing mixing. qc contains optional neighbors/slalom; cs contains coverage, purity and reporting/conditional screens. Diagnostics are always retained. There are no legacy argument aliases. fit$settings records the resolved public groups.
Functional annotations currently mean fixed nonnegative marker weights for multi-effect, supplied as a labelled vector or rsids/weight table. Annotation coefficient learning and Bayesian mixture annotations are unsupported. There is no separate vg update; nug=4 is reserved.
Saved PIPs can still be grouped without refitting using getCredibleSets(); its separate CS2/CS3 contract is unchanged.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
section: From an individual-level BED fit to regional marker support
text:
From an individual-level BED fit to regional marker support
First fit the whole selected marker panel using pre-adjusted phenotypes, as in the Bayesian regression guide. Then prepare sparse LD from that same Glist and use it to interpret the saved posterior in named regions:
G <- gbase::gprep(bedfiles="cohort.bed", ids=phenotypes$id)
fit <- gbayes::bayes(data=phenotypes, Glist=G, trait="height",
  method="bayesR", algorithm="mcmc", ve=.8, vb=.2,
  updateB=FALSE, updateE=FALSE, updatePi=FALSE,
  nburn=1000, nit=4000, nchains=2, seed=31)

G <- gbase::gprep(Glist=G, task="sparseld", out_prefix="build/ld/cohort",
  r2=0, max_distance_bp=0, max_distance_variants=49)
regions <- list(locus=G$sparseLD$marker_metadata$marker_id[101:150])
mapped <- gmap::gmap_bed(fit, G, regions)
summary(mapped)
plot(mapped, region="locus", trait="height")
The saved-posterior adapter accepts scalar bayesfit results from bayes() and joint BayesC/BayesR bayesfit results from mbayes(), as well as the standalone gbayes_fit result. It checks physical sample and marker selections and training HWE coding before constructing marginal-PIP groups. For joint fits, each trait’s marginal PIPs are interpreted separately. The joint activity probabilities and component-colocalisation outputs have their own probability meanings.
The 101:150 marker range is illustrative; choose a biological region in reference order. Here r2=0 and the 49-marker window retain every pair in that contiguous 50-marker region. Set the window to span the largest region you intend to interpret. gmap_bed() checks the saved fit against the Glist’s selected people, physical BED marker offsets, alleles and frequencies. It rejects incomplete within-region LD unless control=list(allow_incomplete_ld=TRUE) is explicitly supplied; those groups are then labelled approximate. Regions are bounded to 2048 markers by default.
The returned PIPs and effect summaries are from the global BED fit. Native gmap groups these marginal PIPs using within-region LD. These groups are not component credible sets, do not carry guaranteed coverage and are not regional refits. Inspect chain behavior and parameter summaries on fit itself. The same call accepts a saved joint-trait BED BayesC/BayesR fit and returns separate labelled regional views for each trait.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Prepare summary statistics
Each study has a checked data frame with rsids, ea, nea, b, seb and n, or uses the shared-marker gact matrix layout. checkStat owns alignment. The saved historical example uses older column labels, converted explicitly below.
library(gmap)
G <- gbase::gprep(bedfiles = "build/examples/gmap-workflow/reference.bed")
example <- readRDS("build/examples/gmap-workflow/workflow.rds")
stat <- lapply(example$gwas, function(x) {
  rename <- c(marker="rsids", allele1="ea", allele2="nea", beta="b", se="seb")
  for (name in intersect(names(rename), names(x)))
    names(x)[names(x) == name] <- rename[[name]]
  at <- match(x$rsids, unlist(G$rsids))
  x$chr <- unlist(G$chr)[at]; x$pos <- unlist(G$pos)[at]
  gbase::checkStat(G, x, excludeMAF=NULL, excludeMAFDIFF=NULL,
    excludeHWE=NULL, excludeMISS=NULL)
})
regions <- example$regions
# To rerun the saved example and compare raw/precomputed inputs for all methods:
# source("tools/validation/verify_gmap_interface.R")
The helper supports continuous outcomes analysed by ordinary linear regression with an intercept and conventional standard errors: a separate y ~ marker regression for each marker, without other covariates. All markers within a trait must use the same individuals. Supply the sample phenotype variance, not the residual variance or an assumed value of one.
For centered genotype \(x_j\) and outcome \(y\), the OLS identities give:
\[
d_j=x_j^\mathsf{T}x_j
= \frac{(n-1)s_y^2}{(n-2)\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)^2+\hat\beta_j^2},
\qquad x_j^\mathsf{T}y=d_j\hat\beta_j.
\]
Optional gmap_stat() returns information = d and score = d * beta. The main interface performs this conversion region by region when needed. The native model combines these with the regional LD correlation matrix \(R\):
\[
X^\mathsf{T}X \approx D^{1/2} R D^{1/2},\qquad D=\operatorname{diag}(d_j).
\]
The marginal conversion is exact under the stated OLS contract. The full matrix is exact only with matching in-sample LD, apart from storage precision. This example uses an independent panel, so its off-diagonal entries are approximations. The SuSiE summary-statistic documentation also explains the role of in-sample LD in recovering an individual-data fit.
Covariate-adjusted, mixed-model, logistic, robust-SE, meta-analysis and varying-sample-size summaries are outside this helper’s contract. It cannot recognise the generating analysis from numbers alone. Supplying equal n does not prove identical samples. Correctly prepared cross-products can still be passed directly to gmap(); z-only conversion is deferred.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
section: A small simulation with known truth
text:
A small simulation with known truth
The complete script generates binomial dosages with correlated neighbours and uses gsim() for continuous phenotypes. The artificial coordinates have no biological interpretation.







Setting
Value




GWAS cohorts
Two disjoint cohorts of 10,000 individuals each


LD reference
Independent 4,000-individual panel from the same generator


Regions
Two artificial chromosomes, 20 markers each


Genotype construction
Allele frequency 0.3; adjacent copy probability 0.8


Shared region
m08 affects both traits


Distinct region
m25 affects A; m36 affects B


Effects
0.12 and 0.14 per standardized dosage; converted to raw-dosage units


Residual variance
Known simulation value 1, fixed during fitting


Seeds
Genotypes 20260915; gsim 20260916 and 20260917



The LD reference retains all within-region correlations, is prepared once, and caches one eigensystem per region. Each call reuses that preparation across traits. The script fits traits separately; it is not a joint multivariate Bayesian model. Marginal GWAS results are calculated separately in each cohort.
Full LD is the default. An explicit ld$threshold = c(.995, .99, .95) tries successively smaller masses when earlier attempts fail the convergence rule. The eigendecomposition is not repeated. For a region with several traits, one threshold is accepted only when every trait passes. Multi-effect fits use their native convergence flag; BayesC and BayesR use the configured maximum between-chain PIP range. The selected threshold, achieved mass, retained rank and score-projection change are in diagnostic_summary; eigen_attempts retains one lightweight row per attempted trait and threshold.
fit$diagnostic_summary
fit$eigen_attempts

# Exact full-rank likelihood, without fallback
full <- gmap(stat, G, sets = regions, method = "multi_effect", ve = 1, vb = .04,
  control = list(multi = list(effects = 3L)))
If no attempted likelihood passes, the last complete fit is returned with status = "provisional" and a warning; the threshold is therefore never hidden. Only positive directions are retained, materially indefinite LD is rejected, and every truncated likelihood explicitly projects the score into the retained space. Residual-variance learning currently requires the full-rank setting.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Fit the three methods
mc <- list(nburn = 1000L, nit = 5000L, nrun = 2L, swap = FALSE)
bayesc <- gmap(stat, G, regions, method = "bayesC", ve = 1, vb = .04,
  pi = c(.95, .05), control = list(mcmc = mc), seed = 31)
bayesr <- gmap(stat, G, regions, method = "bayesR", ve = 1, vb = .04,
  pi = c(.95, .01, .01, .03), control = list(mcmc = mc), seed = 31)
multi <- gmap(stat, G, regions, method = "multi_effect", ve = 1, vb = .04,
  learn = list(updateB = TRUE),
  control = list(multi = list(effects = 3L, maxiter = 500L)))
These deliberately specified priors differ between methods; the example is not a ranking experiment. effect_variance is on the original GWAS effect scale. BayesR uses its default variance multipliers. Multi-effect can reduce unneeded component variances to zero. Residual variance is fixed in this example; the known simulation value is not a general recommendation for data. A regional fit also omits the other region’s small genetic contribution, so fixing the residual variance at one is a deliberate working approximation. The multi-effect fit uses full rank because its saved components are used for colocalisation below; component colocalisation does not accept a truncated likelihood.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Learn parameters when needed
Initialization and learning are separate. Multi-effect defaults to learning component variances; BayesC/BayesR weakly learn pi and vb by default, keeping ve=vy fixed. The Dirichlet prior has alpha=1000*pi (learn$concentration=1000), and nub=20 centres the effect-variance prior mean on initial vb. Use learn=list(updateB=FALSE, updatePi=FALSE) for fixed mixture parameters.
learned <- gmap(stat, G, regions, method = "bayesR", ve = 1, vb = .04,
  nub = 6, learn = list(updateB = TRUE, updatePi = TRUE),
  control = list(mcmc = mc))
learned$initialization
learned$parameters
Bayesian effect/residual learning uses scaled inverse chi-square priors with scale (df-2)/df times the starting variance; mixture learning uses starting-pi-centred Dirichlet concentrations. Multi-effect updateB uses native variance optimization. Residual learning requires the reference people and full complete LD:
learned_multi <- gmap(list(A = stat_in_sample), G_in_sample, regions,
  method = "multi_effect", vy = var(y), ve = 1, vb = .04,
  ld = list(insample = TRUE), learn = list(updateB = TRUE, updateE = TRUE),
  control = list(multi = list(effects = 3L)))
Normalization is response_ss=(n-1)*vy and likelihood_dimension=n-1 for an intercept-only model. Sample identity cannot be established from counts. External-panel or incomplete LD cannot support this residual-learning claim.

Inspect estimates, sets and chains

The top-marker PIPs exceed 0.99999. Each fit returned one complete set. All four multi-effect fits converged in two sweeps. The largest BayesR PIP range between the two chains was 0.014. These strong signals make an easy workflow demonstration, not a demanding fine-mapping evaluation.
BayesC/BayesR report PIPs pooled over the two chains. Chain-specific PIPs and ranges are available; agreement alone does not certify convergence. Their sets group marginal PIP mass within LD neighbourhoods. Multi-effect sets represent component assignment probabilities. These set probabilities are not interchangeable, and this one simulation does not establish coverage. The sum of PIPs is the expected number of active markers, not necessarily the number of independent signals.
gmap_sets() keeps the native interpretation in its meaning column: marginal_pip_mass for BayesC/BayesR neighbourhood groups and component_assignment for multi-effect credible sets. Its summary table also retains completeness, pairwise LD purity, incomplete-LD, duplicate and fit-status fields. The member table gives the markers, posterior weights and LD to the lead.
gmap_bfdr() uses only marker PIPs. At threshold \(t\), its expected number of false discoveries is \(\sum_{j:PIP_j\ge t}(1-PIP_j)\) and BFDR is that value divided by the number selected. With target, it returns the largest marker group defined by a PIP threshold whose BFDR is no larger than the target. This posterior summary does not provide a frequentist FDR guarantee.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Compare the traits without refitting
shared <- gmap_coloc_components(
  multi, multi, G, trait1 = "A", trait2 = "B",
  control = list(complete_region_coverage = TRUE,
                 non_overlapping_samples = TRUE)
)
summary(shared)
shared$estimates
shared$component_status
plot(shared, region = "shared")
plot(shared, region = "distinct")



Component-pair colocalisation probabilities in the shared and distinct regions.


H0 means neither trait is associated; H1/H2 mean only one is associated; H3 means distinct causal variants; H4 means a shared causal variant. These are component-pair probabilities, not a single region-wide posterior. The defaults are per-variant priors \(p_1=p_2=10^{-4}\) and \(p_{12}=10^{-5}\). In this run, shared-region H4 was 0.999999999991; distinct-region H3 rounded to 1, with H4 about \(3.24\times10^{-45}\). These values reflect this strong, artificial example and its specified priors, not general performance. Changing these priors reuses the saved evidence. No eligible component pairs means there is no eligible comparison; it is not evidence for H0.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Numerical checks and saved results
The script compares the converted scores and diagonals against direct cross-products from the simulated individuals. It also fits all three methods from both routes, with the same LD and seeds, and checks PIPs and posterior means. That validates the conversion; it does not validate the external-LD approximation or establish calibration. The LD file checksums are checked before and after fitting.
The run on 15 September 2026 used gsuite 0.43.0, gsim 0.9.0 and R 4.4.1. The largest score/diagonal discrepancy was \(1.82\times10^{-12}\); the largest posterior-mean discrepancy was \(1.11\times10^{-16}\). PIPs agreed to numerical precision. Approximate observed times for four region/trait fits per method were 0.69 s (BayesC), 6.16 s (BayesR) and 0.36 s (multi-effect). The whole script took 17.91 s, including preparation, repeat fits for verification, colocalisation and figures. These are illustrative elapsed times on one laptop, not a benchmark; another package-build process was also active.
example$conversion
example$equivalence
example$timing
summary(example$fits$bayesr)
summary(example$coloc)
workflow.rds contains the summaries, prepared statistics, truth, fitted objects and checks. report.txt records summaries and package versions. The directory also contains two figures and compact CSV tables. Saved fits can be plotted without the LD files; a new gmap_coloc_components() call requires the reference files so that eligibility and reference checks can run.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
ABF colocalisation
For at most one causal variant per trait, compare the aligned GWAS tables directly. This route uses native gmap ABFs; it does not require an LD object, gmap_stat() or a Bayesian fine-mapping fit. The example’s two cohorts are disjoint, and each selected region contains one generating causal variant per trait, so it is suitable for illustrating this model.
markers <- regions$shared
first <- gwas$A[match(markers, gwas$A$marker), ]
second <- gwas$B[match(markers, gwas$B$marker), ]
abf <- gmap_coloc(
  first, second, region = "shared",
  phenotype_sd1 = sqrt(example$phenotype_variance[["A"]]),
  phenotype_sd2 = sqrt(example$phenotype_variance[["B"]]),
  p1 = 1e-4, p2 = 1e-4, p12 = 1e-5)
abf$shared_variant_probability
Each table requires rsids, chr, pos, ea, nea, b and seb. Rows and alleles must match exactly. ea is the effect allele; effects and standard errors are on the phenotype scale per allele. Phenotype standard deviations are supplied here, unlike the variances passed to gmap_stat(). The effect-prior SD is the specified fraction of each phenotype SD. Binary/log-odds, z-only and p-value-only inputs are not supported, and phenotype SD is never inferred.
H0 means neither trait is associated, H1/H2 one trait alone, H3 distinct causal variants and H4 a shared causal variant. Here these are regional probabilities under the single-causal model. The earlier multi-effect results instead apply to individual component pairs; they must not be added into a regional posterior. Marker probabilities are conditional on H4, not marginal fine-mapping PIPs.
Use separate calls to examine alternative association priors. Regional coverage and sample independence are scientific assumptions of this model and must be established by the caller. Selected MR instruments alone do not provide complete regional data. Evidence for shared association is not by itself evidence for a causal effect of one trait on another.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
Chain disagreement is a warning
BayesC/BayesR sets remain available when chains disagree. Inspect fit$diagnostic_summary: chain_agreement_pass, chain_disagreement, max_pip_range, and reporting_allowed distinguish diagnostics from reporting. Bayesian converged is NA and a disagreeing fit has status chain_warning; its reporting_allowed remains TRUE. Multi-effect nonconvergence still gates its optional reporting screen. Do not use a Bayesian convergence field as an automatic set-removal rule. QC, purity and conditional-support screens are unchanged.
Non-finite posterior summaries remain ineligible for reporting; the warning-only policy applies to chain agreement, not numerical failures.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
section: Optional regional QC and reporting for all methods
text:
Optional regional QC and reporting for all methods
Neighbor-sign and SLALOM-style QC run before fitting and can be enabled for multi_effect, BayesC or BayesR. QC and conditional screening require one study, finite aligned Z-scores and fixed residual variance. They remain opt-in and do not repeat checkStat alignment. QC uses full regional LD; reporting uses the original, untruncated LD among retained markers, even with ld$threshold below one.
screened <- gmap::gmap(stat, G, loci, method = "bayesR",
  qc = list(neighbors = TRUE, slalom = TRUE),
  cs = list(reporting = TRUE, conditional = TRUE))
screened$neighbor_sign
screened$slalom
screened$reporting
Reporting checks pairwise LD purity and duplicate sets. The conditional screen retains one primary set and requires conditional support for additional sets. Bayesian chain disagreement remains a warning; it does not veto supported sets. Non-finite fits remain ineligible. fit\(reporting records selected candidate
indices; fit\)sets, native details and gmap_sets() retain all candidate sets. For a region and study, select the screened subset with:
at <- screened$reporting[["locus1"]][["trait"]]$selected
reported <- screened$sets[["locus1"]][["trait"]]$sets[at]
These screens detect statistical incompatibility, not proven allele errors; true effects and reference mismatch can also produce exclusions. Compare screened and unscreened fits when interpreting a locus.

Defaults and what they do
The default method is multi_effect. Select method="bayesC" or "bayesR" for the mixture samplers. These are working defaults, not universally optimal settings. Explicit values override initialization.

title: From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
text:
First-round simulation comparison: 36 cases
Saved benchmark results, not a new run of gmap 0.2.4. Six synthetic loci, each with 20 markers and 10,000 individuals, were each analysed under matched LD, external-reference LD and four single-marker sign-error scenarios (36 correlated cases). Neighbor-copy probabilities .55, .8, .95 give decaying LD; each is repeated with same-direction or opposite-direction causal effects. The causal markers are m05 (primary) and m15 (secondary). This is a small, controlled simulation, not realistic human haplotype LD or independent held-out validation.
All rows below use the same retained markers after neighbor-sign then SLALOM QC, followed by shared reporting: pairwise r-squared at least .5, exact duplicate removal, one primary set retained, and conditional Bonferroni P below .05 for additional sets. title: Genetic covariance models
text:
gcorr_covariance() requires a finite labelled continuous-trait covariance matrix, compatible named units and, for model fitting, the full joint sampling covariance of lower-column moments.
library(gcorr)

traits <- c("A", "B", "C")
G <- matrix(c(1, .3, .2, .3, 1, .4, .2, .4, 1), 3,
  dimnames = list(traits, traits))
labels <- c("A|A", "B|A", "C|A", "B|B", "C|B", "C|C")
V <- diag(.001, 6)
dimnames(V) <- list(labels, labels)
input <- gcorr_covariance(G, V, continuous = TRUE,
  units = setNames(rep("standard deviations", 3), traits))
