title: REML through packed ssSNPBLUP equations
text:
The experimental standalone YAML interface can estimate unstructured genetic and residual covariance matrices using the same conditional packed PCG equations as prediction. Natural covariance matrices in YAML are starting values. Numerical computation belongs to greml; the Python frontend validates inputs, prepares files and labels outputs. Existing R interfaces are unchanged.


The initial route supports an ordinary pedigree, one genetic channel per trait, and a shared unstructured residual covariance across independent observation blocks. Missing traits are integrated using the observed submatrix of the current residual covariance. Fixed effects and additional identity random effects are retained. analysis.estimate selects whole genetic, residual and additional identity-effect covariance blocks; omitted blocks remain fixed. Genetic channels may include random-regression coefficients and need not have the same width as the residual trait vector. Marker centering, normalization, genomic scaling, ridge/blend and any pedigree adjustment are held fixed throughout REML. This is conditional on the supplied genomic construction, rather than simultaneous estimation of its base parameters.
The method is EM-REML. Conditional genetic coordinates have independent prior blocks with row precisions Qnn, the genomic residual precision and marker identity, all sharing the genetic covariance K. Each update uses posterior second moments of those coordinates, including coefficient covariance from the fixed-effect equations. Dividing their contracted moments by the total number of genetic and marker levels gives the genetic EM update. Residual updates use posterior residual moments, with missing components integrated conditionally. Fixed covariance blocks retain their supplied natural values exactly.
The exact pedigree factor, ancestral reduction and packed genotype provider are reused across covariance states. The current implementation copies the sparse topology/maps when making a new numeric state; it does not refactor the pedigree. Record precisions, right-hand sides and the PCG preconditioner are refreshed. Qnn reuse avoids another pedigree factor for each new preconditioner; the shifted-pedigree option does build its covariance-dependent preconditioner factor. The existing final prediction solve independently checks the fitted model.
The fit does not assemble a global equation matrix, full inverse, dense genomic relationship or marker cross-product matrix. The optional exact likelihood reference materializes bounded small coefficient matrices. Source records and trait-pattern metadata, sparse maps and factors, coefficient vectors and the selected record cache still consume memory. Old/new numeric states can coexist during refresh; this is not a bound on process RSS.



Use the complete packed REML example (models/multitrait-packed-reml.yml). The main estimation controls are:
analysis:
  task: reml
  estimate: [genetic, residual]
  optimizer:
    maximum_iterations: 200
    score_tolerance: 1.0e-6
    step_fraction: 1.0
  traces:
    method: exact
    maximum_solves: 10000
estimate selects whole covariance blocks; omit a block to fix it. Packed EM does not yet support fixing individual Cholesky coordinates. step_fraction is the EM update fraction in (0,1], not a likelihood line-search control.
Exact traces solve every conditional coefficient unit column at each covariance state. They are intended for small reference problems, not industrial data. For a bounded stochastic calculation, replace the trace controls explicitly:
  traces:
    method: stochastic
    probes: 64
    seed: 4401
    maximum_solves: 10000
    maximum_score_mcse: 0.001
The stochastic option uses a common deterministic Rademacher probe bank across covariance states and streams one query at a time. The example numbers above are syntax examples, not a calibrated industrial recommendation. Score error is in natural variance/covariance coordinates and depends on data and scaling; the probe count alone does not establish adequate precision.
Each state uses one response solve plus probes stochastic solves, or one plus the conditional coefficient dimension for exact traces. maximum_solves caps their total across all states. It excludes the initial setup and subsequent independent final prediction solve, which have separate timing/iteration metrics. Every REML solve must pass both transformed and original augmented equation residual checks. The internal solve uses a numerical margin; the requested acceptance tolerances are unchanged.
Convergence requires the maximum absolute free score plus twice the maximum free-score Monte Carlo standard error to be no larger than score_tolerance. The MCSE must also meet maximum_score_mcse. Exact traces have zero sampling MCSE, subject to PCG numerical error. A stochastic moment matrix that is not SPD is rejected without clipping, jitter, silent probe increases or an exact fallback.
A stochastic candidate must pass one final score/precision check using an independent probe bank. Its additional response and probe solves count against the same total cap, and history marks the validation state. Failed independent validation rejects the fit; its probes never guide another update or select another validation bank. This check can add a qualification state after the last permitted covariance-update state. Score convergence does not establish uniqueness or statistical identifiability of an arbitrary covariance model.



Results include variance_components.csv, parameters.csv, reml_history.csv, likelihood.json and convergence.json, plus native natural-score and score-MCSE vectors. History records scores, MCSE and cumulative solve counts. Converged fits then produce the ordinary prediction tables. Failed fits retain diagnostic parameter states and history but publish no qualified prediction tables.
Likelihood reporting is optional, as described below. It does not control EM updates or replace score convergence. Exact EM has its usual likelihood monotonicity, but stochastic moment updates carry no likelihood-ascent certificate. Reported score MCSE describes trace estimation at the evaluated parameter state; it does not include variance-component estimation uncertainty or provide confidence intervals for the fitted parameters.
Focused tests compare natural scores with an independent dense restricted likelihood and finite differences, verify a joint analytic covariance optimum, check missing-trait EM updates and fitted predictions, and exercise stochastic work/precision rejection. This is not a 50K or industrial runtime qualification. EM can require many covariance updates, each with many PCG solves; prediction timings cannot be reused as REML runtime estimates. The native reml stage covers every covariance evaluation, final stochastic check and optional likelihood diagnostic. reml_likelihood reports the determinant diagnostic separately. Existing fine-grained data/operator profile counters are not an aggregate REML profile; use that stage and the explicit solve totals when assessing cost.
FA, serial/grouped residuals, genetic groups, metafounders, coordinate constraints and joint PEV output are outside the current packed REML interface. The existing compiled sparse-direct REML implementation retains its broader covariance/constraint support and likelihood reporting.



Omit analysis.likelihood for zero global determinant/operator-product work. To report the restricted-likelihood change from the supplied starting covariances to the final fitted covariances, add one block under analysis:
  likelihood:
    method: slq
    maximum_operator_products: 6144
Defaults are probes: 32, seed: 4402, lanczos_steps: 32, check_steps: 64, maximum_mcse: 1.0 and maximum_depth_change: 0.5. All can be set explicitly. These illustrate controls, not calibrated production precision. The work cap must cover 2 * probes * (lanczos_steps + check_steps) equivalent vector products: both start/final states at both depths. It is independent of the REML trace-solve cap. Earlier Lanczos breakdown can reduce actual products.
The matrix-free stochastic Lanczos quadrature (SLQ) diagnostic uses common Rademacher probes at the two covariance states and both depths, with a seed stream separate from the score traces. Paired differences give an MCSE for the likelihood change. depth_change is the absolute change in the estimate when increasing Lanczos depth; it is a sensitivity check, not a truncation error bound. A small sampling MCSE alone cannot qualify Lanczos accuracy.
For a small exact reference, use:
  likelihood:
    method: exact
    maximum_dimension: 256
This materializes and factors the start/final conditional coefficient matrices, using 2 * coefficient_dimension products. The explicit dimension cap protects against accidentally selecting a dense reference on a large model. It is a caller-selected work/shape limit, not an application RAM ceiling.
Both methods evaluate -0.5 times the change in log|R_observed| + (n + marker_columns) log|K| + log|C| + y'Py. C is the full conditional coefficient matrix, including fixed and nuisance effects. Observed residual submatrices retain missing-trait covariance. The genetic normalization includes latent marker levels. Other prior and coordinate constants cancel because data, design, genomic construction and fixed additional covariances are unchanged. A stable residual-plus-prior quadratic evaluates y'Py. The initial numeric model is retained for this comparison, so requesting likelihood can increase memory.
likelihood.json and run.json.estimation.likelihood report scale: relative_to_start, value, mcse, depth_change, operator products, seconds, message and a status:

not_requested: no diagnostic requested.
not_attempted: covariance fitting did not reach convergence.
qualified: the diagnostic completed and, for SLQ, met the requested targets.
unqualified: a finite SLQ estimate missed one or both precision targets.
failed: a numerical/resource diagnostic failed; no value is published.

Unqualified/failed optional likelihood leaves a separately qualified covariance fit and predictions accepted. No probe increase or exact fallback occurs. This is a start-to-final diagnostic, not an absolute likelihood, per-iteration ascent certificate, or evidence for a global optimum. Do not compare its raw value across models with different starting covariances, fixed designs, data or genomic construction. The compiled sparse-direct route reports its existing absolute restricted likelihood with scale: absolute in the same output block.
The complete exact example (models/multitrait-packed-reml.yml) and SLQ example (models/multitrait-packed-reml-slq.yml) share inputs. Small tests compare exact changes with an independent marginal likelihood (including nonzero markers and missing traits), and paired SLQ estimates/MCSE with an eigenvalue oracle. No industrial likelihood runtime or precision qualification follows from those checks.



The packed EM implementation also estimates unstructured covariance matrices for independent additional-effect levels. It refreshes their small precision templates with each covariance state while preserving level assignments and the pedigree factor. The EM sufficient statistic is the sum of posterior mean outer-products and conditional covariance blocks over those levels. The same exact or stochastic inverse actions supply all covariance-block moments.
Genetic random-regression channels can have a different dimension from the residual trait vector. Covariance matrices retain their declared channel order; residual matrices retain trait order. Whole-block analysis.estimate selection, solve budgets, score/MCSE qualification and optional likelihood controls are unchanged. The likelihood diagnostic includes the determinant changes of every estimated additional-effect prior.
See the complete additional-effect example (models/packed-additional-covariance-reml.yml). Small exact references cover multivariate additional-effect scores and EM updates, an analytic variance optimum, likelihood changes, fixed-block preservation, prediction refits and random-regression channel dimensions. These checks do not establish industrial REML throughput or identifiability of arbitrary collections of effects. FA and serial-parameter REML remain on the compiled route.

Each state uses one response solve plus probes stochastic solves, or one plus the conditional coefficient dimension for exact traces. maximum_solves caps their total across all states. It excludes the initial setup and subsequent independent final prediction solve, which have separate timing/iteration metrics. Every REML solve must pass both transformed and original augmented equation residual checks. The internal solve uses a numerical margin; the requested acceptance tolerances are unchanged.
Convergence requires the maximum absolute free score plus twice the maximum free-score Monte Carlo standard error to be no larger than score_tolerance. The MCSE must also meet maximum_score_mcse. Exact traces have zero sampling MCSE, subject to PCG numerical error. A stochastic moment matrix that is not SPD is rejected without clipping, jitter, silent probe increases or an exact fallback.
A stochastic candidate must pass one final score/precision check using an independent probe bank. Its additional response and probe solves count against the same total cap, and history marks the validation state. Failed independent validation rejects the fit; its probes never guide another update or select another validation bank. This check can add a qualification state after the last permitted covariance-update state. Score convergence does not establish uniqueness or statistical identifiability of an arbitrary covariance model.

title: REML through packed ssSNPBLUP equations
text:
Results include variance_components.csv, parameters.csv, reml_history.csv, likelihood.json and convergence.json, plus native natural-score and score-MCSE vectors. History records scores, MCSE and cumulative solve counts. Converged fits then produce the ordinary prediction tables. Failed fits retain diagnostic parameter states and history but publish no qualified prediction tables.
Likelihood reporting is optional, as described below. It does not control EM updates or replace score convergence. Exact EM has its usual likelihood monotonicity, but stochastic moment updates carry no likelihood-ascent certificate. Reported score MCSE describes trace estimation at the evaluated parameter state; it does not include variance-component estimation uncertainty or provide confidence intervals for the fitted parameters.
Focused tests compare natural scores with an independent dense restricted likelihood and finite differences, verify a joint analytic covariance optimum, check missing-trait EM updates and fitted predictions, and exercise stochastic work/precision rejection. This is not a 50K or industrial runtime qualification. EM can require many covariance updates, each with many PCG solves; prediction timings cannot be reused as REML runtime estimates. The native reml stage covers every covariance evaluation, final stochastic check and optional likelihood diagnostic. reml_likelihood reports the determinant diagnostic separately. Existing fine-grained data/operator profile counters are not an aggregate REML profile; use that stage and the explicit solve totals when assessing cost.
FA, serial/grouped residuals, genetic groups, metafounders, coordinate constraints and joint PEV output are outside the current packed REML interface. The existing compiled sparse-direct REML implementation retains its broader covariance/constraint support and likelihood reporting.

title: REML through packed ssSNPBLUP equations
text:
Omit analysis.likelihood for zero global determinant/operator-product work. To report the restricted-likelihood change from the supplied starting covariances to the final fitted covariances, add one block under analysis:
  likelihood:
    method: slq
    maximum_operator_products: 6144
Defaults are probes: 32, seed: 4402, lanczos_steps: 32, check_steps: 64, maximum_mcse: 1.0 and maximum_depth_change: 0.5. All can be set explicitly. These illustrate controls, not calibrated production precision. The work cap must cover 2 * probes * (lanczos_steps + check_steps) equivalent vector products: both start/final states at both depths. It is independent of the REML trace-solve cap. Earlier Lanczos breakdown can reduce actual products.
The matrix-free stochastic Lanczos quadrature (SLQ) diagnostic uses common Rademacher probes at the two covariance states and both depths, with a seed stream separate from the score traces. Paired differences give an MCSE for the likelihood change. depth_change is the absolute change in the estimate when increasing Lanczos depth; it is a sensitivity check, not a truncation error bound. A small sampling MCSE alone cannot qualify Lanczos accuracy.
For a small exact reference, use:
  likelihood:
    method: exact
    maximum_dimension: 256
This materializes and factors the start/final conditional coefficient matrices, using 2 * coefficient_dimension products. The explicit dimension cap protects against accidentally selecting a dense reference on a large model. It is a caller-selected work/shape limit, not an application RAM ceiling.
Both methods evaluate -0.5 times the change in log|R_observed| + (n + marker_columns) log|K| + log|C| + y'Py. C is the full conditional coefficient matrix, including fixed and nuisance effects. Observed residual submatrices retain missing-trait covariance. The genetic normalization includes latent marker levels. Other prior and coordinate constants cancel because data, design, genomic construction and fixed additional covariances are unchanged. A stable residual-plus-prior quadratic evaluates y'Py. The initial numeric model is retained for this comparison, so requesting likelihood can increase memory.
likelihood.json and run.json.estimation.likelihood report scale: relative_to_start, value, mcse, depth_change, operator products, seconds, message and a status:

not_requested: no diagnostic requested.
not_attempted: covariance fitting did not reach convergence.
qualified: the diagnostic completed and, for SLQ, met the requested targets.
unqualified: a finite SLQ estimate missed one or both precision targets.
failed: a numerical/resource diagnostic failed; no value is published.

Unqualified/failed optional likelihood leaves a separately qualified covariance fit and predictions accepted. No probe increase or exact fallback occurs. This is a start-to-final diagnostic, not an absolute likelihood, per-iteration ascent certificate, or evidence for a global optimum. Do not compare its raw value across models with different starting covariances, fixed designs, data or genomic construction. The compiled sparse-direct route reports its existing absolute restricted likelihood with scale: absolute in the same output block.
The complete exact example (models/multitrait-packed-reml.yml) and SLQ example (models/multitrait-packed-reml-slq.yml) share inputs. Small tests compare exact changes with an independent marginal likelihood (including nonzero markers and missing traits), and paired SLQ estimates/MCSE with an eigenvalue oracle. No industrial likelihood runtime or precision qualification follows from those checks.

title: REML through packed ssSNPBLUP equations
text:
The packed EM implementation also estimates unstructured covariance matrices for independent additional-effect levels. It refreshes their small precision templates with each covariance state while preserving level assignments and the pedigree factor. The EM sufficient statistic is the sum of posterior mean outer-products and conditional covariance blocks over those levels. The same exact or stochastic inverse actions supply all covariance-block moments.
Genetic random-regression channels can have a different dimension from the residual trait vector. Covariance matrices retain their declared channel order; residual matrices retain trait order. Whole-block analysis.estimate selection, solve budgets, score/MCSE qualification and optional likelihood controls are unchanged. The likelihood diagnostic includes the determinant changes of every estimated additional-effect prior.
See the complete additional-effect example (models/packed-additional-covariance-reml.yml). Small exact references cover multivariate additional-effect scores and EM updates, an analytic variance optimum, likelihood changes, fixed-block preservation, prediction refits and random-regression channel dimensions. These checks do not establish industrial REML throughput or identifiability of arbitrary collections of effects. FA and serial-parameter REML remain on the compiled route.

title: Weighted, spatial and non-additive mixed models
text:
All these models use the same gsuite run model.yml command. Inputs, natural covariances, execution settings and outputs stay in the model file. See the YAML specification for complete syntax.
These are small numerical references. They do not qualify industrial REML throughput, large spatial blocks or large dominance/cross-product relationships.

title: Weighted, spatial and non-additive mixed models
section: Observation precision and known measurement error
text:
Observation precision and known measurement error
The residual covariance of one response unit is \(D^{-1/2}R(\theta)D^{-1/2}+sS\), where \(D\) contains positive precision weights, \(S\) is a supplied positive-semidefinite measurement-error covariance and \(s\) is an optional nonnegative variance multiplier. It is not a standard deviation. Missing responses select the corresponding covariance submatrix before inversion.
model:
  residual:
    type: independent
    covariance: residual
    precision_weights: {trait1: weight1, trait2: weight2}
    measurement_error: {covariance: sampling_error, scale: error_scale}
The names on the right refer to mapped input columns or named covariances. A single weight column can apply to every trait. Weights are precision weights, not frequency counts or likelihood powers; zero weights are rejected. Known error is fixed and is excluded from variance estimation. Its multiplier must agree within a residual unit. Supply covariance matrices, not inverses. See the weighted observation example (models/multitrait-observation-precision.yml).
These modifiers currently apply to independent/grouped/supplied residual blocks. Packed REML with these modifiers is rejected; use compiled REML.

title: Weighted, spatial and non-additive mixed models
text:
Spatial field trials
covariances:
  trial_A:
    type: spatial_ar1
    variance: 1.2
    nugget: 0.3
    row_correlation: 0.45
    column_correlation: 0.30
model:
  residual:
    type: spatial_ar1
    group: trial
    row: plot_row
    column: plot_column
    block: field
    covariances: {A: trial_A}
For observed plots \(i,j\) in a field, covariance is \(v\rho_r^{|r_i-r_j|}\rho_c^{|c_i-c_j|}+e\,1_{i=j}\). variance and nugget are positive variances; correlations lie strictly between minus one and one. Trials have separate named parameter blocks. Optional fields are independent replicates sharing a trial’s parameters. Actual integer gaps are retained, missing plots are marginalized and duplicate cells are rejected.
The initial implementation is univariate and stores dense matrices within each observed field: storage grows quadratically with its observed plot count. It does not allocate the entire rectangular grid. See the spatial trial example (models/spatial-field-trial.yml).

title: Weighted, spatial and non-additive mixed models
text:
Selected prediction uncertainty
Define a named prediction once, then reference its level or prediction-grid record in output.uncertainty.contrasts. The same channel, incidence and basis definitions determine the prediction and its uncertainty. Exact output includes PEV and optionally cross-contrast PEC. Direct sessions reuse their accepted factor; packed sessions retain pedigree transforms and the PCG preconditioner. Coefficient right-hand sides stream one at a time.
maximum_solves explicitly bounds inverse actions. Stochastic diagonal output also requires probes, deflation_rank, seed and maximum_mcse in PEV units. The existing independent-sketch estimator operates in target space. Outputs retain raw estimates, MCSE and qualification flags; negative stochastic estimates are not clipped. Sampling qualification is separate from point-fit acceptance. The existing genetic reliability estimators and their limits are unchanged.
Uncertainty is conditional on covariance parameters and excludes their estimation error. The initial contrast YAML route uses a solve task and excludes inherited group effects. Fit covariances first, then refit them for conditional uncertainty. See the contrast example (models/prediction-contrasts.yml).

title: Weighted, spatial and non-additive mixed models
text:
Additional-effect REML
analysis.estimate can select genetic, residual and additional independent-effect covariances on packed EM-REML. Omitted blocks stay fixed. Genetic regression channels may have a different width from the residual trait vector. Small precision templates refresh with each covariance state while level assignments, the exact pedigree factor and genotype provider are retained.
The same inverse actions supply all posterior moments. Score/MCSE gates, the independent final probe check and total solve accounting are unchanged. Optional likelihood changes include the determinants of estimated additional priors. Whole unstructured blocks are free or fixed and must have distinct names; shared parameter tying is not supported by YAML REML. FA, serial parameters, finer coordinate constraints and weighted/known-error REML remain on the compiled route. See the additional-effect example (models/packed-additional-covariance-reml.yml) and packed REML details.

title: Weighted, spatial and non-additive mixed models
From Gaussian regression to the linear mixed model
text: Contents · Abbreviations

title: From Gaussian regression to the linear mixed model
text:
1 Why start here?
An animal’s phenotype reflects its genetic value, its environment and unexplained variation. We want to distinguish these contributions, predict genetic values and describe how uncertain those predictions are. Relatives carry information about one another, and animals with few records should not be treated as if their performance were known precisely.
Linear mixed models express these ideas through means and covariances. This chapter connects the Gaussian regression model to best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) and the animal model. It assumes familiarity with means, variances, normal distributions and basic matrix multiplication. We begin with known covariance parameters. Estimating them is a separate problem, introduced near the end.
By the end, you should be able to explain shrinkage, construct the mixed-model equations, distinguish a breeding value from a phenotype, and understand how a pedigree supplies information for an animal without its own record.
These notes complement the existing Bayesian linear regression notes. The central connection is that a Gaussian distribution for random effects produces the same quadratic penalty that appears in Gaussian-prior regression.

title: From Gaussian regression to the linear mixed model
text:
2 A statistical model for observations
Write the linear mixed model as
\[
y=X\beta+Zu+e,
\]
with
\[
u\sim N(0,K),\qquad e\sim N(0,R),\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(u,e)=0.
\]
We assume joint Gaussianity, so the zero cross-covariance also implies independence. Throughout the derivation, \(K\) and \(R\) are known positive-definite matrices and \(X\) has full column rank. Singular covariance models and redundant fixed-effect columns need additional care and are deferred to later chapters.

Here \(K\) denotes the entire random-effect covariance. Later we will reserve \(G\) for a genomic relationship matrix, avoiding two meanings for the same symbol.

2.1 Conditional and marginal distributions
Conditional on \(u\),
\[
y\mid u,\beta\sim N(X\beta+Zu,R).
\]
Integrating over the random effects gives
\[
y\mid\beta\sim N(X\beta,V),\qquad V=ZKZ^\top+R.
\]
These are two views of the same model. The conditional view helps us predict individual effects. The marginal view helps us estimate fixed effects and covariance parameters. Related observations can be correlated through \(K\), through \(R\), or both.


2.2 What makes an effect fixed or random?
A fixed effect is represented by an unknown coefficient without a probability distribution in this model. A random effect is assigned a distribution whose covariance specifies how information is shared and how strongly estimates are regularized.
For example, herd can be fixed when the aim is to adjust for a particular set of herd differences, or random when a population distribution of herd effects is appropriate. This is a scientific modelling decision; it is not determined solely by how many herds occur in the data. In either case we must consider confounding, connectedness and whether the assumptions suit the study design.

title: From Gaussian regression to the linear mixed model
section: 3 Shrinkage in the simplest possible example
text:
3 Shrinkage in the simplest possible example
Suppose an animal has \(r\) independent records after adjustment for a known population mean \(\mu\):
\[
y_j=\mu+u+e_j,\qquad
u\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2),\qquad e_j\sim N(0,\sigma_e^2).
\]
The record mean has residual variance \(\sigma_e^2/r\). Multiplying its Gaussian likelihood by the Gaussian distribution for \(u\) gives
\[
u\mid\bar y,\mu\sim N\left(
\lambda(\bar y-\mu),
\left[\frac{1}{\sigma_u^2}+\frac{r}{\sigma_e^2}\right]^{-1}
\right),
\qquad
\lambda=\frac{\sigma_u^2}{\sigma_u^2+\sigma_e^2/r}.
\]
The prediction is the adjusted record mean multiplied by a number between zero and one. With little information, it stays close to the population mean. With more independent records, it moves towards the animal’s observed mean. Larger residual variation produces more shrinkage; larger between-animal variation produces less.
For \(\sigma_u^2=1\), \(\sigma_e^2=3\) and \(\bar y-\mu=2\):

This particular calculation assumes independent residuals and no additional permanent animal effect. Repeated records with shared environmental effects contain less independent information than this simple formula assumes.

title: From Gaussian regression to the linear mixed model
text:
4 Deriving the mixed-model equations
This is the classical mixed-model prediction construction (Henderson, 1975; Robinson, 1991).
For known \(K\) and \(R\), consider the quadratic objective
\[
Q(\beta,u)=
(y-X\beta-Zu)^\top R^{-1}(y-X\beta-Zu)+u^\top K^{-1}u.
\]
The first term penalizes lack of fit in units of residual covariance. The second penalizes random effects according to their covariance. It is not an arbitrary extra penalty: it comes from the Gaussian distribution of \(u\).
Let \(r=y-X\beta-Zu\). Setting the derivatives to zero gives
\[
X^\top R^{-1}r=0,\qquad
Z^\top R^{-1}r=K^{-1}u.
\]
Rearranging yields Henderson’s mixed-model equations:
\[
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
X^\top R^{-1}X & X^\top R^{-1}Z\\
Z^\top R^{-1}X & Z^\top R^{-1}Z+K^{-1}
\end{bmatrix}}_{C}
\begin{bmatrix}\hat\beta\\\hat u\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}X^\top R^{-1}y\\Z^\top R^{-1}y\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The precision matrix \(K^{-1}\) stabilizes the random-effect block. Even if two animals have identical incidence columns, the covariance model can make their joint prediction well defined. It cannot, however, repair arbitrary non-identifiability in the fixed-effect part.
In the special case \(K=\sigma_u^2I\) and \(R=\sigma_e^2I\), multiplying both sides by \(\sigma_e^2\) places \(\alpha I=(\sigma_e^2/\sigma_u^2)I\) in the random-effect block. Thus the familiar ridge parameter is a ratio of variance components. The intercept and other fixed effects are not penalized in this formulation.

title: From Gaussian regression to the linear mixed model
section: 5 BLUE, BLUP and the Bayesian connection
text:
5 BLUE, BLUP and the Bayesian connection
Define
\[
B=(X^\top V^{-1}X)^{-1}.
\]
An equivalent solution is
\[
\hat\beta=BX^\top V^{-1}y,\qquad
\hat u=KZ^\top V^{-1}(y-X\hat\beta).
\]
The first expression is generalized least squares. The second uses the covariance between effects and observations, \(\operatorname{Cov}(u,y)=KZ^\top\), to predict effects from adjusted records. The mixed-model and marginal expressions agree; neither requires an explicit dense inverse in a practical large-scale implementation.
BLUE means best linear unbiased estimator of an estimable fixed-effect contrast. BLUP means best linear unbiased predictor of a random-effect contrast, where “best” means minimum mean squared prediction error within the linear unbiased class under the assumed covariances. Unbiasedness averages over both random effects and residuals. It does not mean \(E(\hat u\mid u)=u\): shrinkage generally prevents that conditional equality.
The linear optimality result needs the specified first and second moments; Gaussianity additionally supplies the conditional-distribution interpretation. With \(\beta\) known,
\[
E(u\mid y,\beta)=KZ^\top V^{-1}(y-X\beta).
\]
With an improper flat prior on \(\beta\), known covariances and a proper resulting posterior, the joint posterior of \((\beta,u)\) is Gaussian, with mean equal to the mixed-model solution and covariance \(C^{-1}\). A proper informative prior on \(\beta\) changes these equations. These equivalences do not make a fixed-covariance BLUP analysis a fully Bayesian variance-component analysis.

title: From Gaussian regression to the linear mixed model
text:
6 Introducing the pedigree animal model
Pedigree relationships and their sparse precision representation underpin the animal model (Henderson, 1976).
For additive genetic values \(a\), write
\[
y=X\beta+Za+e,\qquad
a\sim N(0,\sigma_a^2 A),\qquad e\sim N(0,\sigma_e^2I).
\]
\(A\) is the numerator relationship matrix. Under the ordinary pedigree model, \(A_{ii}=1+F_i\), where \(F_i\) is the inbreeding coefficient, and off-diagonal entries describe additive relationships relative to the chosen founder base. The genetic covariance is \(\sigma_a^2 A\), not \(A\) alone.
Consider two unrelated, non-inbred founders and their offspring:

Their relationship matrix is
\[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1/2\\0&1&1/2\\1/2&1/2&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
With an intercept, \(\sigma_a^2=1\) and \(\sigma_e^2=1\),
\[
y=\begin{bmatrix}8\\12\end{bmatrix},\quad
X=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix},\quad
Z=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Solving gives \(\hat\mu=10\) and \(\hat a=(-1,1,0)^\top\). The parents’ deviations are shrunk from \((-2,2)\) to \((-1,1)\). The offspring prediction equals their average, zero, because its unobserved Mendelian sampling term has conditional mean zero. Zero here means the model’s genetic reference level; it does not mean that the offspring’s true breeding value is known to be zero.

6.1 Information from an offspring record
If the offspring A3 also has a phenotype of 14, its record changes the estimated intercept to 11 and the genetic predictions to \((-1,1,1)^\top\). Information can travel through relationships in both directions; it is not limited to passing parental predictions to offspring.

title: From Gaussian regression to the linear mixed model
section: 7 What uncertainty belongs to a prediction?
text:
7 What uncertainty belongs to a prediction?
The prediction error is \(a-\hat a\), rather than the observed residual \(y-X\hat\beta-Z\hat a\). These quantities answer different questions. For the general model, let
\[
P=V^{-1}-V^{-1}XB X^\top V^{-1}.
\]
The prediction error covariance of the BLUP is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(u-\hat u)=K-KZ^\top PZK.
\]
This includes uncertainty from estimating fixed effects. It equals the random-effect block of \(C^{-1}\) when \(C\) uses the unscaled precision convention above. If the equations are multiplied by \(\sigma_e^2\), their inverse must also be rescaled before interpreting its entries as variances.
Under this known-covariance model, a common reliability measure is
\[
\mathrm{Rel}_i=1-\frac{\mathrm{PEV}_i}{K_{ii}}.
\]
In the example the parent prediction-error variances (PEVs) are \(0.75\) and their reliabilities are \(0.25\). The offspring PEV is \(1\) and reliability is zero: its prediction is available, but this balanced example supplies no information about its genetic value beyond the prior variance after allowing for the unknown mean.
Reliability concerns uncertainty in a genetic value. Predicting a new phenotype also involves residual variation and possibly new environmental effects. With estimated covariance parameters, a plug-in PEV generally does not include all variance-component uncertainty.

title: From Gaussian regression to the linear mixed model
section: 8 Known covariances, REML and Bayesian inference
text:
8 Known covariances, REML and Bayesian inference
For restricted likelihood see Patterson and Thompson (1971); for the broader likelihood and Bayesian quantitative-genetics framework see Sorensen and Gianola (2002).
The derivations so far condition on covariance parameters, denoted collectively by \(\theta\). These may include genetic and residual variances and, for several traits, covariance matrices.
Supplied-covariance solving computes \(\hat\beta\) and \(\hat u\) at specified \(\theta\). It answers the prediction problem without estimating \(\theta\).
restricted maximum likelihood (REML) followed by prediction estimates \(\theta\) from residual contrasts and then substitutes \(\hat\theta\) into the prediction equations. Up to constants independent of \(\theta\), the restricted log likelihood is
\[
\ell_R(\theta)=-\tfrac12\left\{
\log|V|+\log|X^\top V^{-1}X|+y^\top Py+(n-p)\log(2\pi)
\right\}.
\]
The resulting predictor is commonly called empirical BLUP. Because its covariances depend on the data, it is generally no longer linear in \(y\).
Fully Bayesian inference assigns priors to \(\theta\) and integrates over its posterior. A posterior mean such as \(E(u\mid y)\) averages over covariance uncertainty rather than evaluating a prediction formula at a single estimate.
These are different inferential tasks. A numerical linear solver does not by itself estimate variance components or quantify their uncertainty.

title: From Gaussian regression to the linear mixed model
text:
9 Connecting the equations to gsuite
In a supplied-covariance standalone YAML (a human-readable model-configuration format) model, \(X\) is specified by fixed, the grouping/incidence information by the random-effect group, and \(K\) by the relationship and covariance declarations. For the three-animal example, the central model declarations would be:
relationships:
  A: {type: pedigree, input: pedigree}
covariances:
  genetic: [[1.0]]
  residual: [[1.0]]
model:
  data: observations
  fixed: '1'
  random:
    genetic:
      group: individual
      relationship: A
      covariance: genetic
  residual: residual
analysis: {task: solve}
This is a model fragment, not a complete runnable file: input tables, trait mapping, execution and output declarations are also required. For complete existing examples see the YAML example catalog and the pedigree analysis tutorial. Interface support and qualification are described in the model catalog; the equations alone do not establish support for an arbitrary model.

9.1 An illustrative multitrait model
The framework accommodates many combinations of traits, relationships and random effects. As one illustration, a four-trait model for animal \(i\) and trait \(t\) can be written
\[
y_{it}=\mu_t+a_{it}+h_{\operatorname{herd}(i),t}
+f_{\operatorname{family}(i),t}+c_{it}+e_{it}.
\]
Here \(a\) denotes genetic values, \(h\) herd effects, \(f\) family effects and \(c\) individual-environment effects. Assume independence between these effect classes, with covariance between traits within each class. With effects stacked trait by trait, representative covariance blocks are
\[
\operatorname{Var}(a)=\Sigma_a\otimes H,\quad
\operatorname{Var}(h)=\Sigma_h\otimes I_h,\quad
\operatorname{Var}(f)=\Sigma_f\otimes I_f,\quad
\operatorname{Var}(c)=\Sigma_c\otimes I_{\rm animal}.
\]
For one complete four-trait record per observed animal and the same ordering, \(R=\Sigma_e\otimes I_{\rm observed}\). Missing trait records require selecting the corresponding rows and covariance entries. Different stacking conventions change Kronecker order, not the statistical model.
\(H\) combines pedigree and genomic information; its construction, genomic adjustment and pedigree blending belong to the single-step chapter. SNP-effect and animal-effect representations will be connected explicitly there.
With exactly one visit per animal, an independent individual-environment component and an unrestricted within-record residual component cannot generally be estimated separately: only their sum is identified from those records. They can nevertheless be specified separately when their covariance matrices are supplied, as in the four-trait benchmark. This is one example of the broader model framework, rather than a development endpoint. Biological naming does not establish statistical identifiability.

title: From Gaussian regression to the linear mixed model
text:
10 Model, formulation and computation
The statistical model specifies \(X\), \(Z\), \(K\), \(R\) and the target of inference. A formulation expresses that model in particular unknowns, for example animal or marker effects. A numerical method solves the resulting equations, using direct factorization or an iterative algorithm.
A preconditioner changes how an iterative solver reaches a solution. If it is used only for that purpose, it does not change the model’s target equations. An approximate preconditioner can therefore produce the same accepted solution as an exact one, while taking a different number of iterations. Adding a ridge to the model covariance, changing blending or dropping an effect changes the target and needs a separate scientific justification.
Numerical residual checks assess whether the specified equations were solved. They do not demonstrate that the model fits the biology or predicts new data well. Those require model checking and appropriately designed validation.

title: From Gaussian regression to the linear mixed model
text:
11 Guided reading

Refresher: Bayesian linear regression notes. Revisit Gaussian priors and posterior precision, then identify the analogous \(K^{-1}\) term in this chapter.
BLUP interpretation: Robinson (1991) explains random-effect prediction and its connections across statistical traditions.
Foundations and selection: Henderson (1975) develops estimation and prediction under a selection model. Read after the derivation, focusing on its assumptions. The small example here does not model selection.
Inference beyond supplied covariances: Sorensen and Gianola (2002) connects likelihood estimation and Bayesian analysis in quantitative genetics.

Continue with the advanced notes and their shared bibliography.

title: From Gaussian regression to the linear mixed model
text:

title: 2. Prediction and uncertainty at supplied covariances
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: 2. Prediction and uncertainty at supplied covariances
text:
1 Equivalent prediction systems
The covariance and mixed-equation representations describe the same known-covariance prediction problem (Henderson, 1975; Robinson, 1991).
Set
\[
B=(X^\top V^{-1}X)^{-1},\qquad
P=V^{-1}-V^{-1}XB X^\top V^{-1}.
\]
The known-covariance best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) for fixed effects and best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) for random effects are
\[
\hat\beta=BX^\top V^{-1}y,\qquad \hat u=KZ^\top Py.
\]
Equivalently, solve \(C\hat x=b\), where
\[
C=\begin{bmatrix}
X^\top R^{-1}X&X^\top R^{-1}Z\\
Z^\top R^{-1}X&Z^\top R^{-1}Z+K^{-1}
\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}X^\top R^{-1}y\\Z^\top R^{-1}y\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Eliminating \(u\) connects the mixed-model equations to the marginal equations through the Woodbury identity:
\[
V^{-1}=R^{-1}-R^{-1}Z
(K^{-1}+Z^\top R^{-1}Z)^{-1}Z^\top R^{-1}.
\]
This is an algebraic equivalence, not a recommendation to form the matrices densely. Efficient implementations apply covariance/precision operators, exploit sparse structure and reuse factors across right-hand sides.
BLUP unbiasedness is unconditional over the random effects and residuals. It is not conditional unbiasedness for each realized breeding value. Under Gaussianity, known covariances and a flat prior for identifiable fixed effects, the mixed-model solution also equals the joint posterior mean and mode. Integrating over uncertain covariances generally changes that conclusion.

title: 2. Prediction and uncertainty at supplied covariances
section: 2 Prediction targets, PEV and uncertainty accounting
text:
2 Prediction targets, PEV and uncertainty accounting
The distinctions between prediction error and coefficient uncertainty are central to BLUP (Robinson, 1991). Additional error from estimating covariance parameters is treated by Kackar and Harville (1984).
For a genetic contrast \(t=l^\top u\),
\[
\mathrm{PEV}(t)=l^\top(K-KZ^\top PZK)l.
\]
For a target combining fixed and random coefficients, \(t=l_\beta^\top\beta+l_u^\top u\), set \(l=(l_\beta^\top,l_u^\top)^\top\). Under the known-covariance assumptions,
\[
E[(\hat t-t)^2]=l^\top C^{-1}l.
\]
The mixed fixed/random blocks matter. Adding a fixed-effect variance to an animal PEV without their cross-covariance is generally incorrect. A new phenotypic observation may add residual variance and new random effects; if its residual is correlated with training records, the full joint covariance must be used rather than simply adding a scalar residual variance.
For a random contrast with nonzero prior variance \(l_u^\top K l_u\), its known-covariance reliability can be written \(1-\mathrm{PEV}(t)/(l_u^\top K l_u)\). Inbreeding changes animal-specific prior variances. Reliability of a contrast is not the average reliability of its constituent animals.
Exact selected solves, selected inverse calculations and stochastic uncertainty estimators are computational choices for a specified uncertainty target. They have different work and approximation properties. A stochastic preconditioner diagonal is not a stochastic PEV estimate; uncertainty controls must retain their own qualification limits. See prediction-error documentation.

title: 2. Prediction and uncertainty at supplied covariances
text:
3 Unknown and unobserved targets
For an unobserved random target \(u_*\), let \(K_{*u}=\operatorname{Cov}(u_*,u)\) and \(K_{**}=\operatorname{Var}(u_*)\). With the same fixed-effect treatment as above,
\[
\hat u_*=K_{*u}Z^\top Py,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(u_*-\hat u_*)=K_{**}-K_{*u}Z^\top PZK_{u*}.
\]
An animal without a phenotype can therefore receive a prediction through relationships. For an independent new environmental level with no connecting information, its random-effect prediction is zero and its prior uncertainty remains. A future phenotype with a nonzero fixed-effect design row requires the joint fixed/random target calculation, including cross terms.

title: 2. Prediction and uncertainty at supplied covariances
text:
4 Contrasts and connectedness
For two breeding values, \(\mathrm{PEV}(a_i-a_j)=\mathrm{PEV}(a_i)+
\mathrm{PEV}(a_j)-2\mathrm{PEC}_{ij}\), where PEC denotes prediction-error covariance. Two animals can each have modest marginal reliability while their within-family contrast is relatively precise, or appear individually precise while a poorly connected between-group contrast remains uncertain.
Report the uncertainty of the actual selection or comparison target. Rankings and differences between populations cannot be assessed from a list of marginal PEVs alone. Simultaneous ranking uncertainty is also a different question from one-animal marginal intervals.

title: 2. Prediction and uncertainty at supplied covariances
text:
5 Prediction after covariance estimation
The two-stage uncertainty problem is studied by Kackar and Harville (1984); fully Bayesian integration is a different inferential construction (Sorensen and Gianola, 2002).
Substituting \(\hat\theta\) into the BLUP and PEV formulas produces empirical predictions and conditional plug-in uncertainty. It does not propagate all uncertainty in \(\hat\theta\). Parametric bootstrap and full Bayesian analysis can address broader uncertainty under their respective assumptions, but they have different targets, computational costs and calibration requirements.
A Gaussian conditional interval for a breeding value is not automatically a frequentist confidence interval with exact coverage after model selection, variance estimation or selection of the animals being reported.

5.1 Prediction when the representation is learned
Let \(\psi\) collect measurement, feature or loading parameters and let \(\theta\) collect covariance parameters, with \(\mathcal D\) denoting all analysis data. In a fully specified Bayesian joint model, the law of total variance gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}(t\mid\mathcal D)
=E_{\theta,\psi\mid\mathcal D}
[\operatorname{Var}(t\mid\mathcal D,\theta,\psi)]
+\operatorname{Var}_{\theta,\psi\mid\mathcal D}
[E(t\mid\mathcal D,\theta,\psi)].
\]
A plug-in calculation conditions on one learned representation and generally omits the second term. This posterior identity is not an automatic frequentist PEV correction; calibration under an empirical fitting procedure needs its own assessment (Kackar and Harville, 1984; Sorensen and Gianola, 2002).
For annotation-informed prediction, uncertainty concerns learned marker shrinkage as well as covariance parameters. For phenomics it may also concern calibration, trajectories and latent scores. Specify whether the target is a transmissible genetic value or a future phenotype conditional on candidate measurements. The model progressions in functional information and phenomics make those choices explicit.






Implementation in gsuite



Fixed-covariance prediction is available through the standalone solve task and development R model interfaces. Selected pedigree PEV and reliability use retained direct factors; standalone selected contrasts and packed genetic uncertainty have their own exact/stochastic controls. Availability is target- and route-specific. These outputs condition on supplied or fitted covariances; they do not implement the full learned-representation uncertainty decomposition developed above.


Next: variance-component estimation.

title: 4. Pedigree, genomic and combined relationship models
text:
Genomic prediction models differ in their assumptions about genetic effects, their reference populations and the information they use. The choice of marker-effect or animal-effect equations is sometimes only a change of representation. Changing the prior distribution, relationship kernel or genomic blending generally changes the statistical model.
Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

The prediction target is the additive genetic value relative to a declared base. Total genotypic value, marker association and individual future phenotype are different targets.

title: 4. Pedigree, genomic and combined relationship models
section: 2 Pedigree BLUP as the relationship baseline
text:
2 Pedigree BLUP as the relationship baseline
The sparse pedigree-inverse construction is due to Henderson (1976).
For an additive animal model, \(K_a=\sigma_a^2A\). If animal \(i\) has known sire \(s\) and dam \(d\), pedigree recursion gives \(A_{ij}=(A_{sj}+A_{dj})/2\) for earlier animals and \(A_{ii}=1+A_{sd}/2\). Unknown parent contributions follow the specified founder assumptions. Animals must be topologically ordered for this recursion, while external identities must remain stable across all outputs.
A structural representation writes \(a=P_{\rm ped}a+\varepsilon\), where \(P_{\rm ped}\) contains known parental half-contributions and \(\varepsilon\) contains independent Mendelian innovations under the pedigree model, taking \(\sigma_a^2=1\) for this relationship construction. With their correctly computed variance diagonal \(D_{\rm ped}\) on the relationship scale,
\[
A^{-1}=(I-P_{\rm ped})^\top D_{\rm ped}^{-1}(I-P_{\rm ped}).
\]
Parental inbreeding changes innovation variances. The simple diagonal values for unrelated, non-inbred founders must not be applied indiscriminately to inbred pedigrees. This representation explains why pedigree precision can be sparse even though the relationship matrix itself is dense.
For founder mean and covariance assumptions, genomic compatibility and crossbred prediction targets, see genetic bases and crossbreeding.
Pedigree best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) uses expected relationships under this inheritance model. Genomic models can capture variation in realized marker sharing around those pedigree expectations; their base, scale and target must still be specified.

title: 4. Pedigree, genomic and combined relationship models
section: 3 Marker coding and the genetic reference population
text:
3 Marker coding and the genetic reference population
Let \(M_{ij}\in\{0,1,2\}\) count a consistently chosen allele at marker \(j\). For reference allele frequencies \(p_j\), define
\[
W_{ij}=M_{ij}-2p_j,\qquad
d=\sum_j2p_j(1-p_j),\qquad G=WW^\top/d.
\]
This common construction uses one overall normalization. It differs from standardizing every marker to unit variance before taking a cross-product. Both are legitimate covariance specifications, but they imply different marker weighting. Rare variants can receive much greater relative weight under per-marker standardization.
Frequencies calculated in the training sample, the full genotyped population or an external base need not give the same \(W\). Under mean imputation at these same frequencies, a missing centered dosage is zero. That is an imputation assumption, not evidence that the genotype is observed. Marker filtering, imputation and frequency estimation should be recorded separately.
Reversing an allele consistently changes one column of \(W\) to its negative. Its contribution to \(WW^\top\) is unchanged, while the corresponding estimated marker effect changes sign. Inconsistent allele alignment between training and prediction data changes predictions.

title: 4. Pedigree, genomic and combined relationship models
section: 4 SNP-BLUP and GBLUP: an exact covariance equivalence
text:
4 SNP-BLUP and GBLUP: an exact covariance equivalence
In single-nucleotide polymorphism best linear unbiased prediction (SNP-BLUP),
\[
y=X\beta+ZWm+e,\qquad m\sim N(0,\sigma_m^2I).
\]
The induced genetic covariance is
\[
K_a=\sigma_m^2WW^\top=\sigma_a^2G,
\qquad \sigma_m^2=\sigma_a^2/d.
\]
Consequently SNP-BLUP and genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP) give identical fitted genetic values when their covariance scales, fixed-effect spaces, observations and residual models match. This is the equivalence examined by (VanRaden, 2008).
With one record per genotyped animal and \(R=\sigma_e^2I\), marker equations contain the penalty \(\lambda I\), where
\[
\lambda=\frac{\sigma_e^2}{\sigma_m^2}
=\frac{d\sigma_e^2}{\sigma_a^2}.
\]
The factor \(d\) must not disappear when transferring variances between parameterizations. An intercept is normally unpenalized.
For a new individual with centered genotype row \(w_*^\top\),
\[
\hat a_*=w_*^\top\hat m
=\operatorname{Cov}(a_*,y)V^{-1}(y-X\hat\beta).
\]
This expression also clarifies kernel prediction: predictions for a new individual require training-to-new cross-covariances, not just the training kernel. Compatible uncertainty additionally needs the target’s prior variance.
\(G\) is often singular because of centering, limited marker rank or duplicate genotypes. A Gaussian model with a positive-semidefinite genetic covariance can still be valid when \(R\) makes \(V\) positive definite. The marginal formula or marker model then remains usable without an ordinary inverse of \(G\). Adding a ridge solely to permit inversion is not an exact reparameterization of the original singular model.

4.1 Why use one representation rather than another?
An explicit genomic matrix for \(n_g\) genotyped animals costs \(O(n_g^2)\) storage. A marker formulation can apply \(W\) and \(W^\top\) without constructing it, including from packed dosage data. Conversely, a retained relationship factor may make repeated solves attractive when its dimension and fill are manageable. Trait count, missingness, factor reuse and uncertainty requests also matter. Comparing only equation counts does not determine which representation is faster.

title: 4. Pedigree, genomic and combined relationship models
section: 5 Weighted markers and several genomic components
text:
5 Weighted markers and several genomic components
With \(m\sim N(0,\tau^2D)\) for a nonnegative diagonal \(D\),
\[
K_a=\tau^2WDW^\top.
\]
Fixed externally supplied weights still define a Gaussian mixed model. Weights estimated adaptively from the same phenotypes create a larger estimation procedure; treating them as known afterwards omits their estimation uncertainty.
For biological feature definitions, annotation overlap and feature-dependent marker priors, see Chapter 14.
A multi-kernel model instead writes
\[
a=\sum_k a_k,\qquad
a_k\sim N(0,\sigma_k^2G_k),\qquad
K_a=\sum_k\sigma_k^2G_k.
\]
Possible partitions include chromosomes, functional annotations or variant classes. Each kernel needs its own scale convention. Highly similar kernels can leave component variances weakly identified even when total genetic prediction is stable. Overlapping annotations do not automatically yield independent biological variance contributions: the model defines how that overlap is allocated.

title: 4. Pedigree, genomic and combined relationship models
text:
6 Single-step models: retaining non-genotyped animals
Partition the pedigree matrix into non-genotyped (\(n\)) and genotyped (\(g\)) animals. The pedigree conditional model can be written
\[
a_n=T a_g+\varepsilon_n,\qquad
T=A_{ng}A_{gg}^{-1},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_n)=\sigma_a^2C_n,
\]
where \(C_n=A_{nn}-A_{ng}A_{gg}^{-1}A_{gn}\). Retain this conditional distribution but replace the marginal genotyped covariance by \(\operatorname{Var}(a_g)=\sigma_a^2G_b\). The resulting joint relationship is
\[
H=\begin{bmatrix}
C_n+TG_bT^\top&TG_b\\G_bT^\top&G_b
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
For nonsingular matrices this gives
\[
H^{-1}=A^{-1}+E_g^\top(G_b^{-1}-A_{gg}^{-1})E_g.
\]
Here \(E_g\) selects genotyped animals from the complete animal vector. This provides a common basis for single-step genomic BLUP (ssGBLUP) and its marker-effect representation, single-step SNP-BLUP (ssSNPBLUP). Phenotypes on non-genotyped relatives remain in the model; they are not simply discarded or treated as additional genotypes. See (Christensen and Lund, 2010).
An ssSNPBLUP formulation expresses the genomic part through marker effects and retains the additional pedigree-related terms needed to reproduce \(H\). It is not ordinary SNP-BLUP with missing genotype rows filled by zero. Equivalence requires matching the complete latent covariance, including blending, adjustment and any additional genetic component.

6.1 Marginal and conditional pedigree precision are different
Partition animals into non-genotyped (\(n\)) and genotyped (\(g\)), and write \(Q=A^{-1}\). The marginal precision for the genotyped breeding values is
\[
A_{gg}^{-1}=Q_{gg}-Q_{gn}Q_{nn}^{-1}Q_{ng}.
\]
It is not generally the principal block \(Q_{gg}\). The latter is the conditional precision of \(a_g\) given \(a_n\). Applying the Schur complement can involve a solve with \(Q_{nn}\) without constructing the dense marginal inverse. This distinction is essential when interpreting timings labelled “pedigree solve” or comparing apparently similar single-step implementations.


6.2 Adjustment, pedigree blending and identity ridge
One moment adjustment is \(G_*=\alpha\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top+\gamma G\), chosen to align specified pedigree and genomic moments. Blending then might be
\[
G_b=(1-w)G_*+wA_{gg}.
\]
The model used for our four-trait comparison has \(w=0.05\), adjustment of \(G\) to \(A\), and no independent identity ridge. In contrast, \((1-w)G_*+wI\) assigns the additional variation to independent genotyped-animal directions. It is not the same as 5% pedigree blending.
Without the adjustment intercept, a pedigree blend admits the representation \(a_g=Wm+r_g\) with independent \(r_g\) having covariance \(w\sigma_a^2A_{gg}\) and an appropriately scaled marker covariance. An adjustment intercept contributes an additional rank-one covariance term. It must be represented consistently; a negative adjustment intercept cannot be interpreted on its own as the variance of an independent scalar effect.
The pedigree block \(A_{gg}^{-1}\) is generally dense even when \(A^{-1}\) is sparse. Schur-complement solves or equivalent latent systems avoid explicitly forming that dense inverse. Their cost is real model algebra, distinct from the cost of decoding markers.


6.3 APY and other approximations
The algorithm for proven and young (APY) partitions genotyped animals into a core and a remaining (noncore) group. The name is historical: the core need not consist exclusively of older or proven animals. It retains a core-dependent conditional prediction and approximates the conditional covariance among remaining animals, typically by a diagonal. Thus an APY relationship approximation can change the target model; its predictions depend on core choice and approximation quality. It should not be described as merely a different preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) preconditioner for an unchanged exact system. An approximate operator used only inside a preconditioner is a separate case. For the original recursive construction see Misztal et al. (2014); for an applied treatment of the core/noncore construction see Garcia et al. (2020).

title: 4. Pedigree, genomic and combined relationship models
text:
7 Bayesian marker-effect distributions
Gaussian SNP-BLUP assigns one common marker variance on the chosen coding scale. The original BayesA/B models allow heterogeneous marker effects (Meuwissen et al., 2001). Important families include:








Family
Representative prior
Implication




BayesA
Gaussian effects with marker-specific inverse-chi-squared variance mixing
Heavy-tailed marginal effects; no point mass at zero


BayesB
A point mass at zero plus a heavy-tailed active component
Selection and marker-specific active shrinkage


BayesC-type models
A point mass at zero plus a common Gaussian active component
Selection with a shared active-effect variance


BayesR-type models
A finite mixture of zero and several Gaussian variance classes
Several degrees of shrinkage



The precise prior includes mixture probabilities, variance scales and their hyperpriors. Names alone are insufficient to reproduce an analysis; some implementations fix a quantity that others estimate. BayesC-type extensions are described by Habier et al. (2011). For BayesR, see Erbe et al. (2012) and Moser et al. (2015).
Conditional on mixture assignments and variance parameters, parts of these models are Gaussian. Integrating over those unknowns gives a non-Gaussian posterior and generally nonlinear prediction in \(y\). Matching the prior’s second moment to a GBLUP covariance therefore does not make the posterior predictions equivalent. Posterior mean, posterior mode, variable-selection probability and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draw are also different outputs.
Posterior inclusion probabilities describe marker inclusion under a declared prior and linkage disequilibrium (LD) structure. They are not automatically probabilities that a marker is causal. Prediction performance does not establish fine-mapping resolution.

title: 4. Pedigree, genomic and combined relationship models
text:
8 Beyond additive, single-trait prediction
An additive/dominance genomic covariance construction and its interpretation are developed by Vitezica et al. (2013).

8.1 Dominance and epistasis
An additive-plus-dominance model uses independent effects with \(K=\sigma_a^2G_a+\sigma_d^2G_d\). Dominance coding must be defined relative to allele frequencies and the intended statistical decomposition. Simply adding squared dosage columns does not specify an orthogonal dominance model.
A Hadamard-product kernel such as \(G_a\circ G_a\) can represent an interaction covariance, but its interpretation depends on coding, centering and whether self-interactions and lower-order effects are included. Kernel labels are not sufficient evidence that estimated components correspond to unique biological mechanisms.
An additive breeding value concerns transmission to offspring under the specified model. Adding dominance or interaction predictions produces a different target, often a component of an individual’s total genotypic value.


8.2 Multitrait, reaction norms and factor structure
For a common additive kernel and trait-major stacking, \(K_a=\Sigma_a\otimes G\) (or \(\Sigma_a\otimes H\) in single-step). Genetic correlations share information across traits but do not guarantee that adding any trait improves prediction in every population.
Reaction norms model genetic coefficients over an environmental basis. If \(a_i(z)=b(z)^\top u_i\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i,u_j)=G_{ij}\Sigma_u\), then
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\{a_i(z),a_j(z')\}
=G_{ij}b(z)^\top\Sigma_u b(z').
\]
A factor-analytic trait/environment covariance, \(\Sigma_a=\Lambda\Lambda^\top+\Psi\), reduces the covariance parameterization and imposes structure. It is not automatically the same as a full unstructured multitrait model. Cross-environment prediction depends on the environmental information available at prediction time as well as the genetic kernel.


8.3 Genomic technologies and uncertain input genotypes
Low-coverage sequencing and imputation expand the ways genomic information can be obtained; Lamb et al. (2021) provide a cattle prediction proof of concept. Their availability does not make uncertain dosages exact measurements. Under a simple zero-mean prior with independent marker effects of fixed variance \(\tau^2\), also independent of the genotype data \(\mathcal D_g\), the induced covariance is
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(a\mid\mathcal D_g)
=\tau^2 E(WW^\top\mid\mathcal D_g),
\]
where centering frequencies and scaling are held fixed. Substituting \(\bar W=E(W\mid\mathcal D_g)\) instead uses \(\tau^2\bar W\bar W^\top\) and omits
\[
\tau^2\sum_j\operatorname{Cov}(W_{\cdot j}\mid\mathcal D_g).
\]
This is an illustrative covariance identity, not a complete likelihood for sequence data or a claim that every prediction requires full genotype integration. It shows what must be assessed when dosage uncertainty is consequential. Shared imputation uncertainty can also connect animals.
Structural variants, changing variant sets and breed-specific frequencies likewise require explicit representation and base conventions. Richer functional information then changes the prior on these variants, rather than repairing inconsistent allele alignment or scaling. See functional information and genetic bases.

title: 4. Pedigree, genomic and combined relationship models
section: 9 Choosing and assessing a genomic model
text:
9 Choosing and assessing a genomic model
For an evaluation, record the scientific target, training and prediction populations, marker coding and frequencies, kernel normalization, covariance parameters, adjustment/blending rule and treatment of non-genotyped animals. Specify whether covariance parameters are supplied, estimated by restricted maximum likelihood (REML) or integrated in Bayesian inference. Computational choices should preserve the intended model or make the approximation and its consequences explicit.
Qualification should connect three levels: an independent small covariance reference, a representative model fit with original-equation residual checks, and prediction validation designed for the intended deployment. Randomly splitting close relatives can answer a different question from prediction across generations or populations. Hyperparameters, marker selection and phenotype-derived weights must be learned inside the training procedure.

title: 4. Pedigree, genomic and combined relationship models
text:
10 Reading alongside this chapter

(VanRaden, 2008): marker/relationship equivalence and genomic relationship construction.
(Meuwissen et al., 2001): the original dense-marker prediction study and heterogeneous effect priors.
(Christensen and Lund, 2010) and (Aguilar et al., 2010): joint pedigree/genomic evaluation including non-genotyped animals.
Existing Bayesian regression notes: Gaussian shrinkage, mixture indicators and posterior inference.







Implementation in gsuite



The standalone command implements packed ssSNPBLUP, supplied-genomic ssGBLUP, APY, pedigree and additional relationship constructions; see the complete YAML examples and raw-genotype APY guide. APY industrial preparation remains unqualified. The development component/pedigree R adapters have a narrower relationship contract and do not themselves construct a single-step relationship. Bayesian marker models are accessed through gbayes, with their own input and prior contracts.


Next: multiple components and identifiability.

title: 6. Multitrait, repeated-record and longitudinal models
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: 6. Multitrait, repeated-record and longitudinal models
section: 1 Multitrait models and the one-visit benchmark
text:
1 Multitrait models and the one-visit benchmark
The following specification uses the general multivariate mixed-model framework (Sorensen and Gianola, 2002); its one-visit identifiability example is an algebraic consequence of the stated covariance structure.
With effects stacked trait by trait, the four-trait model has
\[
y=X\beta+Z_a a+Z_h h+Z_f f+Z_c c+e,
\]
where \(h\) denotes herd effects, \(f\) family effects and \(c\) permanent individual-environment effects, with mutually independent components and
\[
K_a=\Sigma_a\otimes H,\quad
K_h=\Sigma_h\otimes I_h,\quad
K_f=\Sigma_f\otimes I_f,\quad
K_c=\Sigma_c\otimes I_{\rm animal}.
\]
Here \(I_h\), \(I_f\) and \(I_{\rm animal}\) are identity matrices on their respective effect domains. For complete observations at one visit, \(R=\Sigma_e\otimes I_o\), where \(I_o\) is the identity on observation units. An observed-record selector \(S\) gives the observed covariance as \(S V_{\rm complete}S^\top\) when some traits are missing. Removing missing responses without consistently selecting incidence rows and residual blocks does not preserve the model.
Trait order and stacking order are mathematical inputs. For animal-major ordering, a permutation changes \(\Sigma\otimes H\) into \(H\otimes\Sigma\); the biological covariance is unchanged only when every associated vector and operator is permuted consistently.

1.1 Separating individual environment from residual variation
With one visit per animal and unrestricted trait covariance matrices, the individual-environment and residual components contribute
\[
(\Sigma_c+\Sigma_e)\otimes I_o
\]
to the observed covariance. Consequently, a change \(\Delta\) added to \(\Sigma_c\) and subtracted from \(\Sigma_e\) preserves the likelihood whenever both remain admissible. Supplied values define a valid prediction problem, but the data alone cannot estimate this split.
The ambiguity does not automatically imply ambiguity in genetic prediction: holding their sum fixed preserves \(V\) and, with unchanged genetic cross-covariance, preserves \(\hat a\). Predictions of \(c\) itself depend on the selected split. Repeated visits, defensible covariance restrictions or external information can supply additional identification.

title: 6. Multitrait, repeated-record and longitudinal models
section: 2 Multitrait covariance is not repeated-measurement covariance
text:
2 Multitrait covariance is not repeated-measurement covariance
Traits may be different biological outcomes measured together or at different occasions. In a conventional multitrait model, \(\Sigma_a\) describes genetic covariance between traits and residual covariance applies to traits sharing a residual unit. Two measurements on different visits do not share a residual block merely because they concern the same animal.
For an unstructured \(t\)-trait covariance, each component requires \(t(t+1)/2\) parameters. Genetic correlations \(\Sigma_{a,ij}/\sqrt{\Sigma_{a,ii}\Sigma_{a,jj}}\) share information across traits. Whether this improves prediction depends on sample size, covariance estimation and the relevance of the additional trait information to deployment. Trait rescaling must transform every affected covariance block consistently.

title: 6. Multitrait, repeated-record and longitudinal models
text:
3 Longitudinal random regression
Random-regression estimation of genetic covariance functions is developed by Meyer (1998).
Represent an animal’s trajectory by \(a_i(t)=b(t)^\top u_i\), with a supplied basis \(b(t)\). If \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i,u_j)=A_{ij}\Sigma_u\), then
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\{a_i(t),a_j(s)\}=A_{ij}b(t)^\top\Sigma_u b(s).
\]
The prediction target may be a value at a particular age, a change between ages, a slope or an integrated trajectory. Each corresponds to a linear combination of coefficients and needs the full coefficient prediction-error variance (PEV) block. Extrapolation outside the observed time range can be highly sensitive to basis choice even when the numerical system is well solved.
Centering/scaling time improves conditioning. Changing from one full-rank basis to another preserves the model only if the coefficient covariance is transformed accordingly. Truncating the basis changes the model.

title: 6. Multitrait, repeated-record and longitudinal models
text:
4 Residual correlation and irregular visits
The combination of random regression and parametric within-animal environmental correlation is treated by Meyer (2001).
For discrete equally spaced visits a first-order autoregressive [AR(1)] model can use \(R_{rs}=\sigma_e^2\rho^{|k_r-k_s|}\). The distance uses the true visit index, not row adjacency after deleting missing visits. For irregular times, an exponential model uses \(R_{rs}=\sigma_e^2\exp(-\phi|t_r-t_s|)\) with \(\phi>0\). A heterogeneous form multiplies the correlation by occasion-specific standard deviations. Duplicate times, residual units and independent blocks must be declared explicitly.
Genetic random regression, permanent environmental random regression and serial residuals explain different covariance structures. With sparse follow-up, those structures can be difficult to distinguish. Increasing basis dimension without additional independent information does not resolve this.

title: 6. Multitrait, repeated-record and longitudinal models
text:
5 Factor-analytic trait or environment covariance
Sparse average-information fitting for factor-analytic and reduced-rank covariance models is described by Thompson et al. (2003). Its multi-environment setting provides methodological background, not evidence for every livestock application.
A factor-analytic covariance has \(\Sigma=\Lambda\Lambda^\top+\Psi\), with a diagonal nonnegative specific covariance \(\Psi\). It can reduce dimensionality and share information across environments. Loading rotations require constraints for interpretation; the implied covariance can be identified even when individual loadings are not uniquely oriented.
Factors do not automatically have biological labels. Their rank and specific variance assumptions should be assessed against prediction and covariance fit. A factor-analytic model is a structured alternative to a full unstructured covariance, not necessarily an exact computational shortcut.

5.1 Learning genetic dimensions from rich phenotypes
The genetic and environmental factor structures need not have the same rank or loadings. Choosing factors from total phenotypic variance alone can emphasize recording conditions rather than genetic covariance relevant to the objective. The genetic latent-factor work in Melsen et al. (2025) illustrates a plant-breeding route; its covariance estimation and replication assumptions must be checked before transferring the procedure to animal records.
With repeated high-dimensional features, a factor model may be combined with random regression. Estimation then concerns the loadings, coefficient covariance and residual process jointly or through an explicitly qualified staged procedure. Rank, time basis and smoothing choices are model choices to assess inside training, not numerical settings that automatically preserve a full unstructured model. The phenomics progression connects this covariance to trajectory and integral prediction targets.

title: 6. Multitrait, repeated-record and longitudinal models
text:
6 Genotype-by-environment interaction
For a Bayesian reaction-norm formulation including uncertainty in the environmental covariate, see Su et al. (2006). That setting is broader than the supplied-basis example here.
Environments can be treated as correlated traits or represented through measured covariates in a reaction norm. An environmental mean effect belongs in the mean model; a genetic response to environment belongs in genetic covariance. A prediction in a new environment requires observed covariates or a declared cross-environment covariance. An arbitrary new environment label does not supply either.
Existing route-specific examples are in the pedigree tutorial, multitrait guide and longitudinal guide.






Implementation in gsuite



Implemented routes include incomplete multitrait pedigree models, longitudinal pedigree random regression, and standalone trait, basis, serial-residual and factor-analytic constructions in the YAML examples. Factor-analytic covariance is implemented natively and exposed through YAML, while the component R covariance constructor remains a separate exposure gap. Its stochastic optimisation and uncertainty limits differ from exact fitting; see model/backend coverage. The joint learned measurement models developed in the phenomics chapter are broader extensions.


Next: missing data and selection.
For applications to automated measurements and high-dimensional traits, see large-scale phenomics.

title: 8. Binary, ordinal, count and survival traits
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: 8. Binary, ordinal, count and survival traits
section: 1 The observation distribution is part of the model
text:
1 The observation distribution is part of the model
Disease status, calving scores, numbers of treatments and time to removal are not continuous Gaussian measurements merely because they can be entered in a numeric column. Their support, exposure and observation process help determine an appropriate likelihood. The genetic relationship model can remain familiar while the conditional observation model changes.
A generalized linear mixed model specifies
\[
\eta=X\beta+Zu,\qquad u\sim N(0,K(\theta)),\qquad
g(\mu_i)=\eta_i,
\]
with conditionally independent responses from a declared distribution and \(\mu_i=E(y_i\mid u)\). Conditional independence is an assumption: repeated events, shared exposure and serial recording may require additional structure. The statistical construction and approximate inference for generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) are developed by Breslow and Clayton (1993); Bayesian quantitative-genetic treatments are given by Sorensen and Gianola (2002).








Response

Important distinction




Binary outcome
Bernoulli with probit or logit link
Status during a defined window differs from lifetime susceptibility
