Category spacing is not assumed equal

Poisson or negative binomial, with exposure where needed

Time to event
Survival model with censoring and a declared time origin
An unobserved event time is not an observed failure time



These are starting points, not automatic choices. A Gaussian approximation may be useful for a particular target and design, but its scale and limitations must be assessed rather than inferred from successful numerical convergence.

title: 8. Binary, ordinal, count and survival traits
text:
2 Binary traits and latent liability
For a probit model, write
\[
\ell_i=x_i^\top\beta+z_i^\top u+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad \varepsilon_i\sim N(0,1),\qquad
y_i=\mathbf1(\ell_i>0).
\]
Then \(\Pr(y_i=1\mid u)=\Phi(\eta_i)\). Fixing the liability residual variance sets the otherwise unidentified scale. A threshold location or equivalent intercept constraint is also required. The liability interpretation of threshold traits has a long quantitative-genetic foundation (Dempster and Lerner, 1950).
A logistic model instead uses \(\Pr(y_i=1\mid u)=\{1+\exp(-\eta_i)\}^{-1}\). Genetic variances on logit and probit scales are not directly interchangeable. Under a latent-logistic convention the residual variance is \(\pi^2/3\), whereas the probit construction above fixes it at one. Neither convention says that the observed binary residual variance is constant.
If additive and other independent liability components have variances \(\sigma_a^2\) and \(\sigma_c^2\) in a specified reference population, the probit liability heritability is
\[
h_\ell^2=\frac{\sigma_a^2}{\sigma_a^2+\sigma_c^2+1}.
\]
Its observed-scale counterpart depends on prevalence, covariates and the population being averaged. Ascertainment and selective recording also matter. A liability-scale variance ratio should therefore not be reported as a universal heritability of the recorded zero/one outcome.

title: 8. Binary, ordinal, count and survival traits
text:
3 Ordered categories and count models
For ordered categories, let \(y_i=k\) when \(\tau_{k-1}<\ell_i\leq\tau_k\), with ordered thresholds and end points \(\tau_0=-\infty\), \(\tau_J=+\infty\). With unit normal liability residual,
\[
\Pr(y_i=k\mid u)=
\Phi(\tau_k-\eta_i)-\Phi(\tau_{k-1}-\eta_i).
\]
Thresholds, the intercept and residual scale need identifying constraints. Scoring categories as 1, 2 and 3 in a Gaussian model instead assumes a metric that the ordering itself does not supply. Category definitions and assessor consistency are also part of the measurement process.
For counts with exposure \(t_i>0\), a Poisson model can use
\[
y_i\mid u\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(t_i\lambda_i),\qquad
\log\lambda_i=x_i^\top\beta+z_i^\top u.
\]
The known \(\log t_i\) is an offset. A treatment count in a short observation period is not comparable to the same count over a year without accounting for exposure. The conditional Poisson variance equals its mean; unexplained heterogeneity may motivate a negative-binomial distribution or additional effects. Extra zeros alone do not establish a separate zero-generating class. Exposure errors, unrecorded events and clustering are alternative explanations.

title: 8. Binary, ordinal, count and survival traits
text:
4 Survival, censoring and frailty
A proportional-hazards mixed model may specify
\[
\lambda_i(t\mid u)=\lambda_0(t)
\exp\{x_i(t)^\top\beta+z_i(t)^\top u\}.
\]
The shared random effects are often called frailties on this scale. For an observed time \(T_i\) and event indicator \(\delta_i\), with independent censoring conditional on the model, the likelihood contribution is
\[
\lambda_i(T_i\mid u)^{\delta_i}
\exp\left\{-\int_0^{T_i}\lambda_i(s\mid u)\,ds\right\}.
\]
Left truncation, interval censoring, competing events and recurrent events require their corresponding likelihoods. Ducrocq and Casella (1996) develop mixed survival models for genetic analysis; their likelihood is different from assigning a Gaussian residual to recorded lifespan.
An additive effect on log hazard is not an additive effect on mean lifetime. Its sign also depends on whether the event represents death, disease, recovery or a desirable transition. For productive life, removal can reflect management, fertility and production decisions as well as biological survival. Treating all culling as non-informative censoring is a substantive assumption. See missing data and selection.

title: 8. Binary, ordinal, count and survival traits
section: 5 Prediction and estimation after the likelihood changes
text:
5 Prediction and estimation after the likelihood changes
For conditionally independent observations, the marginal likelihood has the form
\[
p(y\mid\beta,\theta,\phi)=
\int \left\{\prod_i p(y_i\mid\eta_i,\phi)\right\}
\varphi(u;0,K(\theta))\,du,
\]
where \(\phi\) denotes any additional observation parameters. The integral is generally not the Gaussian restricted maximum likelihood (REML) objective from variance-component inference. Laplace approximations, quadrature, working-response methods and posterior sampling make different approximations or target different inferential objects. Their performance must be assessed for rare events, small groups and the covariance structures of interest; an early approximation is not a universal reference for every modern implementation (Breslow and Clayton, 1993; Sorensen and Gianola, 2002).
The conditional mode of \(u\), its posterior mean and a predicted response probability are different outputs. In particular,
\[
E\{g^{-1}(\eta_i)\mid y\}
\ne g^{-1}\{E(\eta_i\mid y)\}
\]
in general. Response-scale prediction requires integration over the uncertainty appropriate to the target, including future environmental effects when relevant. A genetic contrast on the link scale can remain meaningful, but its translation to risk or rate depends on the covariate and exposure context.
Likewise, an inverse Hessian at a mode is a local curvature approximation. It is not automatically the exact Gaussian prediction-error variance (PEV) formula from prediction and uncertainty, nor a calibrated interval after variance estimation and selection.

5.1 Learned measurements and recorded events are different observations
A disease label, its observation window and a classifier’s estimated disease probability describe different quantities. Treating a learned probability as an observed binary diagnosis discards its measurement interpretation. A staged analysis needs an appropriate uncertainty model; a joint analysis might link a latent health state to both diagnostic observations and sensor features. Its identifiability depends on calibration and reference information, not only on the flexibility of the classifier.
Likewise, automated event counts need exposure and event-detection definitions. Missed detections can differ from biological absence. Observation models must separate these processes where the data support that distinction, with likelihood and uncertainty checks appropriate to the chosen construction. See phenomics for measurement and recording design.

title: 8. Binary, ordinal, count and survival traits
text:
6 Qualification and practical interpretation
Verify likelihood contributions and derivatives on small independent examples, including limiting probabilities, zero exposure handling, ordered thresholds and censoring patterns. Working-equation residuals certify an inner numerical problem; outer likelihood, gradient or posterior diagnostics are still needed. For sampling methods, assess mixing and effective information as well as elapsed time. See the algorithmic reference and qualification framework.
Simulation should assess parameter recovery and interval coverage under the intended prevalence, exposure and recording design. Deployment validation should assess probability calibration and a suitable proper prediction score as well as discrimination. For survival outcomes, evaluation must account for censoring and the time horizon. Genetic accuracy is a different target from classification accuracy of individual observed outcomes.
These observation models connect directly to longitudinal traits and large-scale phenomics. More frequent recording can improve information, but it also makes event definitions, exposure and the observation process more consequential.






Implementation in gsuite



The standalone mixed-model specification and development mixed-model R coverage linked from these notes provide Gaussian model routes. This review does not establish a general threshold, count or survival animal-model workflow in those interfaces. The separate association package includes binary-trait association analysis, which is a different task from the general genetic evaluation models derived here. This chapter supplies the broader theory of observation models rather than a claim that every likelihood is already exposed.


Next: genetic bases and crossbreeding.

title: 10. Breeding objectives, selection response and mating decisions
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: 10. Breeding objectives, selection response and mating decisions
section: 1 Prediction supplies information for a decision
text:
1 Prediction supplies information for a decision
A genetic evaluation estimates or predicts quantities under a model. A breeding programme must then decide which animals contribute, how often, to which mates, and towards which objective. The best estimate of one trait is not necessarily the best selection criterion for the programme.
Define a breeding objective as a function of genetic outcomes, costs and constraints. A common linear approximation is aggregate merit
\[
H=c^\top a,
\]
where \(a\) contains additive genetic values for objective traits and \(c\) contains declared economic or scientific weights. The same mathematical form can represent different objectives. Units and reference conditions are therefore essential: a weight per kilogram is not a weight per genetic standard deviation. Hazel’s selection-index framework connects an objective to correlated selection information (Hazel, 1943).
The objective traits need not be the recorded traits. An inexpensive sensor feature can provide information about health without receiving its own economic weight. Conversely, an important but poorly measured welfare or environmental trait does not cease to be part of the objective because its prediction is difficult.

title: 10. Breeding objectives, selection response and mating decisions
section: 2 Combining information without counting it twice
text:
2 Combining information without counting it twice
Let \(z\) be centered information available at selection, with covariance \(P_z\), and let \(C_{az}=\operatorname{Cov}(a,z)\). A linear index \(I=b^\top z\) minimizing \(E[(H-I)^2]\) satisfies
\[
P_z b=C_{az}^\top c.
\]
The off-diagonal covariances account for redundant information. Adding a new record does not contribute independent information merely because it came from a different device or file. A derived genomic score and an estimated breeding value (EBV) trained on the same records can overlap extensively.
If a coherent joint evaluation already supplies \(\hat a=E(a\mid\mathcal D)\), then the posterior-mean predictor of a linear objective is \(\hat H=c^\top\hat a\). Its prediction-error variance is
\[
\operatorname{PEV}(H)=c^\top C_{\rm PE}c,
\]
using the complete trait prediction-error covariance matrix. Weighting each trait EBV again by its reliability does not generally recover this predictor. Reliability is relevant to uncertainty and decision risk, but is not a generic additional shrinkage coefficient. See prediction and uncertainty.
Combining published evaluations from different sources instead requires a model for their bases, information overlap and error covariance. Treating them as independent measurements without justification can overstate precision.

title: 10. Breeding objectives, selection response and mating decisions
text:
3 Expected response and correlated change
Under joint normality and truncation selection on \(I\), with standardized selection intensity \(i\), the expected vector response among selected parents is
\[
\Delta a=i\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(a,I)}{\sigma_I}
       =i\frac{C_{az}b}{\sqrt{b^\top P_zb}}.
\]
The corresponding change in the objective is \(\Delta H=c^\top\Delta a\). The single-objective expression \(i\,r_{HI}\sigma_H\) follows when \(r_{HI}\) is the accuracy of the criterion for \(H\). These formulas require the stated distribution and selection design; they do not replace a population-dynamic model for every breeding scheme.
Genetic correlations determine correlated responses. Giving one trait zero objective weight does not guarantee zero change in that trait. Similarly, maximizing a weighted objective does not ensure that every individual trait moves in its preferred direction. Report the expected response vector, not only the index score.
Dividing by a generation interval \(L\) gives a schematic response per year. Real programmes may have distinct selection pathways, ages, overlapping generations and dissemination delays. Faster generation turnover can improve annual response but also increase the rate at which relatedness accumulates. Long-term comparisons need both calendar-time response and genetic diversity.

title: 10. Breeding objectives, selection response and mating decisions
text:
4 Objectives, restrictions and uncertainty
Economic weights can be local derivatives of programme profit with respect to trait performance, holding the declared production conditions fixed. Prices, costs, biological limits and farming systems can change those derivatives. Sensitivity analysis should therefore examine plausible alternative objectives rather than imply that one set of weights is permanent.
Some outcomes are better represented by explicit restrictions, such as a lower bound on an expected health response, than by a small compensatory weight. Desired-gain or restricted-index approaches impose different decision criteria from unconstrained economic maximization. If restrictions are incompatible with the available genetic variation and information, an optimizer cannot make them scientifically feasible.
Uncertainty in EBVs, covariance parameters and objective weights is also distinct. A posterior mean is optimal for some quadratic-loss prediction problems, not for every risk-sensitive decision. Alternatives may evaluate downside outcomes, uncertain constraints or expected utility. Their assumptions and consequences should be explicit; numerical optimization cannot determine the ethical or economic acceptability of a trade-off.

title: 10. Breeding objectives, selection response and mating decisions
section: 5 Contributions and the control of relatedness
text:
5 Contributions and the control of relatedness
Selecting a ranked list leaves the number of descendants per parent unspecified. Optimum-contribution selection makes those contributions part of the decision. Meuwissen develops selection for maximum gain under a prescribed inbreeding constraint (Meuwissen, 1997).
For a simplified diploid random-mating generation, let \(w_i\geq0\) be each candidate’s fraction of parental gene contributions, with \(\mathbf1^\top w=1\), and let \(A\) be an additive relationship matrix on a declared base. A schematic optimization is
\[
\max_w\; w^\top\hat H
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\tfrac12 w^\top A w\leq f_{\max},\qquad
\mathbf1^\top w=1,\quad w\geq0.
\]
The factor \(1/2\) converts additive relationship to coancestry in this convention. Sex-specific contribution totals, reproductive capacity, existing cohorts and other practical bounds usually add constraints. Expected group coancestry is a diversity criterion, not automatically the realised inbreeding of every planned offspring or an exact annual inbreeding rate. A rate constraint needs a reference cohort and a time or generation definition.
Using genomic rather than pedigree relationships changes which sharing is penalized, and its normalization and base matter. A numerical coancestry limit cannot be transferred blindly between different relationship scales. See genetic bases and crossbreeding. The variance available after several rounds of selection also need not remain equal to the initial reference variance.

title: 10. Breeding objectives, selection response and mating decisions
section: 6 Mating allocation is a further decision
text:
6 Mating allocation is a further decision
Given selected parental contributions, a mating plan allocates pairs. Under a purely additive model, the expected offspring breeding value from parents \(s,d\) is \((\hat a_s+\hat a_d)/2\), but the Mendelian sampling variance and prediction uncertainty still affect offspring distributions. If an EBV omits a base-group contribution, that deviation alone is not the required total parental value.
For conventional pedigree relationships, expected offspring inbreeding is \(F_{sd}=A_{sd}/2\). This statement uses the corresponding pedigree base and inheritance assumptions; a genomic relationship coefficient on another scale should not be inserted without establishing its interpretation.
Allocation can reduce close matings while retaining selected contributions. It does not generally undo the longer-term concentration of ancestry created by heavy use of a few parents. Conversely, controlling average coancestry does not rule out every undesirable individual mating.
Recessive defects, dominance, heterosis and breed-specific commercial targets can introduce pair-specific objectives and restrictions. Their prediction requires additional information and models. An additive EBV alone does not identify the best pair for a non-additive outcome. Crossbreeding systems also need to distinguish parental purebred merit from expected crossbred performance.

title: 10. Breeding objectives, selection response and mating decisions
text:
7 Learning from realised outcomes
Selection changes the data subsequently observed. Records from selected parents or surviving offspring are not a random sample of the original population. Evaluation of realised genetic trends must distinguish genetic change from management change and account for the information used in selection. Forward validation and prospective outcome tracking complement retrospective accuracy comparisons; see missing data and selection and model checking and validation.
Assess gain, correlated responses, diversity, inbreeding, realised contributions and delivery to the commercial population. A favourable index trend in a nucleus does not establish that all intended outcomes reached farms, especially when environments or crossing systems differ.

title: 10. Breeding objectives, selection response and mating decisions
section: 8 What a reproducible decision analysis should retain
text:
8 What a reproducible decision analysis should retain
Keep the objective definition and weights, trait units and reference population, the joint evaluation and uncertainty source, candidate eligibility, relationship matrix convention, contribution bounds, mating restrictions and time horizon. Separate predicted outcomes from realised outcomes and model assumptions from operational constraints.
Small independent examples should verify index weights and response algebra, coancestry normalization, feasibility and the effect of changing constraints. Population simulations can then assess multi-generation gain, variation and uncertainty under a specified breeding scheme. These are qualifications of a decision procedure, beyond qualification of the underlying prediction solver.






Implementation in gsuite



Genetic predictions and selected joint contrasts from standalone output and prediction uncertainty can supply inputs to an index or decision analysis. The reviewed interfaces do not establish a complete optimum-contribution selection or mating-allocation optimizer. Those decision procedures require additional constraints and qualification beyond an accepted mixed-model fit.


Next: large-scale computation.

text:

title: 12. Model checking, validation and software comparison
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: 12. Model checking, validation and software comparison
text:
1 Numerical acceptance and scientific agreement
Backward error, conditioning and iterative refinement are treated by Higham (2002). A residual criterion is a numerical diagnostic, not a biological model-checking procedure.
For \(C\hat x=b\), record the original-system residual \(r=b-C\hat x\). A useful normwise backward-error diagnostic is
\[
\eta=\frac{\|r\|}{\|C\|\,\|\hat x\|+\|b\|}.
\]
A small residual does not by itself guarantee small coefficient error when the system is ill conditioned. The identity
\[
x-\hat x=C^{-1}r
\]
shows why scaling and conditioning matter. A solve in transformed variables must be checked after reconstructing the original target, under the declared original-system acceptance criterion.
A symmetric positive definite (SPD) preconditioner used solely to accelerate preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) preserves the target equations; finite stopping error still depends on convergence. Refinement changes how accurately a backend solve is performed. Neither should be confused with adding a ridge to \(K\), which changes the statistical model. Residual acceptance, variance-component optimizer convergence and scientific predictive validity are three separate assessments.
Practical equivalence is a scientific judgment about the size of differences; it does not retrospectively turn a failed numerical gate into a pass. The software-comparison section specifies the alignment, error summaries and performance evidence needed for that judgment.

title: 12. Model checking, validation and software comparison
section: 2 Statistical diagnostics after an accepted solve
text:
2 Statistical diagnostics after an accepted solve
Inspect observed patterns, influential groups, residual distributions and variance heterogeneity against the model. Conditional residuals \(y-X\hat\beta-Z\hat u\) have covariance shaped by fitting and shrinkage; they are not independent draws with covariance \(R\). Standardized or whitened diagnostics must use the appropriate fitted residual covariance or a stated approximation. Marginal and conditional residuals address different questions.
A good numerical residual does not diagnose omitted management effects, incorrect parentage or a misspecified residual process. Large scientific residuals do not necessarily imply a failed equation solve either.

title: 12. Model checking, validation and software comparison
text:
3 Validation aligned with deployment
Simulation, validation design and benchmarking in genomic prediction are discussed by Daetwyler et al. (2013). Multitrait-specific validation leakage and remedies are studied by Runcie and Cheng (2019).
A random animal split mostly tests prediction for animals with the relationships and information retained in that split. Forward-generation validation tests a different task; leave-family, leave-population and leave-environment designs answer other questions. Specify what information would genuinely be available at prediction time, including relatives’ future records and environmental covariates.
Marker selection, phenotype-derived weights, hyperparameter tuning and covariance estimation must be fitted within the training procedure for the claimed validation design. If target genotypes are allowed in frequency or kernel construction, state that transductive information explicitly rather than describing the exercise as entirely independent prediction.

title: 12. Model checking, validation and software comparison
text:
4 Accuracy, calibration and uncertainty
In simulation, compare predictions to known latent breeding values. In field data those values are not observed: correlation with phenotype is not genetic accuracy, and heritability-based adjustments require assumptions. Predictive correlation is insensitive to additive shifts and multiplicative dispersion, so also assess bias, regression calibration and prediction error on a clearly specified target.
For held-out phenotypes, mean squared error includes unexplained environmental and residual variation. For breeding values, reliability describes a model-based uncertainty measure rather than an automatically observed out-of-sample accuracy. Interval coverage should be checked against the target actually covered, with repeated simulation or an appropriate external design.
Partial-versus-whole-data prediction comparisons, including the linear-regression (LR) method (Legarra and Reverter, 2018), provide additional validation tools under their assumptions. They do not make true breeding values directly observable or eliminate the effects of an incorrect covariance model.

4.1 Qualifying an information pipeline
Compare a model using new information with a baseline using the same eligible animals, markers, records and prediction-time availability. Distinguish the benefit of obtaining additional measurements from the benefit of a different method for analysing them. An annotation-weighted model and a sensor-assisted predictor may answer different information questions even when both improve a retrospective correlation (Daetwyler et al., 2013; Runcie and Cheng, 2019).
Feature extraction, calibration, annotation selection, factor rank, covariance estimation and tuning learned from the study data belong inside the assessed training procedure. Externally trained, frozen components form a distinct case: record their provenance and assess transfer rather than silently assuming it. Hold out animals and relevant farms, devices, populations or time periods.
For estimation, assess recovery of the intended component or total covariance and interval behaviour, including misspecified annotations and recording error. For prediction, assess the actual genetic or phenotypic target, calibration and uncertainty. Feature enrichment, molecular association and variance explained by fitted scores are not interchangeable measures of success.

title: 12. Model checking, validation and software comparison
text:
5 Comparing software and models
First establish the same data, allele coding, relationship base, covariance scales and prediction target. Align external animal IDs and trait order; exclude marker coefficients when comparing animal genetic values. Check complete coverage, duplicates and nonfinite outputs before error summaries. Report maximum absolute error, per-target root mean squared error (RMSE) and a prespecified absolute/ relative gate. Agreement on predictions alone does not prove equal likelihoods, prediction-error variances (PEVs) or variance estimates.
Then compare setup, factorization, iteration, reconstruction and output time, plus end-to-end time, on documented hardware. Use repeated runs where practical to assess variability. Different stopping criteria and different nodes limit causal claims about algorithmic speed. A smaller time per iteration can coexist with a larger complete runtime.
Finally distinguish two conclusions: equivalent-model software qualification and predictive model comparison. The former asks whether implementations solve the same problem; the latter asks whether a model improves inference or prediction for a scientifically relevant population.

title: 12. Model checking, validation and software comparison
section: 6 A report that can be interpreted later
text:
6 A report that can be interpreted later
Preserve the scientific specification, input identities, code/runtime versions, parameter estimates or supplied covariances, numerical status and uncertainty method. State the validation design and what was learned inside each training set. Keep unsuccessful numerical gates and unsupported uncertainty requests visible; practical agreement is not a replacement for recording those results.






Implementation in gsuite



The standalone runner records separate numerical, estimation and execution status in results and diagnostics. Supplied-truth evaluation checks labelled predictions and reports accuracy, error and calibration summaries. The software validation pages describe existing focused evidence. LMT conversion and other directive/data converters cover restricted model subsets; conversion acceptance is separate from numerical agreement. Deployment validation and inferential calibration remain study-design tasks, not consequences of a successful run.


Next: current developments.
The qualification framework sets out how independent numerical, simulation, validation and performance evidence support different kinds of claims.
For applications to automated measurements and high-dimensional traits, see large-scale phenomics.

title: 14. Genomic-feature information and prior models
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: 14. Genomic-feature information and prior models
section: 1 Biological information as part of the statistical model
text:
1 Biological information as part of the statistical model
A genomic feature can be a variant class, gene, pathway, regulatory region, tissue-specific molecular annotation or a quantitative score. Its statistical role must be specified: it may define a covariance component, an expected marker variance, a mixture probability or a predictor measured on each animal. These choices are not interchangeable.
Retain the marker model from Chapter 4:
\[
y=X\beta+ZWm+e.
\]
\(W\) contains consistently centered marker dosages. In ordinary single-nucleotide polymorphism best linear unbiased prediction (SNP-BLUP), \(m\sim N(0,\tau^2I)\). Feature information allows the marker distribution to depend on an annotation design \(B_{\rm ann}\), with row \(b_j^\top\) describing marker \(j\). The same annotation can be external biological information even when its influence on the trait is estimated from the training phenotypes.
The word “prior” has two uses here. A feature set may be defined before an analysis, without assigning a Bayesian prior to its variance component. A full Bayesian model additionally assigns probability distributions to unknown effects and hyperparameters. Declaring a feature in advance does not mean that its enrichment is known.

title: 14. Genomic-feature information and prior models
text:
2 Feature-specific variance components: GFBLUP
Genomic-feature best linear unbiased prediction (GFBLUP) assigns different variance components to declared marker sets.
Partition markers into a feature set \(F\) and its complement \(B\). Write
\[
a=W_Fm_F+W_Bm_B=f+r,
\]
with independent effects
\[
m_F\sim N(0,\tau_F^2I),\qquad m_B\sim N(0,\tau_B^2I).
\]
For positive normalizers \(d_F,d_B\), define \(G_F=W_FW_F^\top/d_F\) and \(G_B=W_BW_B^\top/d_B\). Then
\[
K_a=\sigma_F^2G_F+\sigma_B^2G_B,
\qquad \sigma_F^2=d_F\tau_F^2,\quad
\sigma_B^2=d_B\tau_B^2.
\]
The feature and background variances can be supplied, estimated by restricted maximum likelihood (REML) or assigned hyperpriors. Their interpretation follows the kernel scaling. Equal marker variances correspond to \(\sigma_F^2/d_F=\sigma_B^2/d_B\), not generally to equal component variances. If \(d=d_F+d_B\) under the same normalization convention, ordinary genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP) is recovered by these matching per-marker variances.
This makes the feature model a direct extension of multiple-component inference. The feature provides a grouping hypothesis; the data determine whether its markers warrant different shrinkage. A small or noisy feature can produce an unstable component estimate, and a boundary estimate need not imply that the underlying biology is absent.

2.1 What does feature enrichment mean?
An effect-size enrichment is \(E_\tau=\tau_F^2/\tau_B^2\). A ratio of total component variances instead includes feature size and normalization. Neither should be reported merely as “the enrichment” without a denominator.
For a declared evaluation population with centered dosage matrices, the average model-implied feature variance is
\[
v_F=\frac{\sigma_F^2}{n}\operatorname{tr}(G_F),
\]
and similarly for background. The ratio \(v_F/(v_F+v_B)\) is a prior population-average component share under the independent-effect model. This is distinct from a variance share calculated from fitted predictions. For posterior draws, feature and background effects can become correlated through the data and linkage disequilibrium (LD); posterior realized variance decompositions need their cross term.

title: 14. Genomic-feature information and prior models
section: 3 Weighted kernels and continuous annotation-dependent variances
text:
3 Weighted kernels and continuous annotation-dependent variances
A more general Gaussian model is
\[
m_j\mid\alpha\sim N(0,\tau_j^2),\qquad
\log\tau_j^2=\alpha_0+b_j^\top\alpha,
\]
which induces \(K_a=W D(\alpha)W^\top\), where \(D\) is diagonal. This general variance-regression formulation accommodates continuous scores and overlapping annotations. Positive variance is automatic, while regularization of \(\alpha\) controls extreme weights and weakly identified annotation effects.
Fixed external weights define one covariance. Learning weights by likelihood or empirical Bayes defines a covariance-estimation problem. Assigning priors to \(\alpha\) and integrating over its uncertainty defines a hierarchical Bayesian problem. Plugging learned weights into a final best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) does not automatically propagate their uncertainty.
Correlated annotation columns make individual coefficients difficult to interpret. Genomic coordinates, annotation version, feature mapping, minor allele frequency (MAF)/LD dependencies and score scaling are part of the model specification.

3.1 From an annotation to a fitted covariance model
Functional resources such as the Farm Animal Genotype–Tissue Expression (FarmGTEx) project expand the information from which marker annotations can be constructed (Fang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2022). Their statistical contribution depends on the rule connecting an annotation to the trait model. An atlas supplies evidence; it does not supply a universally correct variance weight for every trait, tissue and population.
Consider three centered marker columns \(w_1,w_2,w_3\) and an annotation indicating that markers 1 and 3 belong to a candidate functional class. Keeping marker coding and normalization fixed, a simple model is
\[
D(\alpha)=\tau^2\operatorname{diag}(e^\alpha,1,e^\alpha),\qquad
K_a(\alpha)=\tau^2\{e^\alpha(w_1w_1^\top+w_3w_3^\top)+w_2w_2^\top\}.
\]
At \(\alpha=0\) this reduces to equal marker variances. At \(\alpha=\log 2\) the annotated markers have twice the prior variance of the background marker. This is a statement about effect variances, not necessarily a doubling of population genetic variance or of the variance of fitted breeding values. The genotype cross-products and population scale still matter.
If \(\alpha\) is fixed externally, prediction remains a Gaussian mixed-model problem at the declared covariance. If it is learned from the phenotypes, \(\alpha\) becomes a covariance parameter: the same data now inform both shrinkage and breeding values. The model must distinguish that direction from the overall variance scale and competing components. Assigning a prior to \(\alpha\) and integrating over its posterior adds another level of uncertainty. These three analyses can use the same annotation but need not give identical predictions or uncertainty intervals.
For the general variance function above, with fixed \(W\) and no \(\alpha\)-dependent normalization,
\[
\frac{\partial K_a}{\partial\alpha_l}
=W\operatorname{diag}(\tau_j^2 b_{jl})W^\top,\qquad
\frac{\partial V}{\partial\alpha_l}
=Z\frac{\partial K_a}{\partial\alpha_l}Z^\top.
\]
These are the derivative operators entering the restricted-likelihood score in variance-component estimation. Normalizing each learned kernel again would add derivatives of that normalizer. Learning many annotation coefficients requires regularization or hierarchical pooling when the data do not identify their effects independently. A valid covariance parameterization ensures admissibility; it does not guarantee identifiability.
The corresponding mixture-model development learns annotation-dependent allocation probabilities or effect-size classes instead of only a Gaussian variance function. BayesRC provides an established biological-class example (MacLeod et al., 2016). A Gaussian covariance obtained by matching a mixture’s second moment is a separate approximation, not an equivalent posterior analysis.

title: 14. Genomic-feature information and prior models
text:
4 Annotation-dependent mixture distributions
For marker allocation \(c_j\) and mixture variances \(v_k\),
\[
\Pr(c_j=k\mid b_j)=\pi_{jk},\qquad
m_j\mid c_j=k\sim N(0,v_k),
\]
where a component with \(v_0=0\) is a point mass at zero. Annotation information can change the probability of inclusion, the distribution of nonzero sizes, or both. These mechanisms need not produce the same prediction or genetic architecture estimate as a Gaussian model with a matching second moment.
In the original BayesRC construction, predefined variant classes have class-specific mixture proportions learned from the data. MacLeod and colleagues used this to incorporate biological information into a BayesR-type model. Their real-data findings also show why useful priors do not guarantee large prediction gains: informative enrichment and the variance represented by the feature both matter (MacLeod et al., 2016).
An overlapping-annotation extension can instead make mixture probabilities a function of \(b_j\), for example through multinomial or sequential probit/logit links. Such links, their coefficient priors and update rules are part of the model. They are not identical to independent Dirichlet updates of disjoint feature-class probabilities.
The prior probability \(\pi_{jk}\), posterior allocation probability and posterior inclusion probability are different quantities. Inclusion depends on the prior and LD; it is not automatically a causal probability. A posterior enrichment estimate is also conditional on the selected feature definitions and competing annotations.

title: 14. Genomic-feature information and prior models
text:
5 Overlapping features: two different constructions
The independent-component covariance sum is a general mixed-model identity (Sorensen and Gianola, 2002). Its identifiability depends on the resulting covariance directions, not simply the number of annotation labels (Rothenberg, 1971).
In an annotation regression, one marker effect has several predictors of its variance or mixture probabilities. In an additive multi-kernel model, a marker can contribute through several independent latent components. These are different decompositions.
For nonnegative membership weights \(q_{jk}\), consider
\[
G_k=\frac{W\operatorname{diag}(q_{\cdot k})W^\top}{d_k},\qquad
K_a=\sum_k\sigma_k^2G_k.
\]
The equivalent marginal marker variance is \(\tau_j^2=\sum_k\sigma_k^2q_{jk}/d_k\). A marker in two features receives both contributions. This is mathematically valid, but the resulting component variances are not automatically unique biological attributions. Identical or nearly identical kernels can be unidentifiable or weakly identifiable.
Nonnegative weighted kernels preserve positive semidefiniteness. Signed annotation scores cannot simply be inserted as diagonal kernel weights without checking that property. Centering a score is appropriate as a regression covariate but need not be appropriate as a covariance weight.

title: 14. Genomic-feature information and prior models
text:
6 Molecular evidence and its uncertainty
Feature definitions can use coding consequence, regulatory activity, expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL), splicing quantitative trait locus (sQTL), expression, pathways or fine-mapping results. CattleGTEx provides a multi-tissue regulatory resource that can inform such definitions (Liu et al., 2022).
A tissue-specific eQTL annotation is variant-level information. An expression measurement on an individual animal is a different predictor, potentially affected by environment, disease and the phenotype itself. A model using the latter must state when expression is measured and whether it is available at selection time. It does not automatically predict the same additive breeding value as a genotype-only model.
Association evidence from a genome-wide association study (GWAS), colocalization and experimental functional validation also provide different evidence. LD can make several variants or genes appear informative for one locus. Combining an annotation with a GWAS statistic from the same animals does not create independent prior evidence.
Treat uncertain or tissue-mismatched annotations as hypotheses rather than known causal labels. Sensitivity to alternative mappings, irrelevant tissues and matched random features helps determine whether a result reflects useful biology or generic genome structure.

6.1 Molecular measurements change the joint observation model
Suppose \(y\) is a performance trait and \(z\) an expression-derived phenotype. A simple joint model gives their additive effects covariance
\[
\operatorname{Var}\begin{pmatrix}a_y\\a_z\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_y^2&\sigma_{yz}\\
\sigma_{yz}&\sigma_z^2\end{bmatrix}\otimes K,
\]
where \(K\) is the declared pedigree or genomic relationship kernel, with a separately specified environmental and residual covariance. The data must identify the genetic cross-covariance rather than merely the observed association between \(y\) and \(z\). Treating \(z\) as a fixed covariate instead changes the conditioning statement and can change the genetic target. Neither construction establishes molecular mediation without additional assumptions and evidence.
This is a different extension from assigning a marker to an expression-linked annotation. It requires information about when the molecular phenotype is measured, which animals have it, its measurement process and whether candidates will have it at prediction time. The multitrait validation issues in Runcie and Cheng (2019) apply. Tissue-specific annotations can inform prior sharing, but measured expression may also reflect treatment, disease and shared environment.

title: 14. Genomic-feature information and prior models
text:
7 Multitrait and single-step extensions
For feature \(k\), a multitrait Gaussian extension has \(\operatorname{Var}(a_k)=\Sigma_k\otimes G_k\) in trait-major order. Feature-specific trait correlations allow a region to affect several traits differently from the background. They also increase parameter count and require enough independent information to distinguish the kernels and trait covariance structures.
A Bayesian extension can use shared versus trait-specific inclusion, or mixtures of multivariate effect covariances. Shared inclusion does not force identical effect sizes or signs. Sharing annotations does not by itself establish that the same causal variant acts on every trait.
In single-step, define the complete genotyped covariance induced by the feature model and the conditional relationship to non-genotyped animals. Compatibility, reference adjustment and residual pedigree variation still matter. Replacing ordinary single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) shrinkage by a feature prior without revisiting the remaining latent terms is not proof of equivalence to a desired animal-effect model. Their joint covariance, identifiability and inferential properties must be derived and assessed for the combined model.

title: 14. Genomic-feature information and prior models
text:
8 Qualification: prediction, estimation and biology
Genomic benchmarking should match the intended information and deployment population (Daetwyler et al., 2013). Leakage from correlated-trait information is a particular concern in multivariate validation (Runcie and Cheng, 2019).
Start with an unannotated model using the same markers and information. Then compare fixed feature weights, estimated feature variances and a suitable mixture model where the scientific question warrants it. Include a background component so that an imperfect feature need not explain all genetic variation.
Assess informative, irrelevant and deliberately misspecified annotations. Controls should consider feature size, MAF, LD, gene density and annotation overlap: an arbitrary random SNP set need not be an adequate null for a gene-based feature. When many features are searched, selection and tuning belong inside training; an untouched outer validation is needed for the selected procedure’s performance claim.
Report prediction accuracy and calibration separately from component variance, enrichment and feature selection stability. Feature variance is not evidence that an entire pathway is causal. Within-family validation can conceal or exaggerate portability, so include the populations and generations relevant to the intended application. Estimation uncertainty and numerical acceptance remain necessary even when prediction differences are small.

title: 14. Genomic-feature information and prior models
text:
9 Guided reading



Reading

Tissue-specific regulatory annotations in cattle









Implementation in gsuite



Gaussian feature/background models can be expressed using separately supplied, aligned kernels in the component model interfaces; constructing and scaling those kernels remains part of input preparation. Annotation-informed mixture regression is implemented in gbayes, including development scalar bayesRC routes under the documented prior and interface contracts. These implementations do not establish the arbitrary learned Gaussian variance-function, molecular mediation or fully integrated single-step mixture models developed above.

title: Algorithmic reference: from a mixed model to accepted inference
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: Algorithmic reference: from a mixed model to accepted inference
text:
1 Mathematical scope
Consider \(y=X\beta+Zu+e\), with \(u\sim N(0,K)\) and \(e\sim N(0,R)\) independent. This reference derives computational identities for a Gaussian model with positive-definite \(K,R\) and full-column-rank \(X\), unless a different case is explicitly stated. Covariance parameters are fixed within a coefficient solve. The statistical interpretation is developed in Chapters 1–3 (Henderson, 1975; Robinson, 1991).
A complete algorithm must preserve observation identities, effect domains, trait order, covariance scale and prediction targets. A computational ordering is a permutation of the scientific problem, not a redefinition of animal IDs. The equations below are independent of a particular file format or application programming interface (API).

title: Algorithmic reference: from a mixed model to accepted inference
section: 2 What must an implementation be able to apply?
text:
2 What must an implementation be able to apply?
Dense \(X\) and \(Z\) notation is convenient for derivation, but does not require global incidence matrices in memory. An implementation can provide forward and transpose incidence actions, residual precision actions and random-effect precision actions.
For \(v=(v_\beta^\top,v_u^\top)^\top\), set \(h=Xv_\beta+Zv_u\) and \(w=R^{-1}h\). The mixed-equation operator is
\[
Cv=\begin{bmatrix}X^\top w\\Z^\top w+K^{-1}v_u\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
b=\begin{bmatrix}X^\top R^{-1}y\\Z^\top R^{-1}y\end{bmatrix}.
\]
This defines a matrix-free product without changing the target. Independent residual blocks can be factored separately. Multiple traits require the correct within-block covariance action; treating their residual precisions as unrelated scalars changes the model.
For a genomic component \(K_a=\tau^2WW^\top\), the covariance action on a vector or batch \(v\) is \(K_av=\tau^2W(W^\top v)\). An animal-covariance operator is not automatically an efficient animal-precision operator: applying \(K_a^{-1}\) can itself require a solve or a different latent representation. Packed marker products save storage and decoding work, not this distinction.

title: Algorithmic reference: from a mixed model to accepted inference
section: 3 Block elimination and the marginal model
text:
3 Block elimination and the marginal model
Define
\[
S_u=K^{-1}+Z^\top R^{-1}Z.
\]
The random equations imply
\[
\hat u=S_u^{-1}Z^\top R^{-1}(y-X\hat\beta).
\]
Substitution into the fixed equations gives
\[
X^\top V^{-1}X\hat\beta=X^\top V^{-1}y,
\]
because
\[
V^{-1}=R^{-1}-R^{-1}ZS_u^{-1}Z^\top R^{-1}.
\]
Conversely, the marginal solution reconstructs the mixed-equation solution. This establishes an exact check between formulations. It does not say to form \(S_u^{-1}\) or \(V^{-1}\) explicitly: retained factors and linear solves implement the inverse actions (Saad, 2003; Sorensen and Gianola, 2002).

3.1 Singular components and constraints
If a component covariance is positive semidefinite, it can sometimes be represented as \(u=Bv\) with a full-column-rank basis and a positive-definite latent covariance. The observation incidence becomes \(ZB\). Zero-variance directions must be handled consistently in prediction and uncertainty.
A redundant fixed-effect design needs an estimable basis or explicit constraints. Adding numerical jitter to avoid either issue is not generally equivalent to the original model. Determinants and likelihood comparisons also need the correct measure and normalization when rank or parameterization changes. The positive-interior identities here must not be applied unchanged across an arbitrary rank-changing boundary (Self and Liang, 1987).

title: Algorithmic reference: from a mixed model to accepted inference
text:
4 Pedigree elimination and single-step representations
For \(Q=A^{-1}\) partitioned into non-genotyped (\(n\)) and genotyped (\(g\)) animals,
\[
A_{gg}^{-1}=Q_{gg}-Q_{gn}Q_{nn}^{-1}Q_{ng}.
\]
To apply the right-hand side to \(v\), compute \(t=Q_{ng}v\), solve \(Q_{nn}z=t\), then return \(Q_{gg}v-Q_{gn}z\). This is an exact marginal precision action using a conditional pedigree factor. Selecting \(Q_{gg}\) alone gives a different quantity (Henderson, 1976; Legarra et al., 2014).
A single-step formulation may combine this action with marker products and additional pedigree terms. A reconstruction map must recover animal genetic values on the same scale and domain as the original animal-effect model. Moments of adjusted/blended relationships, innovation variances and covariance cross terms belong to that equivalence proof.
When eliminating a block of the coefficient system, the general identity is
\[
\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\B^\top&D\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}x\\z\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}f\\g\end{bmatrix}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(A-BD^{-1}B^\top)x=f-BD^{-1}g,
\]
followed by \(z=D^{-1}(g-B^\top x)\). This explains why a smaller system can still incur substantial repeated solve work. Fewer unknowns do not imply fewer floating-point operations or lower memory traffic.

title: Algorithmic reference: from a mixed model to accepted inference
text:
5 Direct and iterative coefficient solves
Sparse direct methods separate ordering/symbolic analysis, numerical factorization and triangular solves. A retained factor can serve multiple prediction, derivative or uncertainty right-hand sides (RHS). Covariance changes can preserve the symbolic pattern while invalidating the numerical factor (Chen et al., 2008).
For a symmetric positive definite (SPD) system and a fixed SPD preconditioner \(M\), preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) starts with \(r_0=b-Cx_0\), \(z_0=M^{-1}r_0\), \(p_0=z_0\). Its recurrence includes
\[
\alpha_k=\frac{r_k^\top z_k}{p_k^\top Cp_k},\quad
x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k,\quad
r_{k+1}=r_k-\alpha_kCp_k,
\]
\[
z_{k+1}=M^{-1}r_{k+1},\quad
\beta_k=\frac{r_{k+1}^\top z_{k+1}}{r_k^\top z_k},\quad
p_{k+1}=z_{k+1}+\beta_kp_k.
\]
The denominator and inner products assume the required definiteness. A changing or nonlinear preconditioner, indefinite target or inconsistent inner solve needs an algorithm whose assumptions cover that case; ordinary PCG’s guarantees do not transfer automatically (Saad, 2003).
Scaling also matters. If \(M=LL^\top\), the symmetric transformed system is \(L^{-1}CL^{-\top}v=L^{-1}b\), with \(x=L^{-\top}v\). This changes conditioning, not the target solution in exact arithmetic. A model ridge changes \(C\) itself.

title: Algorithmic reference: from a mixed model to accepted inference
text:
6 Residual reconstruction and refinement
Roundoff can make a recursively updated residual differ from \(b-C\hat x\). After reconstructing the original coefficients, recompute the original residual using the declared original operator. Report the precise absolute, relative or backward-error rule used for acceptance.
The identity \(x-\hat x=C^{-1}(b-C\hat x)\) explains why conditioning matters. A small residual is not a dimension-free guarantee on every coefficient or contrast. Conversely, comparing residual norms across differently scaled formulations without reconstructing the same target is not meaningful (Higham, 2002).
Iterative refinement solves a correction equation \(C\delta=r\) and updates \(\hat x\leftarrow\hat x+\delta\). Its effectiveness depends on residual calculation, solve precision and conditioning. Backend refinement steps, explicit correction solves and outer PCG iterations are separate counters. Refinement policy should be evaluated with the same final acceptance rule; reducing corrections is beneficial only if complete accepted work decreases.

title: Algorithmic reference: from a mixed model to accepted inference
text:
7 REML from retained algebra
Set \(P=V^{-1}-V^{-1}X(X^\top V^{-1}X)^{-1}X^\top V^{-1}\) and \(r_y=y-X\hat\beta-Z\hat u\). The minimized joint quadratic is
\[
y^\top Py=r_y^\top R^{-1}r_y+\hat u^\top K^{-1}\hat u.
\]
The determinant lemma and block elimination give
\[
|V|=|R||K||S_u|,\qquad
|C|=|S_u||X^\top V^{-1}X|.
\]
Therefore, for this fixed-rank positive-interior representation,
\[
\log|V|+\log|X^\top V^{-1}X|
=\log|R|+\log|K|+\log|C|.
\]
This provides an independent likelihood identity and shows why covariance normalization and determinant accounting are essential. A coefficient solution alone is insufficient to evaluate restricted maximum likelihood (REML) (Johnson and Thompson, 1995; Patterson and Thompson, 1971).
For \(V_i=\partial V/\partial\theta_i\) and fixed \(X\), differentiation gives \(\partial P/\partial\theta_i=-PV_iP\). Consequently,
\[
s_i=\tfrac12\{y^\top PV_iPy-\operatorname{tr}(PV_i)\},\quad
\mathcal I_{ij}=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(PV_iPV_j).
\]
When \(V\) is linear in the current covariance parameters, average information has the familiar form \(\mathcal A_{ij}=\tfrac12y^\top PV_iPV_jPy\). This reuses derivative actions and solves instead of finite-differencing a complete optimizer (Gilmour et al., 1995; Johnson and Thompson, 1995). Nonlinear parameterizations require consistent chain rules and the appropriate curvature treatment.
An optimizer also requires admissible trial covariances, a step policy, objective/score criteria and boundary handling. An accepted inner solve is not an accepted outer estimation result.

title: Algorithmic reference: from a mixed model to accepted inference
text:
8 Trace approximation and solve error
For probes with \(E(zz^\top)=I\), \(E(z^\top Bz)=\operatorname{tr}(B)\). The sample average is a trace estimator (Hutchinson, 1989). If \(B\) is implicit, each probe can require one or more coefficient solves. Count these RHS, not only the number of probes. Probability bounds established for symmetric positive semidefinite (PSD) matrices have specific assumptions (Avron and Toledo, 2011).
Finite probe error and solve error are different. Reusing probe banks can reduce noise in differences between nearby parameter evaluations, while creating correlated estimation errors. Precision assessment must respect that dependence. Fixed random seeds provide reproducibility, not proof of accuracy or unbiasedness with inexact solves.
Compare approximate scores with deterministic references on tractable problems; then assess optimization and reported uncertainty at representative scale. The Monte Carlo single-step REML literature illustrates the distinction between retaining a statistical target and approximating inverse-related work (Bermann et al., 2025).

title: Algorithmic reference: from a mixed model to accepted inference
section: 9 Target uncertainty without a full inverse
text:
9 Target uncertainty without a full inverse
Let \(L\) collect target coefficient vectors, so that \(L^\top x\) contains the requested fixed/random linear functions. Solve
\[
CU=L,\qquad \operatorname{MSE}(L^\top\hat x-L^\top x)=L^\top U.
\]
There is one RHS per target column before any valid batching or structural reduction. This includes fixed/random cross-covariances. Inverting only the random-only coefficient block generally does not give the complete-model prediction error covariance (Robinson, 1991).
Selected inverse methods can reuse factor structure to obtain particular entries, while selected solves obtain requested target systems directly. Neither observation means that arbitrary full inverse output is cheap. A randomized uncertainty estimator introduces a separate precision problem. All these plug-in calculations still condition on covariance parameters; additional covariance-estimation uncertainty is another inferential layer (Kackar and Harville, 1984).

title: Algorithmic reference: from a mixed model to accepted inference
section: 10 Bayesian computation is a different outer problem
text:
10 Bayesian computation is a different outer problem
With known covariances and a flat prior on identifiable fixed effects, the Gaussian posterior precision is \(C\). If \(C=LL^\top\), a posterior draw can be written \(x^{(s)}=\hat x+L^{-\top}z^{(s)}\) with \(z^{(s)}\sim N(0,I)\). This gives covariance \(C^{-1}\). Solving only for \(\hat x\) returns a posterior mean in this special case, not a draw or a general Bayesian analysis.
With unknown covariance parameters or mixture allocations, conditional coefficient updates form only part of a joint sampler. Hyperparameter, allocation and residual updates must target the same posterior. Integrating over those states can produce nonlinear prediction and additional uncertainty (Habier et al., 2011; Sorensen and Gianola, 2002).
Approximate Gaussian sampling, Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and variational optimization have different error mechanisms. A linear residual gate does not certify sampler mixing or the fidelity of a variational family. Their computational assessment must include the relevant posterior targets, Monte Carlo or optimization diagnostics, and comparison with tractable independent distributions.

title: Algorithmic reference: from a mixed model to accepted inference
text:
11 Algorithm description and acceptance record
An assessable algorithm description specifies its target equations, representation and reconstruction, admissible parameter domain, outer/inner iteration rules, stopping tests and approximation controls. It reports factorizations, operator applications, solve RHS, correction work and resource limits separately.
Its evidence should demonstrate invariance under equivalent formulations and permutations, derivative and likelihood agreement where applicable, and correct behavior when a requested acceptance criterion cannot be met. The qualification framework describes the distinct roles of algebraic, inferential and performance evidence.

title: Abbreviations and method names
text:
Advanced notes: contents
The chapters expand abbreviations in their prose. This glossary also supports readers entering through a table, heading or cross-link. Method and software names are identified separately where their names are not literal descriptions of an estimator. Symbols such as \(A\), \(G\), \(H\), \(K\) and \(R\) are defined in the mathematical context of each chapter.

title: Abbreviations and method names
text:
Notation conventions







Symbol
Convention




\(y\), \(X\), \(Z\)
Observed responses, fixed-effect design and random-effect incidence; observation selectors are applied consistently to all three.


\(\beta\), \(u\), \(a\)
Fixed coefficients, general random effects and additive genetic values.


\(K\), \(K_j\), \(K_a\)
Full random-effect or component covariances, including variance scales, in the general mixed model. Where \(K\) denotes a dimensionless relationship kernel in an extension, that local meaning is stated explicitly.


\(A\), \(G\), \(H\)
Pedigree, genomic and combined relationship matrices; their normalization and reference population must be declared.


\(\Sigma\)
Trait, factor or basis-coefficient covariance, identified by its subscript. Trait-major stacking uses \(\Sigma\otimes A\) (or the stated alternative relationship).


\(R\), \(V\)
Residual and marginal observed-response covariances; \(V=ZKZ^\top+R\).


\(P\)
Residual-forming precision \(V^{-1}-V^{-1}X(X^\top V^{-1}X)^{-1}X^\top V^{-1}\); it is not generally an ordinary Euclidean projection matrix. Parental contributions use \(P_{\rm ped}\).


\(C\), \(b\)
Mixed-model coefficient matrix and right-hand side when writing \(C\hat x=b\); decorated covariance symbols are defined locally.


\(W\), \(m\)
Centered marker dosages and marker effects; \(B_{\rm ann}\) is an annotation design. Kernel normalizers and marker-variance scales are stated separately.


\(\theta\), \(\mathcal D\)
Covariance parameters and analysis data. Additional representation or observation parameters are defined where introduced.


\(H\) in Chapter 10
Aggregate breeding merit, a scalar selection objective; distinct from the single-step relationship matrix.



Subscripts specify the effect, trait or domain. Local symbols such as a feature background set or a Cholesky factor are defined at use. Hats denote fitted or predicted quantities; a supplied covariance and its fitted estimate are not interchangeable. Unless stated otherwise, uncertainty formulas condition on the declared covariances.

title: 15. Large-scale phenomics: from measurements to genetic evaluation
text: Advanced notes: contents · Abbreviations

title: 15. Large-scale phenomics: from measurements to genetic evaluation
text:
1 Biological targets and recorded measurements
Large-scale phenomics combines repeated measurements, many correlated features and automated data acquisition. Cameras, activity sensors, milking robots, feeding stations and spectra can supply information about growth, behaviour, health and adaptation. The statistical problem starts with the biological target: a breeding value for feed efficiency, for example, is different from a prediction of the next recorded feeder visit.
Automated measurements already support animal-breeding research. Graham et al. (2024) studied feeding traits derived from automated milk feeders together with respiratory-disease treatments in calves. Bérat et al. (2025) estimated genetic parameters for behavioural indicators derived from robotic milking records using repeatability models. These are examples of constructing and analysing traits; they do not establish that every sensor feature is a useful selection target.
Distinguish the raw signal, the extracted feature, the modelled phenotype and the breeding objective. An image-derived weight, a daily growth slope and an animal’s additive genetic effect require different definitions and validation. Specify units, observation windows, aggregation rules and the population in which the target will be used. A software update that changes feature extraction can change the operational trait even when the column name stays the same.

title: 15. Large-scale phenomics: from measurements to genetic evaluation
section: 2 A measurement model before a genetic model
text:
2 A measurement model before a genetic model
A useful starting assumption for a continuous feature is
\[
x_{itk}=\mu_k(t)+a_{ik}(t)+p_{ik}(t)
       +d_{s(i,t),k}+\epsilon_{itk},
\]
where \(k\) indexes features, \(a\) is an additive genetic trajectory, \(p\) is a non-genetic animal trajectory, and \(d\) represents specified device, management or recording-batch effects. This is a modelling template, not a universal description of raw sensor data. Counts, proportions, events and censored times may require other observation distributions and links.
Device calibration and common management effects need an identifiable design. If each family is recorded with a different camera, a device effect cannot automatically be distinguished from a genetic effect. Connected reference measurements, overlapping devices and calibration animals can supply information that a more elaborate covariance model cannot create. The principles in components and identifiability apply to measurement systems as well as to conventional environmental effects.
Under the restricted classical-error model \(x=y^*+\delta\), with independent zero-mean error, measurement error increases phenotypic variance without adding genetic variance. That conclusion does not hold automatically for errors that depend on body shape, disease, farm or genotype. Analyse agreement with reference measurements across relevant subgroups, rather than assuming that a high overall correlation establishes unbiased measurement. Separate repeatability of the instrument from repeatability of the animal’s biological state.

title: 15. Large-scale phenomics: from measurements to genetic evaluation
text:
3 Dense and irregular longitudinal records
Many measurements of one animal are not many independent animals. A repeatability model gives records a shared genetic effect and a shared permanent environmental effect. Random regression allows their magnitudes and correlations to vary with age, lactation stage or time since a challenge (Meyer, 1998). For example,
\[
a_{ik}(t)=\boldsymbol\phi(t)^\top\boldsymbol\alpha_{ik},\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\alpha_i,\boldsymbol\alpha_j)
=K_{ij}\Sigma_\alpha,
\]
where the coefficient vector stacks the declared feature and basis-function order. \(K\) may be a pedigree, genomic or combined relationship matrix. This defines genetic covariance across times through the basis and \(\Sigma_\alpha\); residual serial correlation is a separate modelling choice.
Irregular timestamps, unequal recording intensity and long gaps make the residual model consequential. A correlation defined per unit of elapsed time differs from one defined by consecutive row number. Observation windows should also have biological meaning: resistance to a challenge, recovery rate and long-term resilience need not be the same trait. See multitrait and longitudinal models for covariance construction and variance-component inference for estimation. Dense recording improves some aspects of trajectory precision; it does not remove confounding between genetic and environmental trajectories.

3.1 A progression from records to joint genetic trajectories
Start with one calibrated feature and repeated records on each animal. A repeatability model estimates a persistent genetic effect, a persistent non-genetic effect and record-level variation. Replacing those constants by random regressions changes the target from a single level to a trajectory, and changes the unknown covariance parameters from scalar variances to covariances among basis coefficients (Meyer, 1998; Meyer, 2001).
For several derived features, a possible joint measurement model is
\[
x_i(t)=\mu(t)+\Lambda_g f_i^g(t)+\Lambda_p f_i^p(t)
       +d_{s(i,t)}+\epsilon_i(t),
\]
where \(f_i^g\) and \(f_i^p\) are lower-dimensional genetic and non-genetic trajectories, respectively. For example, specify
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\{f_i^g(t),f_j^g(s)\}=K_{ij}C_g(t,s),\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}\{f_i^p(t),f_j^p(s)\}=\delta_{ij}C_p(t,s).
\]
Here \(\delta_{ij}\) is one for the same animal and zero otherwise. \(C_g\) and \(C_p\) must be valid matrix-valued covariance functions across the declared times, not merely admissible matrices evaluated at isolated occasions. Conditional on the device effects and with independent genetic, persistent environmental and residual components, the feature covariance becomes
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\{x_i(t),x_j(s)\}
=K_{ij}\Lambda_g C_g(t,s)\Lambda_g^\top
+\delta_{ij}\Lambda_p C_p(t,s)\Lambda_p^\top
+\operatorname{Cov}\{\epsilon_i(t),\epsilon_j(s)\}.
\]
This separates genetic similarity across relatives, persistent within-animal variation and the remaining recording process. It is a proposed model template, not a claim that every raw image or event stream has a Gaussian likelihood. Loadings, trajectory covariances and measurement variances need constraints, information and estimation. Factor scales and rotations must be fixed by an explicit convention; unrestricted rescaling of both loadings and factor covariances would otherwise preserve the same observed model. Repeated records alone cannot separate the genetic and non-genetic terms if their observed covariance directions coincide.
The progression therefore changes inference as well as prediction. One may estimate a trajectory value, slope or weighted integral rather than just an animal intercept. For \(a_i(t)=\phi(t)^\top\alpha_i\), an integral target is
\[
T_i=\int w(t)a_i(t)\,dt=c^\top\alpha_i,\qquad
c=\int w(t)\phi(t)\,dt.
\]
Its known-covariance prediction-error variance (PEV) is \(c^\top C_{\alpha_i}c\), using the complete prediction-error covariance block \(C_{\alpha_i}\). Time to a threshold, maxima and other nonlinear targets require additional uncertainty calculations; their uncertainty is not generally one diagonal coefficient PEV.

title: 15. Large-scale phenomics: from measurements to genetic evaluation
section: 4 Many features: separate genetic and environmental dimensions
text:
4 Many features: separate genetic and environmental dimensions
With \(q\) features, an unrestricted covariance matrix has \(q(q+1)/2\) parameters. Estimating several such matrices quickly becomes an information problem as well as a computational problem. Factor structures can constrain genetic and environmental covariances separately, for example
\[
\Sigma_g=\Lambda_g\Lambda_g^\top+\Psi_g,\qquad
\Sigma_e=\Lambda_e\Lambda_e^\top+\Psi_e,
\]
with diagonal, nonnegative specific variances and suitable loading constraints. The number of factors, their identifiability and the stability of the resulting prediction targets require assessment (Thompson et al., 2003). Environmental structure must not be forced into genetic factors merely to reduce parameter count.
Phenotypic principal components describe total variation. Their leading directions need not capture the genetic variation most useful for the breeding objective. Melsen et al. (2025) develop a genetic latent-factor approach to high-dimensional secondary phenotypes, distinguishing genetic and residual covariance. Their application is in plant breeding: it provides relevant methodological evidence, not evidence of deployment in animal evaluation. It also does not imply that dimension reduction always improves prediction. Compare against simpler models using the same deployment scenario and training information.

4.1 Estimating a high-dimensional covariance rather than compressing a matrix
Compared with the unrestricted count above, a generic rank-\(r\) factor structure with diagonal specific variances has \(qr+q-r(r-1)/2\) free covariance parameters after accounting for rotations, under interior identification conditions. For \(q=100\) and \(r=5\), these counts are 5050 and 590. Rank restrictions save parameters by changing the model; they are not an exact replacement for every unrestricted covariance.
Joint likelihood or Bayesian estimation can learn loadings and covariance parameters with genetic relationships and the recording design included. Rank selection, constraints and regularization then belong to the fitted procedure. Conditioning predictions on estimated factor scores and treating those scores as exact observations omits uncertainty from that first stage. The factor-analytic likelihood framework is discussed by Thompson et al. (2003).
The 2025 genetic latent-factor approach of Melsen et al. (2025) is useful methodological evidence, but its covariance-learning pipeline exploits replicated plant data and design adjustment. Those assumptions should be distinguished from joint estimation in a related-animal population. Carrying a learned representation across species or recording designs requires checking the information that separates genetic from environmental covariance, not merely reusing the same factor algorithm.

More records of the same feature
Persistent effects, serial correlation and heterogeneous recording error
Within-animal repetition, elapsed time and connections among animals


More correlated features
Genetic and environmental covariance or factor loadings
Cross-feature observations and genetic relationships


Responses to environmental challenge
Genetic trajectory or reaction-norm covariance
Observed exposure, repeated responses and relatives across conditions


Learned or calibrated features
Measurement parameters and uncertainty in derived observations
Reference measurements, connected devices and independent calibration data



A staged analysis can remain appropriate when its sampling covariance and information overlap are handled explicitly. A joint analysis is attractive when stages share substantial uncertainty or informative recording, but it also requires a defensible joint likelihood. More elaborate estimation cannot recover distinctions absent from the design.

title: 15. Large-scale phenomics: from measurements to genetic evaluation
text:
5 How phenomics enters genomic prediction
The statistical role of additional measurements determines the model:







Role
Target and main question




Additional response traits
Can genetic correlations improve prediction of the breeding objective?


Repeated observations of a trajectory
Which genetic features of level, slope or recovery are to be predicted?


Measured predictors available at selection
Is the target conditional performance or an additive genetic value?


Features used to construct a similarity kernel
What covariance does that kernel represent, including shared environment?


Biological information used to specify marker priors
How is evidence mapped to variants, and is the prior independently assessed?



Individual-level phenomic measurements and variant-level functional annotations are different information sources. A sensor-derived similarity matrix is not automatically a genomic relationship matrix. Likewise, conditioning on a heritable downstream phenotype can change the meaning of the genetic effect being estimated. Define the joint model and target before comparing accuracy; see genomic models and genomic-feature priors.
A secondary trait available on selection candidates may legitimately improve prediction. The same analysis would overstate performance for a deployment where that measurement is unavailable. Validation must reproduce the intended availability pattern (Runcie and Cheng, 2019).

title: 15. Large-scale phenomics: from measurements to genetic evaluation
text:
6 Missingness and two-stage analysis
Sensor failure, missed visits, selective recording, treatment and removal can produce different missing-data mechanisms. An absent feeder record may indicate inactivity, equipment downtime or an animal no longer under observation. Converting every absence to zero changes the data model. Record exposure and reason codes where available, and assess whether dropout depends on latent health or performance. The assumptions in missing data and selection remain essential.
Two-stage analysis is often practical: first extract features or fit individual trajectories, then analyse estimated summaries genetically. Estimated summaries have uncertainty, potentially with unequal variances and correlations. Treating them as equally precise observations can distort weighting and uncertainty. Carry forward their sampling covariance where justified, or assess the consequences with a joint-model reference or simulation. Shrunken first-stage predictions also require care to avoid applying shrinkage twice.
Feature learning, scaling, imputation, selection of recording windows and tuning of factor dimension belong inside the training procedure when evaluating generalisation. A frozen externally trained measurement algorithm can be assessed as a distinct case, with its provenance and target-population validity recorded.

title: 15. Large-scale phenomics: from measurements to genetic evaluation
text:
7 Computation and reproducibility at scale
Report animals, independent families or management groups, records, features, time points and missingness patterns separately. Adding records expands data operations; adding genetic coefficients can expand the solve; adding covariance parameters expands estimation. These costs need different remedies. Sparse incidence operators, structured covariance, streamed feature access and factor reuse are discussed in large-scale computation and the algorithmic reference.
Retain a reproducible path from raw measurement to fitted phenotype: animal and device identifiers, timestamps and time zones, units, calibration records, software versions, quality flags and inclusion rules. Benchmark feature extraction, data preparation, covariance estimation, prediction and output separately, as well as end-to-end elapsed time and peak memory. Faster processing of a changed phenotype is not an equivalent-model speedup.

title: 15. Large-scale phenomics: from measurements to genetic evaluation
text:
8 Qualification for the intended use
Validation should test both measurement and genetic inference. Compare reference measurements across devices and biological subgroups; examine genetic and residual covariance stability; and assess prediction accuracy, bias and uncertainty in independent groups (Daetwyler et al., 2013). Split by animal when repeated records are present, and use farm, time, device or family holdouts when those represent deployment. Randomly splitting individual sensor records can place the same animal and recording conditions in training and validation.
For a new phenomics model, establish a small independent numerical reference, then assess parameter recovery and uncertainty under realistic recording and missingness patterns. Finally test transfer to the intended population and recording system. A small solver residual checks the fitted equations; it does not establish a valid measurement model or useful selection response. The model-checking chapter and qualification framework distinguish these claims.






Implementation in gsuite



Implemented building blocks include longitudinal random regression, multitrait prediction and estimation, standalone factor-analytic and measurement-error models, and development Bayesian factor models. These have distinct input, rank, inference and uncertainty limits. Raw-sensor extraction/calibration and the complete joint genetic/environmental trajectory-and-measurement template in this chapter are not established as one end-to-end gsuite workflow by those building blocks.


Next: drivers shaping the future of breeding.
